Abstract 
This  thesis  is  a  descriptive  grammar  of  Koromu  (sometimes  referred  to  as  Kesawai),  a 
language  spoken  in  southeast  Madang  Province,  Papua  New  Guinea.  Koromu  belongs  to 
the Rai  Coast  subgroup  of  the  Madang  branch  of  the  Trans  New  Guinea  family. 
Typologically,  the  most  interesting  features  of  Koromu  are  serial  verb  constructions,  clause 
chains  and  constituents  which  fianction  at the  level  of  both  grammar  and  information 
structure. 
The  initial  chapters  are  part  of  the  description  but  they  also  provide  a  background  to  the 
remainder  of  the  thesis.  Chapter  1  outlines  the  geographical  and  linguistic  settings,  social 
and territorial  organisation,  basic  ethnographic  information  and  some  of  the  recent  history 
of the  Koromu  speech  community's  interaction  with  other  language  groups.  It  also 
provides  a  brief  history  of  research  on  the  Koromu  language,  as  well  as  an  overview  of 
salient  features  of  the  language.  Chapter  2  introduces  the  phonological  inventory,  the 
syllable  and  stress  patterns  and  the  phonological  changes  which  affect  word  formation. 
Chapter  3  presents  basic  clause  stmctures  and  the  various  types  of  verbal  and  nonverbal 
clauses,  while  Chapter  4  provides  an  overview  of  the  morphosyntactic  and  semantic 
characteristics  of  the  major  verbal  and  nominal  word  classes  as  well  as  of  numerous  minor 
word  classes. 
Chapters  5  to 8  focus  particularly  on  nominal  constructions.  Chapter  5  describes  NP  types 
as well  as  functions  of NPs,  NP  listing  and  appositive  NPs.  Chapter  6  is  a  description  of 
possessive  nominal  constructions,  while  chapter  7  describes  postpositional  phrases  and 
chapter  8  discusses  spatial  frames  of  reference. 
Chapters  9,  10  and  11  are  primarily  concerned  with  verbal  constructions.  Chapter  9 
examines  the  morphology  of  independent  and  dependent  verbs.  Chapter  10  describes 
complex  verbal  predicates  in  serial  verb  constructions,  adjunct-verb  constructions  and  verb 
interation.  Experiencer  object  constructions  (in  impersonal  experiential  clauses)  are 
described  separately  in  chapter  11. 

[PDF PAGE 6]
The  final  chapters  are  concerned  with  clause  combining  and  the  interaction  of  grammar 
with  information  structure.  Chapter  12  describes  basic  clause  combining  with  relation  to 
clause  chains,  complement  clauses,  relative  clauses,  nominalised  clauses  with  pao, the 
adverbial  sei  'orientation'  clause  and  clauses  combined  with  adversative  and  disjunctive 
particles.  Chapter  13  examines  the  grammar  and  infoirnation  structure  of  NP  realisation, 
NP omission  and  subject  NP  prominence.  Finally,  chapter  14  is concerned  with  the 
grammar  and  information  structure  of  words,  phrases  and  clauses  in  the  ground 
(background  material)  in  links  (topic-like  elements)  and  tails. 
The  appendices  consist  of  a  list  of  source  texts,  three  sample  texts  with  morpheme  glosses 
and fi^ee translations,  and  a  basic  Koromu  to  English  wordlist  with  an  accompanying 
English  to  Koromu  finderiist.

Conventions  and  abbreviations 
Conventions  in  the  glosses 
• A  hyphen  (-)  indicates  a  morpheme  break 
• =  indicates  a  clitic 
• when  one  Koromu  word  requires  an  English  gloss  with  two  elements,  these  are 
separated  by  full  stops  as  in  mere 'move.up' 
• person  and  number  labels  are  not  separated  by  flillstops 
• underlining  (_)  indicates  vowel  altemation  or  vowel  elision 
• ...  indicates  that  there  are  preceding  or  following  clauses  which  are  not  included 
• a  verb  gloss  in  capitals  indicates  a  grammaticised  verb,  e.g.  here PUT 
When  words  have  more  than  one  meaning,  the  relevant  meaning  is  used  in  the  gloss.

Chapter  1  Introduction 
1.1 Aims 
This  thesis  describes  topics  in  the  grammar  of  Koromu,  a  Trans  New  Guinea  language 
spoken  in  southeast  Madang  Province,  Papua  New  Guinea.  The  introductory  chapter 
provides  background  material  on  the  geographical  setting  (§1.2),  the  linguistic  setting 
(§ 1.3), and  social  and  territorial  organization  (§  1.4) as well  as  an  ethnographic  sketch 
(§ 1.5), an  overview  of  past  and  present  interaction  with  other  language  groups  (§  1.6), a 
brief  history  of  research  on  Koromu  (including  fieldwork  for  this  study)'  (§  1.7), a 
description  of  the  sources  and  contents  of  texts  (§  1.8) and  an  outline  of  salient  features  of 
Koromu  grammar  (§  1.9). 
1.2 The  geographical  setting 
Koromu  is  spoken  by  600  to  700  people^  who  live  in  the  Usino-Bundi  District  in  the 
southeast  comer  of  Madang  Province  (see  Map  1.1).^  The  Koromu-speaking  villages  and 
settlements  are  located  north  and  south  of  the  Ramu  River  {Enae  in  Koromu)  which  flows 
' The  data  used  for  this  research  was  collected  during  various  periods  in  the  field  between  1975  and  the 
present  time  particularly  in  2004  during  fieldwork  for  tliis  thesis  (see  §1.1.7). 
^ In  the  2002  census  the  Kesawai  and  Ariheti  wards  which  comprise  the  Koromu  area  had  a  combined 
population  of  882.  There  are  a  large  number  of  immigrants  within  these  wards  so  it  is  difficult  to  specify  the 
number  of  Koromu  speakers  but  the  number  is  possibly  higher  than  600. 
^ Further  geographical  information  about  the  Usino-Bundi  District  and  the  Madang  Province  can  be  found  in 
Hanson  et  al.  (2001  :l89-203). 

[PDF PAGE 31]
2 Chapter  1 
from  southeast  to  northwest  at  about  170  metres  above  sea  level.  To  the  northeast  and 
southwest  of  the  flat  lowland  valley  are  the  steep  mountains  of  the  Finisterre  and  Bismarck 
Ranges.  The  Finisterre  Ranges  rise  to  1400  to  3300  metres  above  sea  level  to  the  northeast 
while  the  southern  part  of  Koromu  land  is  in  the  foothills  of  Mt.  Otto  (3540  metres)  and  Mt 
Helwig  (2739  metres).  To  the  west  Mt.  Wilhelm  rises  to  4509  metres. 
A number  of  rivers  and  streams  flow  out  of  the  mountains  and  across  several  kilometres  of 
fairly  flat  land  to  join  the  Ramu  River.  The  river  has  numerous,  strong  channels  which 
cover  a  wide  area  and  are  interspersed  with  low  gravel  islands.  It  is  challenging  to  cross  in 
the  dry  season  and  extremely  difficult  to  cross  in  the  wet  season.  Throughout  this  part  of 
the  Ramu  Valley  there  are  patches  of  kunai  grass/  kangaroo  grass,  forest  and  swamp. 
Kunai  grass  also  covers  the  steep  foothills  and  some  of  the  mountains  to  a  height  of  1000  to 
2000  metres.  The  higher  parts  of  the  mountains  are  forested  and  there  are  clumps  of  bush 
along  the  streams  and  rivers  which  flow  down  toward  the  Ramu. 
North  of  the  Ramu  the  settlements  of  Kesawai  1,  Monpea  and  Kesawai  2  are  near  the  Kohu, 
Monpea  and  Pakaia  tributaries  respectively.  South  of  the  Ramu  Waimeripa  is  near  the 
Ramu  River,  Autopa  is  a  little  to  the  west  near  the  Oija  River  and  Korike  is  fiiilher  west 
and downstream  of  Autopa  near  the  Marea  River.  Ariheti  is  almost  due  south  of 
Waimeripa,  Saweti  is  south  of  Autopa  and  the  small  settlements  ofWeisa  are  in  the 
foothills  along  the  Aimi  River  branch  ofthe  Marea  (see  Map  1.2).' 
The  road  between  Madang  and  the  Highlands  Highway  passes  through  the  settlements  of 
Kesawai  1  and Kesawai  2.  It  links  the  area  with  Walium  and  Madang  to  the  northwest  and 
the small  township  of  Ramu  Sugar  and  the  Highlands  highway  to  the  southeast. 
" Kunai  is  al.so  known  as  sword  grass,  laiang  or  Imperatci  cinimlimiceci. 
^ The  southern  river  names  are  on  the  Dunipu  8086  map  (1976).  On  this  map  the  Marea,  a  tributary  ofthe 
Ramu,  is  called  Oru-Rumaka  in  the  Koromu  area  but  the  name  Marea  is  used  by  Koromu  speakers.

Introduction 
1.3 The  linguistic  setting 
This  section  describes  linguistic  affiliations  (§1.3.1)  and  the  name  and  origins  of  the 
Koromu  language  (§  1.3.2). 
1.3.1 Linguistic  affiliations 
The  approximately  1200  languages  of  the  region  that  extends  from  Timor  and  Halmahera  in 
the west,  through  New  Guinea,  to  the  Solomons  in  the  east  are  usually  divided  into  the 
languages  belonging  to  the  Austronesian  family,  and  the  non-Austronesian  (Papuan) 
languages  (Foley  2000:358).  Pawley  estimates  that  there  are  700-800  Papuan  languages 
(2005:68)  and  Ross  that  there  are  perhaps  800  (2005:15).  On  the  basis  of  currently 
available  data  Papuan  languages  are  divided  into  20  families  and  about  a  dozen  isolates 
(Foley  2000;  Ross  2000,  2005).  The  largest  Papuan  language  family  is Trans  New  Guinea 
(TNG)  with  around  400  languages. 
Within  the  TNG  family  "the  largest  well-defined  branch"  is  the  Madang  group  with  about 
100 languages  in  the  linguistically  diverse  Madang  Province  (Pawley  2006:1).^ 
Z'graggen's  (1975,  1980)  tentative  subgrouping  of  Madang  languages  was  based  on 
lexicostatisfics  and  morphosyntactic  typology.  These  factors  are  often  affected  by 
borrowing  from  one  language  into  another  therefore  since  paradigms  of  pronouns  are  rarely 
borrowed  Ross  (2000:2)  has  proposed  a  preliminary  revision  of  the  Madang  subgroups 
based  on  shared  innovations  in  pronominal  morphemes.  Proto  Madang  itself  was 
"characterised  by  the  fact  that  it  has  replaced  the  Proto  TNG  first,  second  and  third  person 
singular  pronouns  *na,  *ijga  and  *ya  by  *ya,  *na  and  *mi  respecdvely"  (Ross  2005:36). 
Koromu  belongs  to  the  Rai  Coast  subgroup  (see  foldout  Map  1.3  at the  back  of  the  thesis). 
The  Rai  Coast  languages  are  spoken  in  the  coastal  lowlands  from  the  Gogol  River  in  the 
west  almost  as  far  as the  Mot  River  in  the  east.  There  are  also  Rai  Coast  languages  in  the 
steep-sided  valleys  of  the  Finisterre  Ranges  as  far  south  as  the  Ramu  River  and,  in  the  case 
^ Formerly  the  Madang  group,  including  Koromu,  was  referred  to  as  the  Madang-Adelbert  Range  sub-phylum 
(Z'graggen  1975,  1980). 

[PDF PAGE 37]
8 Chapter  1 
of Koromu,  Tauya  and  Biyom,  south  of  the  river  on  the  lower  slopes  of  the  Bismarck 
Range. 
In 1975  and  1980  Z'graggen  grouped  the  languages  of  Sinsauru,  Asas,  Sausi,  Kesawai 
(Koromu)  and  Dumpu  in  the  Evapia  language  family.^  However,  Ross's  sub-grouping  of 
the  Rai  Coast  languages  is  quite  different.  He  distinguishes  a  subgroup  of  19  languages 
labelled  Sub-Rai  "characterised  by  the  fact  that  most  of  its  members  have  lost  *///'  '2p'  but 
retained  *ta  '2p'  whereas  the  rest  of  the  Rai  Coast  group  has  done  the  opposite"  (Ross 
2000:17). 
Koromu  and  the  neighbouring  languages  of  Sausi  and  Dumpu  are  members  of  the  Sub-Rai 
group.  Sausi^  is  spoken  in  the  Ramu  Valley  northwest  of  Asas  from  Koromu  and  Dumpu  is 
spoken  along  the  valley  to  the  southeast  (Map  1.3).''  Tauya  and  Biyom  are  also  included  in 
the  Sub-Rai  group.  They  are  spoken  beyond  the  swamps  and  mountains  west  of  the 
Koromu  villages  of  Korike  and  Weisa.  The  Wasembo  language,  spoken  east  of  Dumpu  and 
the  Austronesian  language  of  Mari  is  included  in  the  Sub-Rai  group  in  Ross's  analysis 
(2000:7).  Koromu  is  the  only  Sub-Rai  language  spoken  on  both  sides  of  the  Ramu  River 
and  speakers  of  Koromu  are  widely  respected  for  their  ability  to  cross  the  many  channels  it 
forms  in  their  area.  Elsewhere  the  difficulty  of  crossing  the  river,  the  swamps  and/or  the 
steep  rocky  mountain  slopes  have  formed  natural  banners  preventing  frequent  interaction 
between  groups  of  people. 
Sinsaum  and  Asas  on  the  northern  borders  of  Koromu  are  Rai  Coast  but  not  Sub-Rai 
languages  (Ross  2000:13).  Sinsauru  is  spoken  in  villages  beyond  the  first  mountain  range 
to the  north  and  at  the  small  settlement  of  Sisari  in  the  foothills  above  Kesawai  where 
' Z'graggen  (1975,  1980)  based  some  of  his  language  family  names  on  rivers.  The  river  in  question  is 
probably  the  Monpea  or  the  Pakaia.  Both  tlow  across  Sinsauru  and  Koromu  land.  Evapia  is  probably  the 
Sinsauru  name  since  Sinsauru  has  a  bilabial  fricative  and  Koromu  does  not. 
^ Sausi  was  called  Witi  at  the  SIL  Alphabet  Development  Workshop  in  2000.  Speakers  gave  me  the  name 
Wiya  with  a  wordlist  I  collected  in  1  979.  In  terms  of  communication  as  well  as  comparison  of  word  lists  and 
a short  text,  Sausi  is  the  language  which  is  most  similar  to  Koromu. 
' The  Austronesian  language  of  Mari  is  spoken  immediately  to  the  southeast  of  the  Dumpu  language  area. 

[PDF PAGE 38]
Introduction  9 
children attending  the community  school at Kesawai 1  are cared for by a few adults. Asas 
is spoken at Asas village  about 5'/2 kilometres along the valley northwest of Kesawai 1.'" 
Beyond the steep uninhabited  slopes of Mt. Otto and Mt.  Helwig  south of Koromu there are 
languages of the Gorokan  branch of Trans New Guinea.  Speakers  of the Kainantu-Gorokan 
language of Isabi (Pawley  2006, Ross 2000:7) live in settlements part way up the steep 
slopes of Mt. Otto south and west ofWeisa."  From  Ariheti  it takes one very long day to 
climb  to the nearest Benabena village  of Samiri on the slopes between Mt.  Otto and Mt. 
Helwig.  It  takes another day to reach the main Benabena  villages beyond the mountain 
range. A  party traveling with women  and children would  take twice as long. The  Alekano 
(Gahuku)  villages  are two to three days climb  over the slopes of Mt. Otto by way of the 
Aimi  or Tauya Rivers. 
Apart from the Isabi speakers who have at some time moved over the mountain  range from 
the south the main linguistic  boundary  between the Madang  and the Gorokan languages 
corresponds with the vast tract of extremely steep land on the northern slopes of Mt. Otto 
and Mt.  Helwig. 
There are published grammars of only two languages of the Sub-Rai group, namely Tauya'^ 
(MacDonald  1990)  and Siroi (Wells  1979). There  is also an unpublished  grammar  sketch 
and a published paper on Erima  (Colbum  1980  and 1984 respectively). Siroi  and Erima  are 
both spoken on the coast. Tauya,  which  is spoken in the Upper Ramu  Valley,  has some 
constituents which  are similar in form and/or meaning to Koromu  dependent verb 
inflections  (see §9.4), some phasal and valency-changing verbs (see §10.2.4 to § 10.2.6) and 
ablaut rules (see §2.4.6). Anthropological  writings  on Sumau  (Garia)  include  Lawrence's 
study of cargo-cult (1965) and his ethnographic description (1984). There  are wordlists of 
Asas people  are  said  to  have  moved  out  of  the mountains  to  the  slopes  of  the Ramu  Valley  in  the  recent 
past. Asas  and  Sinsauru  people  say that they  speak the  same  language  but  with  some  differences.  They  call 
their language  Kou.  People  in  the villages  of  Auropa  and  Baipa  to their northeast  speak a  little  differently  but 
are also considered  to speak Kou. 
" Z'graggen  (1980:vi)  assigned  the  Isabi  language  to a Brahman  group  within  the Madang  stock. 
Tauya was  assigned  to  the  Brahman  group  by  Z'graggen  (1980).  It  has  been  reassigned  to  the  Rai  Coast 
group  by Pawley  (1996)  and  Ross  (2000).

1.3.2  The  name  and  origins  of  the  language 
In recent  years  Koromu  speakers  have  said  that  their  language  should  be  called  Koromu 
sakine 'Koromu  language',  hi  his  word  lists  Z'graggen  used  the  name  Kesawai  (1975, 
1980),  a name  used  by  outsiders  to  refer  to the  Koromu  area  north  of  the  Ramu  as  early  as 
1924 (Lane-Poole  1925:187,  26'^  Febmary).  The  name  Taga  used  m  Claasen  and 
McElhanon  (1970)  is  Tok  Pisin  for  the  mustard  chewed  with  betel  nut.'"^ 
It is  said  that  the  Koromu  language  originates  from  the  Koromu  area  around  Weisa  (Menato 
Epati  2000:T2.33)  which  was  referred  to  as  "Koromo"  during  Lane-Poole's  visit  in  1924 
(1925:  196,  April).  Menato  Epati  narrated  a  myth  about  the  origins  of  Koromu  which  is 
summarized  below.  This  myth  resembles  a  myth  told  in  a  number  of  other  areas,  for 
example.  Part  C  of  the  Namite  myth  in  the  Monumbo  language  of  north  coast  Madang 
Province  as  analysed  by  Z'graggen  (1987:745,  747). 
Long  ago  the  people  of  Kesawai  area  did  not  speak  Koromu.  One  day  they  went  to  a 
festival  on  the  south  side  of  the  Ramu  River.  On  the  way  they  were  offered  cooked  cassava 
by an  old  woman  who  had  mucus  on  her  hands.  They  refused  it  and  went  on  their  way.  A 
little  later  a  brother  and  sister  came  by  and  accepted  her  offer  in spite  of  the  mucus.  She 
warned  them  to  leave  the  festival  at  dawn  and  return  home.  They  did  this  and  after  they 
came  over  the  Ramu  the  old  woman  flooded  it  leaving  the  remainder  of  the  people  stranded 
on the  other  side.  As  a  result  there  are  many  Highlanders  and  Koromu  people  south  of  the 
Ramu  River  but  very  few  people  in  Kesawai  to  the  north  (Menato  Epati  2000:T2.33,  see 
Appendices). 
Well-documented  languages  in  other  Madang  subgroups  are:  Amele  (Roberts  1981,  1987,  1991,  2001), 
Kalam  (Lane  2007,  Pawley  1966,  1987,  1993,  2007,  Pawley  and  Bulmer  2003,  Pawley  et  al.  2000),  Kobon 
(Davies  1980,  1981,  1985),  Usan  (Reesink  1987)  and  Anamuxra  (Ingram:  in  press).  There  are  also  some 
anthropological  writings  about  Usino  (Conton  and  Eisler  1976,  Conton  1977). 
It appears  that  the  Kohu  people  did  not  chew  betel  nut  in  1924  since  Lane-Poole  reports  that  in  contrast  to 
all theother  people  he  met  they  had  "pearl-white  teeth"  (1925:191,  20  th March).

Introduction 11 
Reasons for the Kesawai people speaking Koromu  are given in Menato's  text on the lost 
Piri language recorded in 2004 (T5.4). After  the flood most Piri speakers were stranded 
south of the Ramu River  where they learned to speak Koromu.  To  the north a few Piri 
speakers remained. These  people were descended from the older and younger siblings who 
managed to cross the river and return to Kesawai before the great flood.  The  Piri speakers 
eventually learned Koromu  and the Piri language died out. 
1.4 Social  and  territorial  organisation 
Population density in Koromu territory is low and kinship networks are concentrated 
amongst small local groups. Patrilineal  kin groups form the basic units of society which 
inherit and work the land, contribute to bride wealth and perform life stage rituals like 
initiation and burial. In  spite of this patrilineal ideal there is considerable flexibility  and 
people can be incorporated into groups through matrilineal kin or adoption. For  example, 
at Otopa, the Kesawai 1  settlement east of the Kohu River, there are four households of 
patrilineal kin (see Map 1.2).'^ One  of these is affiliated to the group through a woman, 
two families have matrilineal land rights in the vicinity'^ and in one family the husband is 
an adopted highlander married to a Korike woman.The  patrilineal  group at Otopa own 
Sotoko land from the east bank of the Kohu River  to beyond the Monpea River. Menato 
Epati belonged to the group which lives near the Monpea. 
Gardening sites, wild game, the offspring of domesticated pigs and various responsibilities 
and obligations  are shaied among descent groups, assimilated members and neighbouring 
descent groups. The  giving of on/ 'insides'  or 'hospitality'  is one of the highest values in 
the community  and the exchange and fulfillment  of obligations is essential to survival. 
This is the patriiineage  to which  I  am affiliated. 
Several decades  ago  he  and  members  of  his patriiineage  moved  away  from  their  land  in  the  steep foothills 
of the Bismarck  Range.  This  was partly  because  a large number  of  deaths occurred  in  that area. 
His father  was an aid post  orderly  at Kesawai  1  for a period  of  time. 

[PDF PAGE 41]
12 Chapter  1 
Patrilineal  descent  groups  are  exogamous  but  marriages  are  common  between  people  in 
related,  neighbouring  groups.  Rights,  obligations  and  social  bonding  between  a  man,  a 
woman  and  their  families  include  a  'bride  price'  of  pigs,  (Finisterre)  pots,  shells  and 
money,  which  is  given  by  the  man's  family  to  the  bride's  mother,  brothers  and  other  kin.  In 
this  exchange  the  mother,  who  gave  birth  to,  cared  for  and  trained  the  girl,  receives  the  best 
meat.  Once  the  exchange  has  been  made,  and  the  gifts  of  food  have  been  eaten,  the  affinal 
kin  who  have  participated  refer  to  each  other  by  kinship  terms  rather  than  by  personal 
names.  There  are  distinct  consanguineal  and  affinal  kinship  terms  (see  Tables  4.7  to  4.10  in 
§4.3.3.2).  Many  kinship  terms  distinguish  people  of  different  ages,  for  example,  the 
consanguineal  terms  for  the  first  bom,  older  and  younger  siblings.  Some  of  these  tenns 
also  distinguish  same  sex  and  different  sex  siblings.  At  the  same  time  identical  tenns  can  be 
used  for  some  consanguineal  and  affinal  kin,  for  example,  ai-  'elder'  is  used  for  an  older 
same  sex  sibling  and  also  for  that  sibling's  husband  or  wife. 
Sister  exchange  was  a  particularly  common  marriage  practice  in  the  past.  In  sister 
exchange  a  man  and  woman  marry  and  at  a  later  date  one  of  the  man's  sisters  and  one  of 
her  brothers  also  marry.  Any  break  up  in  one  of  these  mairiages  results  in  the  end  of  the 
other  marriage  and  when  a  woman  leaves  a  man  she  has  to  leave  her  children  also. 
Traditionally,  people  lived  in  small  settlements  and  scattered  garden  homesteads. 
However,  under  the  Australian  government  they  were  encouraged  to  live  in  larger  villages 
at Kesawai  1  and  Kesawai  2'^  north  of  the  Ramu  River  and  at  Waimeripa,  Ariheti,'*'  and 
Korike  south  of  the  Ramu.  At  Weisa,  the  southernmost  village,  there  were  three 
settlements.  These  villages  had  populations  of  fi^om  50  to  120  people  and  consisted  of 
patrilineal  descent  groups  and  a  few  matrilineal  and  adopted  kin  living  on  or  near  their 
inherited  land.  There  were  also  some  scattered  garden  homesteads.  The  village  names  can 
also  be  used  to  refer  to  territories  in  which  they  are  located. 
Menato  Epati  believed  that  the  name  Kesawai  was  given  to  the  Koromu  area  north  of  the  Ramu  by  the  first 
German  visitors.  When  these  people  asked  about  the  name  of  the  area  the  respondents  thought  they  were 
talking  about  a  pig  or  dog  and  rephed  Kese-r-a  [rot-PRES-3s]  'It  is  rotten'  (2004:15.22).  Fortunately,  people 
do not  link  the  name  with  the  verb  nowadays  (Sirin  Kesapun:  personal  communication). 
" After  a  large  number  of  deaths  in  the  mid  1970s  the  village  site  at  Ariheti  was  abandoned  and  tlie  people 
relocated  to  Waimeripa  and  the  small  village  of  Saweti  upstream  of  Ariheti  on  the  Oija  River.

Introduction  13 
In recent years people  have returned to the more traditional  residential  pattern of  smaller 
settlements at different  sites within  these territories. For  example,  there are four 
settlements in the Kesawai  1  area near the Kohu  River  (see Map 1.2).  The  patrilineage 
associated with  Sotoko  land  lives on the eastern bank of the Kohu.  The  patrilineage  which 
has inherited  the Hupae  land  west of the Kohu  has subdivided  into  two settlements of five 
to six households.^''  There  is also a small settlement of  two households  with  matrilineal 
land rights  west of the Kohu.^' 
Since settlement  names  refer to the land on which  they are located the name associated with 
a particular  community  of  people can change  if people move  to another part of their land to 
be closer to gardens, to avoid  an area associated with  many  deaths or to break away from 
government  instituted  villages.  The  fact that building  materials  deteriorate fairly  rapidly 
and homes  need to be rebuilt every few years facilitates  these changes. Also  people 
sometimes  build  temporary  shelters near their gardens. These  shelters sometimes  become 
more permanent  and  last for more than one season. For  example,  in the late 1970s there 
was one household  near a garden at Autopa  but between the mid-1980s and 2000  Autopa 
became  a large village  where many  former  Waimeripa  residents lived alongside  incoming 
settlers from the Markham  (see § 1.6.3). Later  between 2000  and 2004 the Autopa  residents 
split into  three or four settlements located near the gardens of particular  kin groups.  In 
2004 only  one group of  four households  remained  at the Autopa  site. ^^

The members  of  the Koromu  speech community  are engaged in a subsistence economy 
based on agriculture.  Crops  are seasonal. For  several months  at the end of  the dry season

Garden  produce  is  supplemented  by  hunting,  fishing  and  bush  foraging.  Pig  husbandry, 
which  is  practised  on  a  small  scale,  is  mainly  for  ceremonial  purposes  such  as  bride  price, 
funeral  payments  and  so  on.  In  recent  years  one  man  has  begun  to  raise  pigs  for  sale  and 
for  exchange. 
The  annual  cycle  of  events  is  affected  by  the  wet  and  dry  seasons.  The  wet  season 
normally  begins  in  December  and  then  there  is  regular  heavy  rainfall  from  January  until 
early  May  or  June.  It  is  usually  very  dry  from  June  until  October  when  there  is  occasional, 
sometimes  heavy  rain.  The  main  garden  preparation  and  planting  begins  in  late  May  and 
early  June  and  planting  continues  into  the  early  wet  season  in  December  and  January. 
Early  in  the  dry  season  the  men  cut  down  trees  in  the  flatter  forested  areas^^  and  constmct 
strong  fences  to  enclose  the  gardens.  The  fences  incoiporate  pig  traps.  Larger  garden  trash 
is used  to  demarcate  family  plots  within  the  garden  and  other  trash  is  stacked  and  burnt  by 
the  women.  Rough  shelters  are  built  nearby  so  diat  people  can  sleep  near  their  work.  Such 
garden  sites  are  shared  by  an  extended  family  and  subdivided  into  plots  for  each  nuclear 
family.  A  nuclear  family  can  work  on  their  own  inherited  land  and/or  within  the  garden

'leaders'  traditionally  performed  rituals  to  protect  the  plants.  After  a couple  of  years  the 
garden  land  is  left  to fallow. 
In times  of  warfare  in the  past  gardens  were  made  close  to the  settlements,  often  on 
hillsides  in  the  foothills.  These  gardens  were  more  difficult  for  enemy  marauders  to  reach 
and they  also  provided  good  natural  vantage  points  which  enabled  people  to  see  strangers 
or enemies  approaching.  In  2004  many  of  the  Kesawai  gardens  were  in  the  foothills  close 
to the  settlements  because  there  had  been  violent  attacks  ft-om illegal  squatters.^^  When 
digging  hillside  gardens  teams  of  men  often  work  in  unison  with  long  digging-sticks. 
During  the  wet  season  women  weed  and  harvest  crops,  carry  produce  home  and  prepare 
and cook  food  while  the  men  do  some  hunting  or  fishing.  Trapping,  hunting  with  large 
spears  and  fishing  with  small  spears  are  common  activities  throughout  the  year  and  dogs 
are a useful  asset  for  hunting  trips.  During  the  very  hot,  dry,  windy  period  in  August  and 
September  hunting  parties  of  men and  women  set  the  grasslands  on  fire.  The  men  hunt  usu 
ihiri 'wild  pigs'  and  iiakiia  'small  game'  as  they  flee fi"om the  flames  while  women  and 
children  cut  and  carry  the  meat  home  to  cook  and  share  it out.  In  addition,  in  recent  years 
there  have  been  more  fish  in  the  Ramu  River.^^  In  the  dry  season  of  2004  groups  of  strong 
men and  women  fished  with  a  large  net  across  die  river  channels. 
The activities  of  the  working  day  are  expressed  by  many  different  verbs.  For  example, 
verbs  which  describe  various  paths  of  movement  such  as  erehe 'move  alongside';  the 
positioning  and  transport  of  things/children  on  different  parts  of  the body  such  as  sahoni 
'bundle  it  on head',  and  distinctive  ways  of  cutting  things  such  as  kesane 'scythe  -with  a 
short knife  (as  women  do)'  and  hoporo  'scythe  -with  a  long  knife  (as men  do)'. 
Illegal  squatters  destroyed  gardens  and  pigs  for  a  number  of  years.  Then  early  in  2004  they  killed  a  young 
man  near  a  garden  in  the  main  valley  (Norman  Papum  Menato  T5.23). 
An agricultural  officer  is  said  to  have  released  fish  tlirther  downstream.  Then  after  the  flooding  in  2003  the 
river silted  up  in  the  Brahman  area.  Since  these  two  events  there  have  been  more  fish  in  the  river.

16 Chapter  1 
Initiation  (of  boys)  and  marriages  occur  early  in  the  dry  season  when  it  is  easier  to  ford  the 
Ramu,  follow  the  rivers,  meet  in  the  open  air  and  find  food  for  large  groups  of  people. 
Other  rituals  and  ceremonies  mark  life  events  at  appropriate  times.  Examples  are  rituals 
following  births,  mother's  rejoining  the  community  after  a birth,  coming  of  age  (girls), 
illness,  healing,  death,  divination,  funeral  payments,  end-of-mouming  ceremonies, 
reconciliation  agreements  and  sangiima^  payments. 
Young  men  learned  the  'secret'  knowledge  of  mythology  and  ritual  through  several  stages 
of initiation  undergone  during  their  teenage  years.  The  ability  to  bring  the  power  of 
supematural  beings  into  secular  activities,  such  as  production  and  use  of  the  material 
culture  was  attributed  to  this  knowledge.  However,  when  the  Kesawai  communities 
decided  they  wanted  a  primary  school,  which  opened  in  1980,  they  also  decided  to 
discontinue  initiation. 
Traditionally  men  became  tamaite  arene  [men  big]  'leaders  or  big  men'  through  a 
combination  of  factors,  particularly  their  ability  to  use  and  control  ritual  knowledge.  In 
addition  their  oratorical,  arbitration,  curing  and  fighting  skills  and  their  ability  to  acquire 
and distribute  material  goods  were  and  are  important  in  acquiring  a  following. 
Illness  was  traditionally  associated  with  spirits,  sorcerers  and  a  person's  behaviour.  Spirits 
of root  ginger,  dead  animals,  trees  killed  by  humans,  ancestors  and  distinctive  places  could 
be offended.  For  example,  spirits  of  ginger  could  cause  a  man  to  be  ill  because  he  had  not 
been  hunting.  Alternatively,  illness  could  be  attributed  to  eating  food  that  had  not  had  a 
garden  ritual  performed  over  it,  was  designated  for  the  elderly  or  that  was  taboo  during  a 
period  ofmouming. 
Koromu  speakers  distinguish  three  types  ot'saiigitma  'sorcei-y'.  In  one  type  the  practitioner 
is believed  to  have  the  power  to  take  the  form  of  a  death  adder  or  other  creature  in  order  to 
attack  a  victim.  In  the  second  type  the  practitioner  is  said  to  wound  a  victim,  pack  the 
wound  with  dried  leaves  and  earth  and  cause  him  to  sicken  and  (usually)  die  several  days 
^^ Sungumu  is  a  Tok  Pisin  word  for  sorcery.  Sangitnui  payment  refers  to  the  practice  of  paying  sanguma 
practitioners  to  stop  causing  illness  and  death. 

[PDF PAGE 46]
Introduction  17 
later.  In  a  third  type  the  practitioner  is  said  to  breathe  on  a  victim  or  operate  magic  from  a 
distance.  The  intention  is  to  cause  illness  and  possibly  death  (Ian  Priestley  1979:4).  The 
first two  types  are  perfomied  with  the  intention  to  kill.  They  are  similar  to  sangiima 
'assauh  sorcery'  described  by  Click  (1972:1029)  and  Laycock  (1996:273-274).  The  third 
type  correlates  with  projective  sorcery  described  by  Click  (1972:1029)  and  exuvial  sorcery 
described  by  Laycock  (1996:271).  Practitioners  are  said  to  enlist  the  aid  of  spirits  to  work 
sorcery  from  a  distance  by  using  a  victim's  personal  leavings  (nail  clippings  etc.). 
Exuvial  sorcery  and  sangiima  were  greatly  feared.  Practitioners  had  the  skills  and 
responsibilities  of  other  tamaite  arene  'big  men'  (personal  observation)  and  were  also 
initiated  into  the  practice  of  sangiima  (Ian  Priestley  1979:  8).  Some  of  these  men  were 
hired  as  killers  by  people  from  other  language  groups  in  both  the  southern  Madang 
Province  and  neighbouring  Highlands  areas.  In  some  cases  ritual  murder  was  committed. 
This  was  a  physical  attack  involving  strangulation,  clubbing  and  the  breaking  of  each  limb 
of the  victim.  The  man  responsible  for  one  such  murder  in  1972  was  the  most  feared 
sangiima practitioner  in  Koromu.  He  spent  three  years  in  prison  in  Madang  (his  own 
account  and  Bob  Solberg  1975:pers.  com.).  In  the  last  year  of  his  life  he  gave  up  the 
practice  oisangiima  (Sirin  Kesapun  1990:pers.com.). 
To some  extent  the  reputation  for  sorcery  and  sangiima  was  a  deterrent  against  attack  by 
larger  neighbouring  groups  and  a  punishment  or  retaliation  for  wrongs  such  as  adultery. 
Therefore  it  is  possible  that  the  sorcery  threat  increased  after  the  implementation  of 
government  control  when  traditional  punishments  were  oudawed.  Before  that  time 
adulterers  for  example,  could  have  been  punished  by  the  wronged  husband  or  a  supportive 
leader  shooting  a  direct  shot  fi^om a bow  and  arrow  into  the  culprit's  thigh.  If  a second  such 
incident  occuired  the  punishment  was  death. 
The  strong  belief  in  the  actual  or  imagined  attacks  of  sangiima  and  sorcery  was  reinforced 
by the  frequent  occun'ence  of  severe  illnesses  and  death  from  malaria,  amoebic  dysentery, 
pneumonia,  and  other  tropical  and  infectious  conditions  (cf  also  Click  1972:1029-1030).

Although  there  is  still  some  fear  ofsarigiima in  the  Koroinu  area  many  Koromu  people 
have  seen  the  effectiveness  of  health  care,  medicine  and  prayer  in  times  when  they  have 
faced  major  life  threatening  situations.  As  Nonnan  Papum  Menato  said  thankfiilly  in  a 
report  in  2000  -  we  have  hope  and  we  don't  die  so  easily  anymore. 
1.6 Past  and  present  interaction  with  other  language  groups 
This  section  describes  interactions  between  members  ofthe  Koromu  speech  community 
and neighbouring  language  communities  (§1.6.1),  interactions  with  people  from  distant 
places  before  the  mid-1970s  (§  1.6.2)  and  developments  since  the  mid-1970s  (§1.6.3). 
1.6.1  Interaction  with  neighbouring  language  communities 
A tradhion  of  interaction  between  the  Koromu  speech  community  and  neighbouring 
language  groups  is  indicated  by  bilingualism,  intemiamage,  trade,  sungiima  fears, 
reconciliation  payments,  stories  and  so  on. 
In the  past  tamiate  areiie  'big  men'  and  some  others  learned  to  speak  the  closest 
neighbouring  language,^''  for  example,  Benabena  and  Alekano  to  the  south  and  Sausi, 
Sinsauru  (Kou),  Asas  (Kou)  or  Dumpu  in  the  north  (see  Map  1.3).  However,  since  1975 
fewer  people  speak  these  languages  because  there  is  more  communication  in  Tok  Pisin. 
In addition,  to  the  preferred  marriages  within  the  Koromu  area  mentioned  in  (§  1.4)  Koromu 
people  have  also  manned  Sausi,  Sinsauru,  Asas,  Dumpu,  Benabena  and  Alekano  (Gahuku) 
people,  and  more  recently,  incoming  settlers.  These  mamages  create  relationships  of 
mutual  help  and  obligation. 
Commodities  from  different  regions  have  been  exchanged  for  generations.  In  2000  on  the 
hillside  behind  Kesawai  1  Tomas  Awai  discovered  a  stone  axehead  made  of  tinggri,  a 
distinctive  light  coloured  homfels.  Axes  of  this  material  were  "made  in  the  Jimi  valley,  at 
or near  the  Ganz  River"  and  "probably  reached  the  Ramu  by  being  traded  down  the  Simbai 
This is  based  on  observation  and  information  from  speakers.

River"  through  Mareng  territoiy  (John  Burton  2000:pers.  com.,  see  Map  1.2).  Lane-Poole 
saw "dozens"  of  stone  axes  in  the  huts  at  the  Kohu  in  1924  (1925:  194,  April  2"'').  The 
Koromu  ai'ea  has  been  a  source  of  betel  nut  and  other  items  for  neighbouring  highlanders

In the  past  sangiima  killers  from  the  Ramu  valley  region  were  hired  to  kill  people  in  the 
Benabena,  Alekano  and  Chimbu  areas  while  sangiima killers  from  both  Koromu  and 
neighbouring  languages  to  the  north  and  northwest  affected  Koromu  people.  Some  deaths 
were  attributed  to  sorcery  and  others  to  assassination  by  physical  means.  Cessation 
payments  were  required  by  killers  and  their  kin,  who  walked  long  distances  to  collect 
payments  from  their  victims  (Priestley  C.  1979,  Priestley  I.  1979).  In  1986  Koromu,  Asas 
and Sausi  people  met  at  Kesawai  1  to bring  a  number  of  killers  to  justice  (personal 
observation). 
There  are  communication  routes  between  language  groups  along  the  Ramu  valley  and  into 
the  mountains  to  the  north  and  south.  Routes  from  Koromu  to  Sinsauru  follow  the  Pakaia 
River,  the  ridges  behind  Kesawai  1,  or the  river  valleys  behind  Asas  village.  These  routes 
ai'e most  commonly  travelled  by  Sinsauru  people.  To  reach  Benabena  and  Goroka  it  is  one 
or two  days  climb  from  Ariheti  up  the  Oija  River  via  Samiri  (Benabena)  to  the  North  Bena 
road  neai-  Megabo  or  along  a  more  direct  route  via  Matahausa  over  the  mountains  to 
Goroka.^'  There  are  also  routes  from  Weisa  up  the  Aimi  River  and  from  Korike  up  the 
Tauya  River  over  the  shoulder  of  Mt.  Otto  to  the  Zokozoi  River  and  down  to  Goroka. 
Nowadays  Weisa  people  sometimes  pay  to  travel  by  road  from  Kesawai  to  Goroka,  where

1.6.2 People  from  distant  places  before  the  mid-1970s 
Chinese  and  Indonesian  bird-of-paradise  hunters  began  operating  near  the  coast  in  the 
lower  Ramu  before  1851  (Swadling  1996:70)."  Between  1871  and  1883  the  Russian 
scientist  Mikloucho-Maclay  spent  three  years  at  Bongu  on  the  Rai  Coast  (Mikloucho-
Maclay  1975).  As  a  result  the  word  makarai,  from  Maclay,  was  presumably  adopted  into 
Bongu  (B27  in  Z'graggen  1980)  because  it  spread  inland  to  Koromu  where  it  is  used  to 
mean  'white  man'.  It  was  also  used  in  the  Benabena  and  Alekano  areas  in  the  1970s 
(Richard  Giddings:  pers.  com.). 
Then,  as  a  part  of  their  colonial  expansion  in  the  Pacific,  Gennany  annexed  Noilh-East 
New  Guinea  in  1884  and  administered  it  until  1914,  when  the  Australians  took  control. 
During  this  period,  German  political  control  extended  inland  only  a  few  kilometres  from 
the coast.  In  Koromu  tradition  (cf  §  1.3.2) the  first  white  men  to  visit  the  area  from  the 
coast  were  German  (Menato  Epati  2004:T5.22).  It  is  difficult  to pinpoint  exactly  when  this 
occurred,  but  German  expeditions  visited  the  middle  Ramu  valley  before  the  end  of  the  19'*' 
century.  Von  Beck  ([1903]:523,  530-538)  records  how  in  1896  a  botanist  called  Dr. 
Lauterbach  led  an  expedition  up  what  he  called  the  Num  (presumably  Nam)  River  from 
Astrolabe  Bay.  They  climbed  over  the  mountains  to  the  Ramu  River  and  then  went 
downstream.  Two  years  later,  in  1898,  Tappenbeck  led  an  expedition  by  steamboat  from 
the mouth  of  the  Ramu  and  established  a  station  140  kilometres  from  the  coast.  Lauterbach 
returned  to  this  station  in  October  1899  and  led  an  expedition  further  upstream  using 
canoes.  He  made  maps,  found  traces  of  alluvial  gold  and  set  up  a  gold  field  station  Most 
of the  information  about  these  Gennan  expeditions  is  confimied  in  German  New  Guinea: 
The Annual  Reports  (Sack  and  Clark  1978:  123,  146,  167)  where  it  is  stated  that  a 
navigable  waterway  extended  as  far  as 5"45'  S  lat.  and  146"E.  If  Lauterbach's  party 
reached  that  longtitude  they  must  have  travelled  through  Koromu  teiritoi-y  and  beyond. 
^^ There  is  perhaps  no  way  of  knowing  how  far  up  the  Ramu  River  they  went. 

[PDF PAGE 50]
Introduction  21 
Subsequently,  during  the  Gennan  administration,  several  gold-seeking  expeditions 
followed  the  land  route  to  the  Ramu.  These  expeditions  must  have  had  an  impact  on  the 
lives  of  people  who  lived  along  that  route  and  in  the  area  where  the  search  for  gold  was 
concentrated.  It  is  possible  that  one  of  them  is  described  in  Menato's  text  about  the  first 
Gei-man  visitors  to  Kesawai  (T5.22,  see  above).  Some  of  the  photos  which  accompany  von 
Beck's  account  support  this  view  (von  Beck  (1903):  537-543).  In  one  photo  a  man  and  his 
son bear  a  striking  resemblance  to  Menato  and  his  son  Norman  Papum  when  Nornian  was  a 
boy.  A  young  woman  in  another  photo  closely  resembles  women  in  another  family.  A 
third  photo  of  the  southem  mountains  must  have  been  taken  from  a  point  a  little  to  the  east 
of Kesawai  1.  Certainly  it  is  only  a  speculation  but  possibly  the  people  in  the  photos  are 
the  forebears  of  Koromu  speaking  people  living  today. 
The  diggers  were  initially  ruthless  with  the  local  people  and,  as  a  result  of  concern  about 
this  and  the  skirmishes  which  followed,  a  contract  established  in  1898  allowed  only  the 
Neu-Guinea  Compagnie"  to  exploit  the  land  (von  Beck  (1903):542).  Patrols  with  Chinese 
and locally  recruited  carriers  were  sent  to  explore  the  Upper  Ramu  in  1900  and  1901  (Firth 
1982:71),  a  prospector  called  Hans  Klink  patrolled  through  and  beyond  Koromu  land  in 
1901 (von  Beck  (1903):  523,  540)  and  a  land  track  was  built  via  the  Nuru  watershed  to  the 
Upper  Ramu  in  1901-02  (Sack  and  Clai'k  1978:234).  However,  after  all  this  the  gold 
project  failed  in  1902  (Firth  1982:163)  and  the  sudden  invasion  of  foreigners  ceased  for  a 
time. 
However,  the  Gemans  also  searched  for  gutta-percha  (wild  rubber)  and  caoutchouc  in  the 
Ramu  Valley  in  1908-09  (Sack  and  Clark  1978:294,  Firth  1982:163,  Lane-Poole 
1925:189).  In  1912  European  and  Melanesian  bird-of-paradise  hunters  visiting  the  Upper 
Ramu  Valley  clashed  with  the  people  whose  birds  they  took  (Firth  1982:99).  In  the 
following  year  the  Gennan  administration  sent  an  expedition  to  the  region  between  the 
Gogol  and  the  Upper  Ramu  looking  for  a site  for  an agricultural  experimental  station  (Sack 
and Clark  1980:80-81). 
" From  1885  to  1899  the  German  government  gave  tlie  Neu-Guinea  Compagnie  a  charter  to  administer  the 
protectorate  (Turner  2001  :xx).

22 Chapter  1 
After  war broke  out between  Gennany  and  Great  Britain  in  1914,  an Australian  military 
government  took  over administration  of  the German  protectorate.  Later  in 1921  Australia 
was granted a mandate  from the  League  of Nations  to administer  the territory of  New 
Guinea  under  a civilian  government. 
In the wet season of  1924 the British-bom  Australian  forester  and explorer  Lane-Poole 
searched for a way to cross the Ramu  River.  Between  26"^ February and 11  * April  he 
stayed four  times at the settlements at the Kohu  River  (Kesawai  1)  (Lane-Poole  1925:187-
199). He  managed  to cross the Ramu  River  and visit  Pakaia,  Waimeripa,  Korike,  Koromo 
(Weisa)  and Mt.  Otto.  He  heard that some  young  men  had  just been forced  to go away  to 
work on plantations  and met one old Korike  man  who  spoke  some  Tok Pisin  which  he  had 
acquired on a Bogadjim  plantation. 
From the end of 1933 until  sometime  in 1934  there was a Lutheran  helper's  station  at 
Waimeripa  (Wagner  and Reiner  1986:160).  Possibly  Lutheran  workers  had travelled 
through  at an earlier date, for example,  in 1920  from the north coast (Wagner  and  Reiner 
1986:132) or in 1926  from Garimari  (Man)  (Wagner  and Reiner  1986:61). 
Government  control,  administered  by  the Australians,  was spreading  into  the Ramu  Valley 
by 1933 (Wagner  and Reiner  1986:160).  The  aims of  full political  control  were  the 
outlawing  of  warfare and homicide,  the regrouping  of  people  in large villages,  the 
instituting  of  village  headmen  and  the imposition  of  a head tax (Lawrence  1984:22).  How 
much this  was realised in the Ramu  Valley  is open to question.  For  example,  in 1943 
Australian  forces  found  the country between  the Ramu  River  and Benabena  was  a vast 
"uncontrolled,  unexplored  and  unmapped"  area (Dexter  1961:241).  People  there had had 
some experience of plantation  ways  but had been infrequently  visited  (1961:46). 
During  the second world  war,  the first .lapanese soldiers  anived  at the Ramu  near  Kesawai 
in Januaiy  1943  (Dexter  1961:235).  Subsequently  small  groups  of  Australian  forces 
patrolled  the Benabena-Matahausa-Weisa  route  between Mt.  Otto  and Mt.  Helwig  into  the 
Ramu  Valley  to prevent Japanese  forces using  the route in the reverse direction  to go south 

[PDF PAGE 52]
Introduction  23 
to the Highlands  (1961 ^SS).^"^ The  Kesawai people fled from the fighting  that ensued to 
the rocky hills below Mt.  Helwig  only returning after the Japanese and Australian  forces 
had gone (Arikao  Tomas 2004: T5.3, T5.5). Tragedy  affected Koromu  people in early 
skinnishes  near Weisa (1961:261)  and Kesawai  changed hands several times before the 
final battle  at Kesawai 1  and the Japanese retreat in December  (1961:704). 
The traumatic events of the war combined with traditional  beliefs in the special power 
associated with  the acquisition and construction of manufactured items created an 
environment  in which cargo cult propaganda from the north was accepted after the war. 
Even in the late 1960s/early 1970s there was an active cult at Kesawai 1  and cargo 
predictions remained in circulation after that. 
After the war a government officer  encouraged Kesawai  1  people  to live in one village near 
the Kohu  River  (Arikao  Tomas pers.com. 1978). Visits by government officers were 
infrequent but they increased when an airstrip was built at Usino in the 1960s and after a 
patrol post was built there in 1965 (Lawrence 1984:26). In  1975 there was still a house at 
Kesawai 1  for the government officer to use. Prior  to 1975 some Koromu  men had worked 
outside the area for periods of time. For  example, Sirin Kesapun  worked in Rabaul,  New 
Britain when he was a young man in the late 1960s or eariy 1970s but by 1975 only one 
Kesawai man was working  outside the area. 
1.6.3 Developments  since the mid-1970s 
Since the mid-1970s there have been major changes in the social and linguistic  situafion in 
the Koromu  area. This  coincides with the period of my observation and participation  in the 
life of Koromu. 
By 1975 the government officer had encouraged people to live in centralised villages at 
Kesawai 1  and 2, Waimeripa,  Korike,  Ariheti and Saweti (see Map 1.2). However,  some 
people still lived in a few smaller settlements at Weisa and scattered throughout the

language  area.  A  very  rough  dry  season  track  (consisting  of  two  wheel  ruts  and  no  bridges) 
led from  the  end  of  the  road  at  Dumpu  into  the  Kesawai,  Sausi,  Usino  area  (see  Map  1.1) 
but the  Koromu  people  had  no  medical  facilities,  schools,  churches,  cash  crops,  tradestores 
and so  on.  There  were  serious  health  and  social  problems  in  the  Koromu  area.  The 
mortality  rate  was  high  and  fear  of sanguma deaths  was  particularly  strong  (cf  §1.5.1). 
Malaria,  pneumonia,  yaws,  dysentery,  ulcers,  leprosy  and  child  malnutrition  were  common. 
In the  mid  1970s  the  govemment  financed  a  gravel  road  linking  Madang,  Usino,  and  the 
Lae-Highlands  highway  (see  Map  1  1). Major  work  on  this  was  undertaken  in  the  dry 
season  of  1975  and  subsequent  years.  Also  the  Ramu  Hydroelectric  Scheme  was  engaged 
in setting  up  power  lines  to  Madang  along  the  same  route  and  the  govemment  bought  land 
from  Kesawai,^^  Asas  and  Sausi  people  and  leased  it  to  applicants  from  more  densely

at the  end  of  the  thesis).  Loans  of  cattle  and  fencing  were  made  to  the  settlers  and  the  local 
landowners.  Provincial  Health  Officers  were  aware  of  the  lack  of  medical  facilities  and  the 
nature  of  health  problems  on  the  highlands  fringe  so  in  1975  when  we  went  to  live  at 
Kesawai  1  my mother  and  I  were  authorised  to  provide  health  care  at  Kesawai  1. 
When  the  gravel  road  was  completed  in  1977-78  the  Usino  airstrip  was  closed  and  the 
patrol  post  moved  to  Walium.  As  the  road  improved  in  1975  the  govemment  officer's 
house  at  Kesawai  1  fell into  disrepair  and  officers  made  one  day  visits  only,  in  the  late 
1970s the  ambitious  cattle  projects  began  to  fail  because  adequate  business  training  and 
transport  to  markets  were  not  provided.  Also  the  Koromu  people  and  settlers  began  to 
petition  the  provincial  govemment  for  a school.  Once  the  community  primary  school 
opened  at  Kesawai  1  in January  1980  the  Kesawai  leaders  decided  that  they  would  no 
longer  hold  initiation  ceremonies  for  young  men  and  boys.  The  May-June  initiations  of 
that year  were  the  last  ones  they  conducted.  It  was  also  in  1980  that  the  Ramu  Sugar 
Company  began  to  build  in  the  Gusap  area  near  the  watershed  between  the  Markham  and 
Ramu  Rivers.  There  is  now  a  small  township  at  Ramu  Sugar. 
Kesawai  refers  to  Kesawai  1  (near  the  Kohu  River)  and  Kesawai  2  (near  the  Pakaia  River).  Kesawai  1  is 
also  known  as  Kohuweti.  However,  Kesawai  1  is  the  name  used  by  people  from  other  areas.

The number  of languages spoken in Koromu,  Asas and Sausi territory have increased 
because of the many settlers who anived  in the mid-1970s (see above), the school teachers 
and aid post orderly who came from 1980 onwards, the Sepik people who acquired land 
leases since the eai'ly 1990s and the few Kainantu  and Chimbu  people  who have remained 
living  neai- an abandoned  timber  project in the hills above Kesawai 1.  Also  since 1990 
there has been a small Bible  training school at Kesawai 1. Some  of the men and women 
who attend are fi'om other parts of mral Papua  New Guinea  so Tok Pisin and English  are 
the languages of instraction. In  addition,  for 17 years until 2004 a group of squatters from 
the Markham  lived illegally  on Kesawai 2 land.^^ In  2004 as a result of all these incoming 
settlers as well as intennaniages  with people from neighbouring  groups there were people 
fi'om about twenty different languages living  on what was formerly Koromu  land (see Map 
1.4 for the main groups). 
Koromu  speakers still outnumber  incoming  migrants. The  settlers who came in small 
groups fi-om the Markham,  the Chimbu,  Goroka  and the Sepik speak their own languages at 
home in their settlements. Individuals  or nuclear family  groups who have settled in the area 
tend to speak Tok Pisin and perhaps a few words of Koromu.  The  lingua franca in this 
multilingual  society is Tok Pisin. At  school Tok Pisin and English  are used and in the 
church at Kesawai 1  Tok Pisin is the main language. Some  settlers and Koromu  people 
have intennamed  and  their young children and others living  near the school at Kesawai 1 
appear to be speaking Tok Pisin as their first language,  although Koromu  children  learn 
specific vocabulaiy,  such as the names of plants and animals,  in Koromu.  Some  Koromu 
children from south of the river live at Kesawai 1  during the school week and are also being 
affected by the use of Tok Pisin in that ai'ea. However,  a number of the Markham  settlers 
(Adzera speakers) have been living  south of the Ramu River  in the Autopa area since the 
late 1980s and some of their children and young adults speak Koromu,  Adzera and Tok 
Pisin (and in some cases English). 
In spite of these massive social changes the Koromu communities  are impressive for their 
resilience and stability,  incoiporation  of  newcomers and the commitment  of  younger people 
to their home area. In  addition,  people have rettimed to living  in smaller scattered

settlements  as  they  were  before  government  officers  did  patrols  on  foot.  By  2004  Sairam

Although  Tok  Pisin  is  used  increasingly  by  the  children  it  is  striking  that  there  is  less  Tok

1.7 A  brief  history  of  research  on  Koromu  including  fieldwork  for  this  study 
This  section  provides  an  overview  of  eariy  published  references  to  Koromu,  my  father's 
early  data  collection,  my  family's  and  my  own  involvement  in  the  Koromu  area  since  1975 
and my  research  on  the  Koromu  language  and  in  linguistics.  The  data  is  archived  in  my

Lane-Poole  commented  that  the  Kesawai  people  he  met  north  of  the  Ramu  spoke  the  same 
language  as  the  people  on  the  south  side  of  the  Ramu  River  (1925:187,  February  1924). 
In their  sui-vey  of  languages  of  the  Finisteire  Range  Claassen  and  McElhanon  (1970:59-60) 
give  veiy  little  infonnation  on  Rai  Coast  languages  spoken  in  the  Ramu  Valley  but  the 
language  they  refer  to as  Taga  is  probably  Koromu  and  they  comment  that  "its  full 
geographic  extent  and  number  of  speakers  is  not  known"  (1970:60).^'^ 
Z'graggen's  (1975)  compai'ative  wordlists  of  Rai  Coast  languages  include  the  first 
published  wordlists  for  Koromu.  Z'graggen  records  300  words  and  some  structural 
elements  and  refers  to  Koromu  as  Kesawai  (B4),  locating  it  correctly  on  both  sides  of  the 
Ramu  River.  Z'graggen  (1980)  provides  no  llnlher  linguistic  data  but  lists  the  villages 
where  Kesawai  (Namuya)"^*^* was spoken  as  Alivetti,  (Kasanum),  Kesawai  1,  Kesawai  2, 
Korigei,  Waimeriba  and  Weissa.  The  total  population  was  given  as  538. 
The  Priestley  family's  involvement  in  Koromu  research  began  in  1975  when  my  father  first 
collected  some  wordlists  and  my  brother  and  I  began  to  collect  data  and  leam  to  speak  the 
language.  As  time  passed  the  linguistic  research  became  largely  my  responsibility. 
However,  my  parents  had  some  linguistic  and  cross-cultural  training  before  they  went  as 
missionaiies  to  Papua  New  Guinea  in  1967  and  they  hoped  to  work  in  a  language  (other 
than  Tok  Pisin).  Initially  they  taught  school  and  worked  in  village  churches  and 
communities  in  the  Yagaiia  and  then  the  Alekano  (Gahuku)  and  Benabena  areas  where  my 
brother,  sister  and  I  grew  up.  During  that  time  my  father  realised  that  there  was  very  little 
linguistic  work  being  done  north  of  the  Benabena  and  he  began  trying  to  find  out  more 
about  the  languages  in  that  area  and  the  people  who  spoke  them.  He  first  heard  about  the 
Koromu  people  fi'om  villagers  in  Megabo  and  Matahausa  in  the  North  Bena  who  told  him 
''  Kaikovu  is  mentioned  in  the  same  locality.  It  probably  refers  to  Kou  (Sinsauru)  since  Kou  people  have 
sometimes  lived  on  the  Ramu  Valley  slopes  along  tlie  Monpea  River  (personal  observation).  "Vocabularies 
for  the  Taga,  Gurumbu  and  Kaikovu  languages  were  collected  by  S.I.L.  members  D.  Trefry  and  D.  Oatridge 
dunng  1964  -1965"  (Claassen  and  McElhanon  1970:74). 
^ Z'graggen  gives  namiiya  as  an  alternative  name.  Namii  means  'namesake',  namuya  is  the  address  form  of 
'namesake'  and  nanntka  means  'one  who  speaks  the  same,  friend'.

1.8 Sources  and  content  of  texts 
The  texts  in  the  corpus  were  spoken  by  a  number  of  different  people  on  a  variety  of  topics. 
From  1978  to  1980  texts  were  recorded  with  26  different  speakers.  21  were  recorded  with

four  from  Kesawai  2  residents.  In  2004  14  people  recorded  texts.  45  texts  were  recorded 
by Kesawai  I  residents  and  five  long  texts  were  recorded  by  Kesawai  2  residents.'*^ Men 
recorded  33,  7  and  38  texts  and  women  recorded  eight,  three  and  twelve  texts  in  die  1978-
1980, 2000  and  2004  audio  collections  respectively.'^'^ 
Overall  the  transcribed  texts  are  narratives  about  recent  events,  personal  histories,  stories 
about  our  shared  past,  procedural  accounts  (for  example  about  gardening,  hunting  and  child 
care),  origin  myths,  animal  origin  myths,  family  histories  and  ideas  about  language

1.9 Salient  features  of  Koroniu  grammar 
This  section  outlines  some  of  the  salient  features  of  Koromu  grammar.  Typologically  some 
of the  most  interesting  features  of the  language  are  serial  verb  constmctions  (§  10.2), clause 
chaining  (§9.2  and  §9.4),  background  material  and  topic-like  elements  (links)  which  occur 
with the  particle  no  'ground'  (chapter  14),  and  the  prominent  subject  encHtic  =te  (§  13.5). 
Syllables  have  the  shapes  (C)V(V)  and  (C)V(V)C  (§2.3.1).  There  are  five  vowels  and  10 
consonants  including  voiceless  stops,  fricatives,  nasals,  a  tap  and  two  approximants  (§2.2). 
Verbal  clauses  are  verb  final  (§3.3.1)  and  in  transitive  clauses  the  preferred  order  is  AOV 
(§3.3.4.2)  but  OAV  (§  14.3.2.2  and  §  14.4.2) and  OVA  (§14.5)  can  occur  in  certain  contexts. 
Epistemic  modality  particles  are  optional  clause  finally  (§3.2.2). 
Common  nouns  form  an  open  class  (§4.3.2).  They  can  be  followed  by  an  adjective,  a 
quantifier  and/or  an  indefinite  specific  article  or  by  post-head  nominals,  adjective  phrases, 
or relative  clauses  (§5.2.3).  Demonstratives  and  pre-head  nominals  occur  before  the  noun 
(§5.2.2).  Closed  classes  of  nouns  include  kinship  nouns  which  have  obligatoiy  possessor 
suffixes  indicating  person  and  number,  or  vocative-type  enclitics  (§4.3.3.2  and  §6.5.3.3). 
Possessor  enclitics  are  optional  with  common  nouns  (§  6.5.3.2). 
Verb  roots  form  an  open  class  (§4.2).  Verbal  inflections  contrast  subject  and  object 
(§3.3.2.2  and  §9.3.2).  Independent  final  verbs  have  portmanteau  tense,  subject  and  mood 
suffixes  as well  as  optional  aspect  and  object  agreement  suffixes  (§9.3).  Dependent  verbs 
in non-final  clauses  have  dependency  suffixes  which  indicate  whether  the  subsequent  verb 
has the  same  or  a different  subject,  the  same,  overlapping  or  sequential  temporal  reference, 
and realis  or  irrealis  status.  Sequences  of  events  can  be  represented  by  clause  chains  of 
dependent  verbs  (§9.4). 

[PDF PAGE 62]
Introduction  33 
One  or  more  bare  verb  roots  and  a  final  verb  can  form  a  serial  verb  construction  which 
expresses  closely  connected  events  (§10.2.8,  §  10.2.9)  or  an  event  marked  for  aspect  or 
valency  changes  (§10.2.4  to  §10.2.7).  Impersonal  experiencer  object  constructions  describe 
involuntaiy  physical  and  psychological  conditions  or  sensations  with  the  experiencer 
indicated  by  the  direct  object.  They  are  syntactically  marked  for  a third  person  singular 
subject  but  no  clear  subject  referent  is  indicated  (chapter  11). 
Minor  word  classes  include  adverbs  (§4.7),  qualifiers  (§4.4),  demonstratives  (§4.14.1)  and 
postpositions  (§4.8).  Pronouns  distinguish  singulai"  and  plural  and  also  have  a  genitive 
fonn  (§4.5)  while  adpositions  follow  a  noun  phrase  or  head  noun  (chapter  7). 
Grammar  and  infomiation  structure  can  be  indicated  by  word  order,  NP  omission  and  the 
prominent  subject  enclitic  =te  (chapter  13).  Background  information  is  expressed  by 
constinaents  in  the  left-most  and  right-most  positions  of  the  clause,  or  in  some  cases 
between  other  clausal  constituents  (chapter  14).  Topic-like  elements  (links)  are  expressed 
by constituents  that  are  located  to  the  left  of  the  main  clause.  They  can  be  followed  by  the 
particle  no  'ground'  and  a  pause  (§14.3),  or  by  an  anaphoric  pronoun  in  the  main  clause 
(§ 14.4).  Some  subordinate  clauses  are  left  dislocations  with  no  'ground'  (§14.3.3).  Head-
tail linkage  at  paragraph-like  boundaries  is  expressed  by  partial  or  complete  repetition  of 
the final  clause  of  the  previous  sentence  (§14.4.3).

Chapter  2  Phonology  and  Morphophonology 
2,1 Introduction 
This  chapter  describes  the  basic  features  of  the  phonology  and  morphophonology  of 
Koromu  in  sections  which  outline  the  phonological  inventory  (§2.2),  phonotactics  (§2.3), 
phonological  changes  in  word  formation  (§2.4),  phonetic  variations  in  rapid  speech  (§2.5) 
and a  summary  of  phonological  changes  and  phonetic  variations  (§2.6).' 
2.2 Phonological  inventory 
Consonants  include  voiceless  stops,  fricatives,  nasals,  a  liquid/tap  and  two  approximants. 
Table  2.1  Consonants Bilabial Alveolar Palatal Velar Glottal 
Stops P t k 
Fricatives s h 
Nasals m n 
Tap r 
Approximants w y 
The  vowels  occur  in  front,  central  and  back  as  well  as  high,  mid  and  low  positions. 
' The  phonological  and  morphophonological  rules  were  originally  described  in  detail  in  my  MA  sub-thesis 
(2002).  Here  the  rules  have  been  revised,  details  have  been  added  and  the  order  of  presentation  is  different.

2.3 Phonotactics 
This  section  describes  syllable  (§2.3.1)  and  stress  (§2.3.2)  patterns. 
2.3.1  Syllable  patterns 
The  open  syllable  patterns  CV,  V,  CVV,  and  VV  have  a  wide  distribution.  The  closed 
syllable  patterns  CVC,  VC,  and  CVVC  can  also  occur. 
CV syllables  occur  initially,  medially  or  finally,  as  in  kani 'fishtrap',  esame 'dog'  and  epo 
'stone'.  All  consonants  can  occur  in  the  syllable  onset  of  CV  syllables.  But  the  liquid  /r/ 
only  occurs  in  initial  position  in  the  enchtic  =rure  'and/with'  (cf  §4.11  and  §5.12.3.1)  and 
in the  reduced  forms  of  the  phasal  verb  siiretre START  (see  §4.2.9  and  §  10.2.4.2)  and 
phasal  and  valency-changing  here/re  PUT  (see  §4.2.10  and  §10.2.5)  which  occur  in 
complex  predicates.  For  example: 
(2.1) ...ne  re  pente... 
eat PUT-  LTD:3p 
'...they  ate  it  up...'Tl.14.19

2.3.2 Stress  patterns 
Stress  is  indicated  by  changes  in  pitch,  duration  and  intensity.  Pitch  rises  between  an 
unstressed  syllable  and  a  subsequent  stressed  syllable  and  then  falls  to a  subsequent  final, 
unstressed  syllable.  Duration  of  the  vowel  nucleus  is  slightly  greater  in  open  stressed 
syllables. 
The main  stress  is  on the  penultimate  syllable  where  it  provides  a  demarcative  function. 
"Alternating  stress"  (as  in Hyman  1975:210)  occurs  on  every  other  even-numbered  syllable 
starting  from  the  syllable  with  penultimate  stress  and  moving  towards  the  beginning  of  the 
word.  When  there  are  more  than  two  stressed  syllables  the  penultimate  syllable  has  the 
main stress  and  the  first  stressed  syllable  is  slightly  more  prominent  than  the  other  (non-
penultimate)  stressed  syllables  in  the  word.  The  position  of  stress  varies  with  the  number 
of suffixes  and/or  enclitics  in  the  word.  Compare  the  following  examples: 
(2.2) ...sdsi  -neka  -ia. 
tell -03p  -Ip 
'...we  told  them.'T  1.7.23 
(2.3)  Sasi  -neka  -id  -te... 
tell -03p  -Ip  -DR 
'We  told  them  and  then...'  T1.7.24 
Syntactically,  suffixes  are attached  to  a  base  morpheme  of  a limited  part  of  speech  (for 
example,  in  the  verbs  above).  In  contrast,  enclitics  are  attached  to  a whole  phrase  or  clause 
(see below).  Phonologically,  an  enclitic  forms  a word  with  a  phrase  or  clause  final  host,  or 
the only  word  in  the  phrase  or  clause.  Monosyllabic  enclitics  are  unstressed  but  when  there 
are two  syllables  the  penultimate  syllable  is  stressed,  as  in the  example  below  (For  details 
of the  possessive  construction,  see  §6.6.1). 
(2.4)  Nhie  keti  pdo  sukhie  =ndpa. 
3p mountain  IGEN  word  =P3p 
'They  are  mountain  (people)'s  words.'  T7.4.15 

[PDF PAGE 70]
Phonology  and  Morphophonology  41 
2.4 Phonological  changes  in  word  formation 
2.4.1  Introduction 
The  formation  of  Koromu  words  and  complex  predicates  (see  chapter  10)  can involve 
phonological  change  at  morpheme  or  word  boundaries.'^  The  most  common  types  of 
change  are  stem  final  vowel  elision  and  regressive  and  progressive  vowel  harmony.  There 
is also  one  initial  vowel  elision  rule,  several  examples  of  final  vowels  being  assimilated  to 
subsequent  vowels  and  one  glide  insertion  rule.  Rules  of  phonological  change  are 
phonological  (§2.4.2),  morphophonemic  (§2.4.3)  or  lexically  conditioned  (§2.4.4).  In 
addition,  there  are  several  ablaut  rules  (§2.4.5). 
2.4.2  Phonological  rules 
The  rules  which  occur  in  purely  phonological  environments  are  vowel  elision  rules 
(§2.4.2.1),  vowel  harmony  rules  (§2.4.2.2)  and  a  rule  of  consonant  assimilation  (§2.4.2.3). 
2.4.2.1  Vowel  Elision  rules 
Phonological  vowel  elision  rules  affect  final  unstressed  vowels  at  syllable  boundaries  in  a 
number  of  environments  before  suffixes,  enclitics  or  words  within  the  same  phrase.  The 
elision  rules  include:  identical  vowel  elision,  vowel  elision  following  nasal  consonants,  and 
/e/ elision  between  alveolar  obstments. 
Rule la:  Identical  vowel  elision 
Identical  vowel  elision  occurs  when  the  final  vowel  of  a root  or  stem  is  the  same  (V,)  as  the 
initial  vowel  of  an inflection.  In  writing  the  final  vowel  of  the  verb  root  is  omitted. 
V,- V/  ^  +  V,-
(2.5.a)  Ka  -hi  (b.)  /Ka  -ae/  ^  K  -ael 
come  -Fls  come  -IMP2s 
'I will  come.'  'You  (singular)  come!' 
For  theoretical  studies  of  Word  Formation  Rules  see  AronofF(1976)  and  Anderson  (1992).

2.4.2.2  Vowel  harmony 
2.4.2.2.1  Introduction 
Vowel  harmony  mles  affect  final  mid  and  central  vowels  at  word  or  morpheme  boundaries 
following  alveolar  and  fiicative  consonants.  The  rules  are  regressive  or  progressive. 
2.4.2.2.2  Regressive  vowel  harmony 
Regressive  vowel  harmony  rules  raise  the  final  mid  front  vowel  following  alveolar 
consonants  and  the  final  central  vowel  following  the  alveolar  fricative.  These  'raising'  rules 
apply  when  the  subsequent  morpheme  has  a  high  vowel.  The  rules  contrast  with  ablaut 
rules  in  which  the  final  high  vowels  of  verbs  are  lowered  to  mid  vowels  before  phasal  and 
valency  changing  verbs  (see  §2.4.5). 
Rule 2a:  Regressive  vowel  harmony  affecting  /e/following  alveolar  consonants 
A final  mid  vowel  Id  following  an  alveolar  consonant  is  raised  to  a  high  vowel  to 
correspond  with  a  high  vowel  in  a  subsequent  CV  syllable,  except  when  C  is  /r/. 
e^  [i]  /  t/s/n/r  _  +C  [i] 
[u] [u] 
In (2.18.a)  te  'get'  retains  final  /e/  while  in  example  (b)  final  /e/  is  raised  to  /i/  when  the 
subsequent  CV  suffix  has  a  high  vowel  and  the  initial  consonant  is  not  /r/. 
(2.18.a)  Te  -r  -i.  (b)  Ti  -hi  =mpe.

'I am  getting  it.'  'I  intend  to  get  (it).'

final /e/  is  raised  and  backed  to  /u/  before  a suffix  with  a  high,  back  vowel  /u/.

2.4.2.2.3  Progressive  vowel  harmony 
Progressive  vowel  harmony  rules  assimilate  mid  front  or  central  vowels  to  a  vowel  in  a 
preceding  syllable.  The  mid  front  vowel  is  affected  following  fricative  consonants  and  the 
central  vowel  is  affected  following  alveolar  consonants.  This  contrasts  with  the  regressive 
rules,  where  the  mid  front  vowel  is  affected  following  fricative  consonants  and  the  central 
vowel  is  affected  following  alveolar  cononants. 
Rule 2c:  Progressive  vowel  harmony  following  fricatives 
When  /e/  follows  a  fricative  /h/  in  a  stressed  or  unstressed  syllable  or  the  fricative  /s/  in  an 
unstressed  syllable  it  is  assimilated  to  the  vowel  in  the  preceding  syllable, 
e^  V,  /  V,  +  h/s_ 
In the  following  example  progressive  vowel  hannony  affects  the  mid  vowel  which  follows 
the fricative  /h/  in  the  suffix  -hera 'F3s'.  This  vowel  assimilates  to  the  central  vowel  in  the 
preceding  syllable. 
(2.21)  Hekeni  tama  -hara. 
fire light  -F3s 
'He  will  light  the  fire.'

2.4.3  Morphologically  conditioned  rules 
Moiphologically  conditioned  rules  of  vowel  elision  and  vowel  harmony  affect  object  and 
present  tense-aspect  suffixes  which  have  a  final  vowel  /e/,  "/e/-eliding  verbs"  and  kinship 
nouns.  This  rule  could  be  said  to  apply  in  a  phonological  environment  following  /e/  final 
suffixes.  However,  it  is  morphologically  conditioned  because  it  only  applies  to  the  final  /e/ 
of "/e/  eliding  verbs"  and  not  to  other  Id final  verbs.  The  /e/  eliding  verbs  are: 
• verbs  whh  a  final  derivational  suffix  -ne 
• the  derived  verb  epone  'follow' 
• phasal,  prohibitive  and  manner  verbs  and  their  corresponding  main  verbs 
• the  monosyllabic  verb  ne  'consume:  drink,  eat,  inhale' 
Rule 3a:  Morphologically  conditionedpre-vocalic  /e/  elision 
The  final  /e/  of  object  and  present  tense-aspect  suffixes  and  of  /e/  eliding  verbs  is  elided 
following  an  alveolar  consonant  (/t/,  /s/,  /n/  or  /r/)  or  iricative  /he/  and  before  a  suffix  or 
enclitic  with  initial  /i/or/a/  such  as:  -/  'Is',  -ia  'Ip',  -anni  '2s',  -amue  '2p',  -ae  'IMP2s',  -
ahe 'IMP2p',  -apii  'nominaliser  (NOM)',  -apesi  'desiderative  (DES)'  (see  chapter  9)  and 
=ama 'group'. 
e ^  0  /  t/s/n/r_  +  i/a... 
In addition,  /e/  is  elided  by  the  identical  vowel  elision  rule  before  initial  /e/  for  example 
before  the  suffix  -e  '3p'  (see  Rule  la  in  §2.4.2.1) 
' This  rule  has  undergone  major  revision  since  the  production  of  my  MA  sub-thesis  (Priestley  2002:36-39). 
In the  MA,  however,  other  rules  are  much  more  detailed  and  include  footnotes  which  indicate  some 
similarities  to  the  nearby  language  of  Tauya.  One  characteristic  which  Koromu  and  Tauya  have  in  common  is 
that  "the  mid  front  vowel  /e/  is  the  vowel  most  susceptible  to  deletion"  (MacDonald  1990:36).

2.4.4  Lexically  conditioned  alternations 
Lexically  conditioned  alternations  of  vowel  elision,  vowel  hamiony  (fi^onting  or  fi onting 
and lowering)  and  glide  insertion  apply  to  individual  words  and  clitics,  namely  ahare  the 
'animate  locative'  postposition,  the  verb  stems  wesu  'show'  and  tii  'give  (to  a  second/third 
person)'  and  the  aspectual  enclitic  =ake  'already,  ahead,  beforehand'. 
Rule 4a:  Lexically  comiitioned  /a/  elision 
The  initial  vowel  of  the  'animate  locative'  postposition  ahare  (see  §7.3.4)  is  elided  when  it 
follows  the  pronoun  sene  '  Ip'  or  nene  '3p'  each  of  which  have  two  identical  front  mid 
vowels. 
(2.49)  Sene  hare  mo  piihu  -ael 
Ip ALOC  here  sit  -IMP2s 
'Sit  here  near  us!'  T  1.27.1 
Rule 4h:  Lexically  conditioned  fronting 
Final  /u/  in  the  verb  stem  wesu  'show'  (see  §4.2.3)  is  fronted  to  /i/  when  the  following 
inflection  has  an  alveolar  consonant  /t/,  /s/  or  /n/  followed  by  the  vowel  /e/.  IVesu  'show'  is 
unchanged  ifthe  recipient  object  is  third  person  singular  and  hence  there  is  no  object 
inflection.

suffix  since  all  of  these  suffixes  have  an  initial  alveolar  consonant  followed  by  /e/.

2.4.5  Ablaut  rules 
The  rules  of  ablaut  and  the  exceptions  to  those  mles  are  examined  in  the  sections  below. 
2.4.5.1  The  rules  of  ablaut 
The  final  high  vowels  of  open  class  verb  roots  are  affected  by  ablaut  before  phasal  (and 
valency-changing)  verbs  (see  §  10.2.4  to  §  10.2.6)  and  the  present  tense-aspect  suffix  (cf 
§9.3.2.3  and  Priestley  2002:26-31).  Ablaut  nales  are  applied  before  phonological  and 
moiphophonemic  rules. 
" The  first  syllable  is  also  the  penultimate  syllable  and  therefore  it  is  a  stressed  syllable.

phasal  and  phasal/valency-changing  verbs.  This  can  be  expressed  as: 
i ^  e  / u ^  o  / phasal  and  phasahvalency-changing  verbs

2.4.5.2  Exceptions  to  ablaut 
2.4.5.2.1  Introduction 
With  some  verbs  ablaut  is  absent  (§2.4.5.2.2)  or  only  partially  implemented  (§2.4.5.2.3). 
2.4.5.2.2  Absence  of  ablaut 
Ablaut  does  not  apply  to  some  verbs  which  also  function  as  verbal  nouns  (cf.  §4.3.2.3  and 
Priestley  2002:31-34),  for  example,  tiiumi  'think'  from  the  mental  process  noun  'thought' 
and uhuru  'be  heavy'  from  the  descriptive  noun  'heaviness'.  Furthermore,  a  linking 
particle  e  occurs  between  the  descriptive  verbal  nouns  uhuni  'heavy'  and  ihi  'finish' 
(§4.3.2.3.3)  and  final  phasal  here  'PUT'  in  causative  constructions.  Compare: 
(2.65.a)  Uhitnt  -a.  (b)  Uhuru  e  her  -a. 
heavy  -3s  heavy  LK.P  PUT  -3s 
'It was  heavy.'  'He/she  made  it  heavy.' 
Also  ablaut  does  not  affect  a main  verb  that  has  an  object  suffix  (cf.  (2.61)  in  §2.4.5.2). 
2.4.5.2.3  Partial  ablaut 
The  semantically  reflexive  verb  root  miku  'submerge/envelop  (self)  in'  which  occurs  in 
miku-a [submerge-3s]  'he  submerged  himself  (in  water)'  is  only  partially  affected  by  ablaut 
when  it  precedes  phasal  and  valency-changing  here  'PUT'  (2.66a).  It  is  not  affected  at  all 
prior  to  other  phasal  verbs  (2.66b). 
(2.66a)  Nuko  hor  -a.  (b)  Nuku  n  -a. 
submerge.in  PUT  -3s  submerge.in  STAY  -3s 
' He submerged  him/her  in  (water).'  '  It is  submerged  (in  water).'

2.5 Phonetic  variations 
2.5.1  Introduction 
Phonetic  variations  can  occur  in  rapid  speech.  They  are  described  below  under  the 
headings  basic  phonetic  variations  (§2.5.2)  and  lexically  conditioned  variations  (§2.5.3). 
2.5.2  Basic  phonetic  variations 
Basic  phonetic  variations  which  occur  in  rapid  speech  include  regressive  vowel  harmony  in 
which  Id  is  raised  to  /i/  (cf.  §2.4.2.1.1),  pre-vocalic  /e/  elision  (cf.  §2.4.3)  and  pre-vocalic 
/u/ elision.'^  Progressive  vowel  harmony  in  which  /e/  is  backed  to  /o/  appears  to  be  a 
matter  of  speaker  choice. 
18 
Variation 1:  Regressive vowel  harmony  following  labial  consonants 
A final  mid  vowel  Id  which  follows  a labial  consonant  can  be  raised  to  the  high  vowel  III 
when  either  the  high  vowel  III  or /u/  occurs  in  the  following  CV  syllable 
e^  i  / p/m/w  C  i/u 
The  verb  root  mene  'be,  stay'  can  be  affected  when  it  occurs  with  the  suffix  -/  '  1 s' or  -ia 
' Ip'.  First  the  pre-vocalic  /e/  elision  rule  applies  when  the  suffix  is added.  Then  the  mid 
front  vowel  /e/  in  the  initial  syllable  is  assimilated  to  the  high  vowel  III.

come  -SR  come  stay  -Is  -DR

This  phonetic  variation  can  also  affect  a loose  temporal  dependency  complex  following  a 
verb  (cf  §9.4.4).  This  complex  morphemic  sequence,  which  has  one  gloss  to  indicate  the 
core  meaning  of  loose  temporal  dependency  and  tense-subject,  consists  ofthe  same  referent 
suffix  -pe followed  by  ne  STAY  inllected  by  a  tense-subject  suffix  and  the  suffix  -te. The 
Possibly  phonetic  variations  are  the  source  of  phonological  alternations.  Anderson  (1992:340)  cites  the 
hypothesis  of  Polish  linguists  Jan  Baudouin  de  Courtenay  and  Mikolaj  Kruszewski  over  a  hundred  years  ago 
which  suggests  that  mechanical  (phonetic)  variations  become  phonological  rules  over  time. 
Although  rules  5a  to  5fare  variations  they  are  listed  as  rules  where  they  fit  in  with  the  numbering  system.
