Chapter  3 Basic  Clause  Structure 
3.1 Introduction 
This  chapter  provides  an  introduction  to  the  characteristics  of  basic  clauses  (§3.2),  to  verbal 
(§3.3)  and  nonverbal  clauses  (§3.4)  with  their  core  arguments  and  to  basic  clause  structure 
with  required  or  optional  oblique  arguments  (3.5). 
3.2 Characteristics  of  basic  clauses 
This  section  introduces  some  of  the  basic  characteristics  of  clause  structure,  including 
distinctions  between  formal  clause  types  (§3.2.1),  the  expression  of  epistemic  modality 
(§3.2.2)  and  the  main  differences  between  verbal  and  nonverbal  clauses  (§3.2.3). 
3.2.1  Formal  clause  types 
3.2,1.1  Introduction 
The  formal  clause  (sentence)  types  in  Koromu  are  declarative,  interrogative,  imperative, 
and exclamative.  They  are  distinguished  from  each  other  by  differences  in syntax  and 
semantics  indicated  by  verbal  suffixation,  intonation  and  the  presence  or  absence  of 
enclitics  and  interrogative  words.  The  illocutionary  force,  or  speech  acts  (see  Van  Valin 
2005:9),  most  commonly  expressed  by  these  clause  types  are  assertions,  questions, 
directions  and  exclamations.  Desiderative  clauses  are  also  mentioned  briefly  here. 
Although  they  ftinction  as  declarative,  interrogative  or  exclamative  clauses  they  have 
fomially  different  verbs  from  any  of  these  clause  types. 

[PDF PAGE 97]
68 Chapter  3 
The  term  mood  is  sometimes  used  in  the  description  of  clause  types  to  refer  to "a  set  of 
syntactic  and  semantic  contrasts  signalled  by  alternative  paradigms  of  the  verb"  (Crystal 
1985:230).  Koromu  declarative  (§3.2.1.2)  and  interrogative  (§3.2.1.3)  verbal  clauses  both 
have  verbs  with  the  full  range  of  tense-subject:person-number  indicative  suffixes  (cf 
§9.3.2.2).  They  are  distinguished  from  each  other  by  intonation  and  by  the  presence  or 
absence  of  question  enclitics  and/or  interrogative  words.  In  contrast,  imperative  (§3.2.1.4) 
and desiderative  (§3.2.1.6)  clauses  have  distinct  verbal  suffixes  (see  §9.3.3  and  §9.3.4) 
while  exclamative  (§3.2.1.5)  clauses  have  an  exclamatory  enclitic  added  to  an  indicative 
clause.  These  distinctive  clause  types  are  introduced  in  the  sections  which  follow. 
3.2.1.2  Declarative  clauses 
The  verb  in  a  declarative  clause  is  inflected  with  one  of  the  six  portmanteau  tense  and 
subject  suffixes  (cf  §9.3.2).'  Declarative  clauses  have  falling  intonation  on  the  predicate 
and are  commonly  used  to  express  assertions

3.2.1.4  Imperative  clauses 
An imperative  clause  has  an  imperative  second  person  singular  or  plural  suffix  on the  verb 
(cf.  §9.3.3.)-  These  clauses  are  used  to  give  directions  or  advice,  request  help  and  express 
friendly  salutations,  as  in  the  instruction  in  (3.3)  above  and  the  direction/friendly  salutation 
below. 
(3.12)  Werai  it  n  -a  =mo.  Yar  -ahe! 
little  do  STAY  -3s  =BM  go  -IMP2p 
'That's  all  (it  was  a  little).  You  go!'  {Yarahel  is  the  type  of  thing  people  say  instead 
of'Seeyou!')T1.20.37 
3.2.1.5  Exclamative  clauses 
Exclamative  clauses  have  an  exclamatoiy  enclitic  =o  following  the  verb  and  falling  or 
rising  intonation  (cf  §4.10).  They  are  used  to  express  exclamations  of  surprise  or  pain  and 
other  extreme  positive  and  negative  feelings.  They  can  be  used  when  exhorting  or  calling 
someone  so  vocatives  are  often  followed  by  the  exclamatory  enclitic  (see  §4.3.3.4).  Rising

3.2.1.6  Desiderative  clauses 
Desiderative  clauses  have  a  desiderative  suffix  -apesi on  the  verb  root  (see  §9.3.4).  There  is 
no verbal  suffix  expressing  tense-subject  on  the  verb  so  this  information  has  to  be 
recovered  from  the  discourse  or  real  world  context  or  from  the  complement-taking 
predicate  when  the  clause  is  a  non-finite  complement  clause  (see  §  12.3.4).  In  the  following 
example,  the  desiderative  suffix  has  scope  over  the  previous  clause  in  which  the  verb  has  a 
same  referent  subject  (cf  §9.4.2).

3.2.2  Epistemic  modality 
Epistemic  modality  particles  are  clausal  operators  (cf  §4.10)  which  occur  clause  finally  and 
have  scope  over  the  clause  which  precedes  them.  The  particles  arepaimo  'apprehensional',^ 
taumo/tauo/taiine 'uncertainty'  and  temo/te  'possibility'  (cf  Priestley  2002:99-102).  The 
particle  ne  indicates  an  'emphatic  statement'.  These  particles  follow  an  inflected  verb  at  the 
end of  declarative,  interrogative  or  desiderative  clauses.  When  the  subject  has  the  same 
referent  in  a  preceding  clause  of  the  same  sentence  the  modality  particle  has  scope  over  that 
clause  as  well. 
Paimo 'apprehensional'  only  occurs  with  a  verb  inflected  for  future  tense  or  desiderative, 
that is,  with  clauses  which  have  iirealis  status. 
(3.16)  "Enaise-ue  -pe  yare  -here  paimo,"  ii  -a  -te... 
leave  -2s  -SR  go  -F3p  APP  quote  -3s  -DR 
' "They  might  leave  you  and  go,"  she  said...'  T  1.15.20 
' Avolitional  auxiliaries  indicating  undesirable  events  occur  in  Tauya  (MacDonald  1990:202-203)  and  Hua 
(Haiman  1980:  141,  142)  and  suffixes  meaning  'for  fear  that'  or  'lest'  occur  in  Rumu  (Petterson  1999:148) 
and  Porome  (Martin  Steer,  personal  communication).

3,2.3  Differences  between  verbal  and  nonverbal  clauses 
Verbal  and  nonverbal  clauses  are  described  in  the  following  two  sections.  There  are  basic 
differences  between  them.  Verbal  clauses  have  an  inflected  verb^  in  the  predicate  (see 
' There  may  be  a connection  between  ne 'emphatic'  and  the  dependency  suffix  -ne 'DR:IR:CS'  (§9.3.3.3). 

[PDF PAGE 103]
74 Chapter  3 
chapter  9).  The  verbs  are  independent  (final)  verbs  inflected  for  tense,  subject  and  mood^ 
or dependent  (medial)  verbs  which,  though  they  have  their  own  core  and  peripheral 
arguments,  are  dependent  for  fiall  specification  of  tense,  subject  and  mood  on  a  subsequent 
more  fially  inflected  verb.  One  or  more  dependent  verbal  clauses  fonn  a  chain  which  ends 
with  a  final  independent  clause.  In  verbal  clauses  negation  is  expressed  by  the  negative 
particle  tai  before  the  verb.  In  contrast,  nonverbal  clauses  do  not  have  verbal  inflections  on 
the predicate  and  do  not  occur  with  tai  'negative'. 
3.3 Verbal  Clauses 
3.3.1  Introduction 
A verbal  clause  consists  minimally  of  an  independent  vei"b with  tense-subject  inflections  or 
a dependent  with  inflections  that  directly  or  indirectly  indicate  tense  and  person  and 
number  of  the  subject  (cf  chapter  9  and  Priestley  2002:  chapters  3  and  5).  There  are  from 
one  to  three  core  arguments  in  the  clause  depending  on  the  semantics  of  the  verbal 
predicate.  The  default  order  of  constituents  is  AOV  in  transitive  clauses  and  AO1O2V  in 
ditransitive  clauses.  Core  arguments  represent  participants  in  the  event  or  state  expressed 
by the  verb  and  are  represented  by  noun  phrases  (cf  chapter  5),  verbal  inflections  (cf 
§9.3.2.2  and  §9.3.2.4)  and  in  some  cases  complement  clauses  (§12.3).  Oblique  arguments 
can also  occur  (see  §3.5). 
The  sections  below  examine  grammatical  relations  (§3.3.2),  subject  and  object  semantic 
roles  (§3.3.3),  types  of  verbal  clauses  (§3.3.4)  and  verbal  clauses  and  negation  (§3.3.5). 
3.3.2  Grammatical  relations 
3.3.2.1  Grammatical  relations  of  core  arguments 
The  morphosyntactic  behaviour  of  Koromu  core  arguments  can  be  discussed  in  terms  of  the 
grammatical  relations  subject  and  object.  Using  the  abbreviations  introduced  by  Dixon 
' The  verb  ia  'be  not'  is  not  inflected  in  independent  clauses  but  it  is  in  dependent  clauses  (§3.3.4.8.3). 
' However,  when  desiderative  mood  is  expre.ssed  tense  and  subject  are  omitted  (i}9.3.7.4)

(1979),  S  is the  single  actant  of  an intransitive  verb,  A  the  agent-like  argument  of  a 
transitive  verb,  and  O  the  patient-like  argument  of  transitive  verbs. 
Evidence  for  these  grammatical  relations  is  found  in  the  person-number  or  switch  reference 
suffixes  which  occur  with  independent  and  dependent  verbs  (§3.3.2.2),  in  subject  and

Further  evidence  for  subject  is  found  in  equi-deletion  of  the  subject  of complement  clauses

possible,  however,  for  subject  and  object  NPs  to be omitted  from  both  verbal  and  nonverbal 
clauses  owing  to  the  prevalence  of  zero  anaphora  in  the  language  (see  §  13.4).

postposition  te  'instrumental'  is  similar  in  fonn  but  only  occurs  with  oblique  arguments  that 
refer  to  inanimate  instruments  (see  §7.4.2.2).  When  =te  occurs  with  an  animate  referent  NP 
it is  clearly  the  'prominent  subject'  enclitic  and  it  confiirns  that  the  NP  is  the  subject.

3.3.3  Subject  and  object  semantic  roles 
Subject  and  object  in  Koromu  are  associated  with  four  common  participator  semantic 
roles  -  agent,  patient,  experiencer,  and  theme  - which  are  'borne  by  what  one  would  think 
of as  actual  participants  in  the  situation  implied  by  the  verb'  (Andrews  2007:140 
[1985:69]). 

[PDF PAGE 109]
80 Chapter  3 
With  certain  cautions  in  mind  an  Agent" is  "a  participant  which  the  meaning  of  the 
verb  describes  as  doing  something,  or  causing  something  to  happen,  possibly 
intentionally  (that  is  because  (s)he  wants  it  to)". 
"A Patient  will  be  defined  as  a  participant  which  the  verb  describes  as  having 
something  happen  to  it,  and  as  being  affected  by  what  happens  to  it"  (2007:137 
[1985:68]). 
An Experience!'  is  "a  participant  who  is  characterized  as  aware  of  something". 
A Theme  is  "a  participant  which  is  characterized  as  being  in  a  state  or  position,  or 
changing  its  state  or  position,  sometimes  treated  as  a kind  of  Patient"  (2007:140 
[1985:70]). 
A number  of  other  semantic  roles  are  associated  with  subject  and  object  in  Koromu.  In  this 
section  1  refer  the  reader  to  examples  eariier  in  this  chapter  which  exemplify  common 
semantic  roles  and  to  chapter  10  where  semantic  roles  which  occur  with  subjects  and 
objects  in  more  complex  verbal  constructions  are  described. 
The  subject  semantic  roles  of  agent,  experiencer  and  theme  are  exemplified  below  (some  of 
the examples  are  repeated  fi^om §3.3.2.2.1).

'1 will strike  you.'  (3.21) 
(3.36)  Experiencer  subject were-neka -i=mo.  [se-03p-1  s=BM 
'1 saw them.'  T  1.15.22 
(3.37)  Theme  subject On men-a.  [yam  be/stay-3s] 
'A yam  is  there.'  (3.24) 
The  italics  are  mine.

with many  transitive  dynamic  verbs  with  here  PUT  (see  §  10.2.5.4.5). 
A number  of  examples  in  §3.3.2.2.1  show  that  O  suffixes  are used  to  refer  to animate  rather 
than inanimate  referents.  Arguments  with  the  semantic  role  of  recipient,  beneficiary  or 
goal are  more  likely  to  have  an  animate  referent  that  can  be  indicated  by  an  O  suffix,  than 
arguments  with  patient  or  theme  roles  (see  (3.28)  above).  Thus  when  both  object  referents 
are animate,  it  is  the  O  (undergoer)  with  the  semantic  role  of  recipient,  beneficiary  or  goal 
which  is  indexed  on  the  verb,  rather  than  the  O  with  the  role  of  patient  or  theme.  So,  while 
English  selects  the  more  patient-like  role  as  the  default  undergoer  ,Koromu,  like  Swahili, 
selects  the  non-patient-like  role. 
3.3.4  Types  of  verbal  clause 
This section  describes  verbal  clause  types.  Three  clause  types  are  based  on  differences  in 
the number  of  core  arguments,  intransitive  (§3.3.4.1),  transitive  (§3.3.4.2)  and  ditransitive 
(§3.3.4.3).  Clause  types  which  deviate  from  these  basic  patterns  are  impersonal 
experiential  clauses  (§3.3.4.5),  verbal  possessive  clauses  (§3.3.4.6),  reflexive  clauses 
(§3.3.4.7),  reciprocal  clauses  (§3.3.4.8)  and  copula  clauses,  (§3.3.4.9). 
" Capitals  indicate  that  a  verb  has  a  grammatical  use. 

[PDF PAGE 112]
Basic  Clause  Structures  83 
3.3.4.1  Intransitive  clauses 
Intransitive  verbal  clauses  describe  events  involving  one  participant  (cf.  §4.2.1).  The  single 
core  argument  representing  this  participant  functions  as  the  subject  of  the  clause  and  is 
represented  by  a  verbal  suffix  which  indicates  tense-subject,  imperative  or  dependency  and 
by an  optional  NP  before  the  verb. 
NPs V  -Tense-subject/imperative/dependency  suffix 
(3.45)  Nene  poho  n  -e. 
3p sit  STAY  -3p 
'They  sat.'  T  1.15.2 
3.3.4.2  Transitive  clauses 
Transitive  clauses  describe  events  with  two  core  arguments  (cf  §4.2.2).  Prototypically, 
someone  or  something  (the  subject)  does  something  to  change  the  state  or  position  of 
another  person  or  thing  (the  object).  The  Koromu  subject  is  indicated  minimally  by  a 
tense-subject,  imperative  or  dependency  suffix  (cf.  chapter  9)  but  also  by  a  subject  NP 
which  can  occur  with  the  'prominent  subject'  enclitic  (cf  §5.11  and  §13.5).  The  object 
is indicated  by  an  NP  and/or  by  an  object  verbal  suffix.  Core  argument  NPs  can  be  omitted 
or they  can  occur  in  a  different  order  (cf  chapters  13  and  14)  but  the  default  word  order  is: 
NPs NPo  V  (-0  suffix)  -Tense-subject/imperative/dependency  suffix 
(3.46)  ...ne  =te  iisii  ho  -ae'}'^ 
2s =PS  pig  cut:butcher  -IMP2s 
'...you  cut  (butcher)  the  pig!'  T2.14.... 
Transitive  clauses  do  not  always  describe  an  agentive  subject  affecting  an object. 
Sometimes  the  subject  NP  is  an  experiencer  and  the  object  NP  has  a  theme  role. 
Home is  a  two  syllable  name.  The  referent  is  not  indicated  by  a  verbal  object  suffix  since  third  person 
singular  objects  are  not  indicated  on  the  verb.

3.3.4.3  Ditransitive  clauses 
Ditransitive  clauses  refer  to events  of  transfer  in which  there  are  typically  three  participants, 
an agent  who  controls  the  transfer,  a  patient  or  theme  which  is  transferred,  and  a  recipient 
or goal  to  which  the  transfer  is  made.  The  subject  and  the  object  recipient/goal  (Oi)  are 
indicated  by  noun  phrases  and/or  verbal  suffixes  while  the  object  theme  (O2)  is  only 
referred  to  by  an  NP.  In  default  word  order  the  recipient  or  goal  object  NP  occurs  before 
the theme  object  NP. 
(NPs) (NPoi)  (NP02)  V  (-0,  suffix)  -Tense/subject  suffix

clauses.  In  the  examples  below  the  object  with  the  role  of  recipient/goal  is  realised  by  an  O 
suffix  and there  is  only  one  object  NP  in the  clause.

'...he  showed  us  the  machine  there...'  T  1.20.24

3.3.4.4  Impersonal  experiential  clauses 
Impersonal  experiential  clauses  describe  physical  or  psychological  conditions  or  sensations. 
The experiencer  object  verb  (see  §4.2.6  and  chapter  11)  which  heads  the  clause  expresses 
the condition  or  sensation  and  is  marked  for  two core  arguments.  The  clause  is  not 
transitive  in  the  sense  outlined  in  §3.3.4.2  above  since  the  subject  suffix  has no  referent  and 
no coiresponding  subject  NP  while  an  object  NP  and  a  corresponding  suffix  refer  to the 
experiencer.  Some  impersonal  experiential  clause  types  include  an  NP  referring  to a  body 
part or  theme/stimulus  but  there  is  no evidence  that  this  NP  is  the  subject. 
NPQ (NP)  V  -O  suffix  -3s  subject  suffix 
The conditions  or  sensations  expressed  by  the  verb  are  not  controlled  by  the  experiencer. 
Therefore  impersonal  experiential  clauses,  like  nonverbal  and  stative  clauses,  can  not  occur 
in imperative  or  intentive  mood.  A  few  examples  are  given  below  but  a  more  detailed 
description  is  given  in  chapter  11.

3.3.4.5  Verbal  possessive  clauses 
Verbal  possessive  clauses'^  indicate  that  one  entity  possesses  another  entity.  They  state 
that  a  possessor  is  at  or  with  the  entity  possessed.  The  possessed  entity  is  subject  of  the 
verb  mene  'be/exist'  and  it  occurs  in  the  position  immediately  before  the  verb  (cf  §4.2.7). 
The  possessor  is  the  unmarked  location  of  the  object.'^  The  NPs  in  this  constmction  are  not 
marked  by  the  genitive  or  possessor  suffixes  (see  chapter  6)  and  the  clause  can  not  occur  as 
an imperative  clause  (§3.2.1.4)  or  fonn  a  causative-like  construction  (§10.2.5.4). 
(3.56)  I  nan  men  -a. 
Is coconut  be  -3s 
'I have  a  coconut,  (lit.  The  coconut  is  at/with  me).'  D160.4 
Verbal  possessive  clauses  contrast  with  nonverbal  possessive  clauses  (see  §3.4.3.3) 
"Languages  usually  employ  existential  and/or  locational  structures  to  express  the  notion  of  possession" 
(Payne  1997:126).  For  example,  English  use.s  'to  have',  Estonian  uses  a  copular  verb  or  particle  'be'  and 
Turkish  uses  a  verb  meaning  'exist'  (1997:126).

3.3.4.6  Reflexive  clauses 
Reflexive  clauses  describe  a  situation  in  which  the  referents  of  the  subject  and  object  can  be 
understood  as  being  the  same  entity.  They  are  not  a  subtype  of  transitive  clauses.  The  verb 
has a  subject  suffix  but  not  an  object  suffix.  There  is  a  single  NP  followed  by  the 
reflexive/emphatic  suffix  -moron 'self  (see  §5.3  and  §5.7)."^ 
(3.57)  I  -moron  were  -r  -i. 
Is -self  see  -PRES  -Is 
'I saw  myself  (...in  a  picture)  D9.25.  5

'Now  you  are  hitting  yourselves'.  D7.19.5

can be  used  to  express  emphasis  in  transitive  (3.59)  constructions.

so.then  Ip  -self  =PS  word  hear  -SR

3.3.4,7  Reciprocal  clauses 
Reciprocal  clauses  describe  events  in  which  two  or  more  participants  act  towards  each 
other  in  the  same  way  at  the  same  time.  Each  participant  is  both  an  agent  and  a  patient  in 
the same  event.  The  verb  has  a  reciprocal  suffix  -a  (see  §9.3.2.5)  and  a  subject  suffix. 
There  is  no  object  suffix.  In  the  following  example  one  NP  represents  the  two  participants. 
Since  NP  omission  is  common  in  Koromu,  it  is  possible  that  a  subject  NP  has  been  omitted  from  the 
position  prior  to  the  NP  with  the  sutTlx -moron  'self. 
" The  verb  pehe can  be  used  to  mean  touch  or  hit.  In  the  examples  given  here  it  combines  with  here  PUT  and 
means  hit(cf.  §10.2.5.4.7).

3.3.4.8  Copula  clauses 
There  are  three  types  of  copula  clause,  copula  clauses  with  mene  'be,  exist',  quasi  copula 
clauses  with  honi  'become'  and  negative  copula  clauses  with  iu  'be  not'. 
3.3.4.8.1  Copula  clauses  with  mene  'be,  exist' 
Copula  clauses  with  the  verb  mene  'be,  exist'  describe  a  temporary  attribute  (cf.  §4.2.7). 
An initial  NP  subject  with  an  experiencer/theme  semantic  role  is  followed  by  a  complement 
which  is  a  qualifier  (an  adjective  or quantifier)  or  an  interrogative.  The  complement 
describes  an  attribute  of  the  referent  of  the  initial  NP. 
(3.63)  Tamaite  tai  imi  -e.  Tamaite  soron  ta  -e. 
men NEG  die  -3p  men  jump  END  -3p 

[PDF PAGE 118]
Basic  Clause  Structures  89 
Tamaite nokono  men  -e. 
men  good/fine  be  -3p 
'The  men  didn't  die.  The  men  jumped.  The  men  were  fine.'  T5.24.25 
In the  exchange  below  interrogative  emu  'how  much'  functions  as  the  complement. 
(3.64.)  Ya  euaii  men  -a?  Ya  mipii  mo  men  -a. 
water  how.much  be  -3s  water  much  here  be  -3s 
'How  much  water  is  there?'  CS10.15  'There  is  a lot  ofwater  here.'  CS10.16 
3.3.4.8.2  Quasi  copula  clauses 
A quasi  copula  clause  describes  the  transformation  of  an  entity.  A  subject  with  an 
experiencer/theme  semantic  role  is  affected  by  something  that  happens.  The  event  is 
described  by  the  verb  horn  'become'  (see  §4.2.7).  A  second  noun  phrase  consisting  of  a 
common  noun  (3.65),  an  adjective  (3.66)  or  a  temporal  noun  (3.67)  represents  the 
transformed  entity. 
(3.65)  (Ni)  henahina  horn  -r  -a. 
she old  woman  become  -PRES  -3s 
'She  is  becoming  an  old  woman.' 
(3.66)  Arene  horn  -r  -a. 
big become  -PRES  -3s 
'She  is  becoming  big.' 
(3.67)  ...si  arisapit,  horn  -a  -te... 
then  afternoon  become  -3s  -DR 
'..  .then  it  became  afternoon  and...'  T1.20.41 
3.3.4.8.3  Negative  copula  clauses 
Negative  copula  clauses  consist  of  a subject  NP  followed  by  a  predicate  nominal,  adjective 
or postpositional  phrase  and  the  defective  copula  verb  ia  'be  not'  (§4.2.8).  Like  a  particle, 
the negative  copula  is  not  inflected  for  tense,  aspect  or  subject  person  and  number  but  like  a

referent  suffix  -te (see  §9.4.3.4.2)  or  the  loose  temporal  dependency  complex  (§9.4.4).  It 
can also  be  the  main  verb  in  a  serial  verb  construction  with  phasal  ne  STAY  (§  10.2.6).^^

3.4 Nonverbal  clauses 
3.4.1  Introduction 
Nonverbal  clauses  consist  of  a subject  NP  and  a  nominal  or  postpositional  predicate.  The 
subject  NP  to  be  omitted  when  it  is  recoverable  from  the  discourse  (see  §  13.4.2).  The 
sections  below  examine  nominal  (§3.4.2)  and  postpositional  clauses  (§3.4.3). 
3.4.2  Nominal  clauses 
3.4.2.1  Basic  characteristics  of  nominal  clauses 
Nominal  clauses  are  formed  by  the  juxtaposition  of  a NP  subject  and  a  NP  predicate.^^ 
NPs NP  predicate 
Nominal  clauses  are  equative,  attributive,  possessive  or  locative  depending  on  the  nature  of 
the NP  predicate  and  its  semantic  relationship  with  the  subject.  To  express  negative 
concepts  the  negative  copula  clause  with  ia  'be  not'  is  used  (see  §3.3.4.8.3  above). 
3.4.2.2  Equative  clauses 
Equative  clauses  have  an  NP  predicate  which  expresses  the  classification  or  identity  of  the 
NP subject.  Classification  (X  is  a  Y)  is  expressed  in  (3.84  ),  see  also  (3.92).  The  first 
example  is  followed  by  a  final  boundary  marking  enclitic  =mo. 
(3.84)  Ni  ososo  =mo. 
3s doctor  =BIVI 
'He/she  is  a  doctor.'

3.5 Required  and  oprional  oblique  arguments  in  clause  structure 
3.5.1  Introduction 
A clause  may  have  oblique  arguments  in  addition  to  the  obligatory  predicate  with  its  core 
arguments,  which  are  expressed  by  verbal  suffixation  and/or  core  argument  NPs.  There  are 
two types  of  oblique  argument,  those  which  are  required  by  the  semantics  of  the  verb  ('core 
oblique'  arguments;  §3.5.2)  and  those  which  are  genuinely  oblique  (§3.5.3). 
3.5.2  Clauses  with  core  oblique  arguments 
Clauses  with  core  oblique  arguments  (see  Van  Valin  2005)  have  a  verb  that  requires  an 
oblique  argument  to  refer  to the  goal  of  the  action.  These  locative  goal  arguments  may  be 
required  by  intransitive  verbs  which  describe  someone's  movement  (cf  §4.2.1.2)  or 
bytransitive  verbs  (or  serial  verb  constmctions)  which  describe  someone  moving  an  object 
to a  place  (cf  §4.2.2.2.3  and  §  10.2.5.4.4).  They  are  represented  by  a postpositional  phrase 
or a  placename,  and  they  behave  like  verbal  objects  and  occur  immediately  before  the  verb. 

[PDF PAGE 128]
Basic  Clause  Structures  99 
In fact,  as  the  second  example  below  shows,  when  there  is  a verbal  object  in  the  same 
clause,  the  locative  goal  argument  occurs  before  the  verb. 
(3.103)  ...somoni  weti  pa  aire  ta  -i. 
night  house  G/L  arrive  END  -Is 
'I arrived  at  the  house  at  night.'  T2.32.36 
(3.104)  ...ah  -ima  no,  wera  hekeni  pa  ene  re  -pe... 
mother  -Pis  GRD  child  fire  G/L  lay  PUT  -SR 
'...my  mother,  lay  the  child  by  the  fire...'  T  1.10.3 
Clauses  with  the  verb  sa 'speak'  can  also  have  a  core  oblique  argument  which  occurs 
immediately  before  the  verb  (cf  §4.2.2.2.1  and  §7.4.1.3). 
3.5.3  Clauses  with  non-core  oblique  arguments 
Genuinely  non-core  oblique  arguments  give  information  about  the  setting  or  circumstances 
of the  situation  described  by  the  predicate  and  the  core  arguments.  They  are  expressed  by 
temporal,  locative,  manner,  'only'  and  sentential  adverbs  (see  §4.7),  manner,  instrument, 
comitative,  reason,  purpose,  similarity  and  resemblance  postpositional  phrases  (see  §4.8 
and chapter  7),  and  placenames  and  temporal  nouns  (see  §4.3.4  and  §4.3.5). 
This  section  gives  some  basic  details  about  the  position  of  non-core  constituents  in  the 
clause,  particularly  sentential,  locative  and  temporal  arguments  (For  further  details  of 
clauses  with  other  oblique  arguments  see  §4.7  and  chapter  7.) 
The  sentential  adverbs,  si 'then'  and  pari 'again,  eventually'  (see  §4.7.6)  modify  the  clause. 
They  occur  in  clause  initial  position  in  both  verbal  and  nonverbal  clauses.  When  both  of 
these  adverbs  occur  in  the  same  clause,  si 'then'  occurs  first.

Chapter  4 Word  Classes 
4.1 Introduction 
This  chapter  examines  word  classes.  These  classes  are  distinguished  on  the  basis  of 
distributional  and  moiphological  criteria  and  some  semantic  and  functional  criteria.  There 
ai'e two  main  open  word  classes,  verbs  (§4.2)  and  nouns  (§4.3).  There  are  a  number  of 
minor  word  classes:  qualifiers  (§4.4),  pronouns  (§4.5),  indefinite  specific  pronouns  (§4.6), 
adverbs  (§4.7),  postpositions  (§4.8),  the  negative  particle  tai  (§4.9),  modality  particles 
(§4.10),  conjunctions  (§4.11),  grammar-information  particles  (§4.12),  interjections  (§4.13) 
and the  semantically  defined  cross-cutting  classes  of  demonstratives  and  interrogatives 
(§4.14). 
4.2 Verbs 
Verbs  are  a  large,  open  word  class.  They  are  distinguished  fi-om  other  word  classes 
because  they  can  be  mai'ked  by  suffixes  which  indicate: 
• tense,  subject:  pei-son  and  number 
• dependency  and  switch  reference 
• aspect 
• object:  person  and  number 
The  main  verb  classes  established  on  the  basis  of  valency  are  intransitive  verbs  (§4.2.1), 
transitive  verbs  (§4.2.2),  experiencer  object  verbs  (§4.2.6),  ditransitive  verbs  (§4.2.3) 
ambitransitive  verbs  (§4.2.4),  and  alternating  transitive  verbs  (§4.2.5).  There  are  also 

[PDF PAGE 133]
104 Chapter  4 
copular  and  quasi-copular  verbs  (§4.2.7)  and  a  negative  copula  verb  (§4.2.8).  In  addition, 
in serial  verb  constructions,  phasal  (§4.2.9)  and  phasal  and  valency-changing  verbs 
(§4.2.10)  occur  in  the  final  position  while  a  manner  verb  (§4.2.11)  can  occur  as  the 
penultimate  or  final  verb.  Further  distinctions  between  types  of  verbs  within  these  classes 
are based  on  the  semantic  nature  of  the  verbs  and  their  core  arguments.  These  semantic 
distinctions  influence  the  fonnal  clause  types  the  verbs  occur  in  (cf  §3.2.1),  the  verbal 
inflections  (cf  chapter  9)  and  complex  predicate  fomiation  (cf  chapter  10).  For  example, 
dynamic  verbs  can  have  tense-subject,  imperative  and  fiature-intentive  suffixes  (cf  chapter 
9),'  while  stative  verbs  cannot. 
4.2.1  Intransitive  verbs 
Intransitive  verbs  take  a  single  argument,  the  subject,  which  is  expressed  by  a  verbal  suffix 
and an  optional  NP  (cf  §3.3.4.1).  The  semantic  subclasses  are  intransitive  dynamic  verbs 
with  agentive  subjects,  intransitive  dynamic  verbs  with  agent  and  theme  subjects, 
intransitive  stative/dynamic  verbs  and  intransitive  stative  verbs. 
4.2.1.1  Intransitive  verbs  with  agentive  subjects 
Intransitive  verbs  with  agentive  (effector)^  subjects  describe  actions  such  as  eta  'vomit', 
hiri 'cry',  kait  'howl',  kerehai  'call  happily',  ko  'whistle',  sipi  'excrete',  mAyakere 
'laugh'.  They  can  occur  in  applicative-like  serial  verb  constructions  (see  §  10.2.5.4.4). 
(4.1)  Hena  yakere  -r  -a.

4.2.1.3  Intransitive  stative/dynaniic  verbs 
The  intransitive  verb  mene  'be,  exist,  stay'  has  a  stative  and  a  dynamic  sense.  The  stative

theme  and  the  existence  of  an  entity  or  a  location  or  temporary  state  of  affairs  is indicated.

4.2.1.4  Intransitive  stative  or  stative/inchoative  verbs 
Intransitive  stative  verbs  have  subjects  with  the  semantic  role  of  patient  or  theme.  These

attains  a  property,  for  example,  kenekene  'be  strong,  tough',  ai  'be/become  soft  or  tender', 
kese 'be/become  wet  or  rotten',  kihi  'be/become  deep',  kiiku  'be/become  heated',  and 
kiikiipe 'be/become  sour  or  dusty'.

These  verbs  cannot  occur  with  imperative  or  intentive  suffixes  (cf  nonverbal  clauses  (see

4.2.2.2.1  Transitive  dynamic  verbs  with  agentive  subjects 
Semantically,  many  transitive  verbs  have  agentive  subjects  and  an  object  with  the  semantic

many  of  these  verbs,  for  example,  ho  'cut',  occur  with  here  PUT,  there  is  an  added  object

indicates  a  more  complete  effect  on a  patient  (cf  §  10.2.5.4.7).

object  with  an  inanimate  referent  (see  alternating  transitive  verbs  in  §4.2.5). 
The  semantic  role  of  the  subject  could  be  described  as  effector  since  it  can  be  an  (inanimate)  force.

4.2.3  Ditransitive  verbs 
Ditransitive  verbs  (cf.  §3.3.4.3)  have  three  core  arguments,  a  subject  and  two  objects.  The 
verbal  O  sutTix  refers  to  the  recipient,  which  is  prototypically  animate,  while  an  object  NP 
typically  refers  to  a  theme  which  may  or  may  not  be  animate  (cf  §3.3.3).  The  O  suffixes 
have  the  same  fomi  as  O  suffixes  which  occur  with  transitive  verbs.  For  example: 
(4.28)  Koia  te  -neka  -i  =mo. 
sweet  potato  give  -03p  -Is  =BM 
T gave  them  sweet  potato.'  T2.32.8 
The  ditransitive  veAs  meaning  'give'  and  'tell,  speak  to'  have  suppletive  forms  according 
to the  number  and  person  of  the  recipient:  si  'give  (to  first  person)'  and  tu/te  'give  (to 
second  or  third  person)'  (cf  Rule  4c  in  §2.4.4),  sasi 'tell  (to  first  person,  second  person,  and 
third  person  plural)'  and  sau  'tell  3s'.  A  third  ditransitive  verb  is  wesii/wesi  'show'  (cf 
Rule  4b  in  §2.4.4). 
4.2.4  Ambitransitive  verbs 
Ambitransitive  verbs  are  verbs  which  can  occur  with  or  without  an  object,  and  therefore 
fianction in  either  intransitive  or  transitive  clauses  (cf  §3.3.4).  When  they  do  have  an  object 
they  can  occur  with  or  without  an  O  suffix  since  an  O  suffix  only  occurs  when  the  object 
has  an  animate  referent.  There  is  a  semantic  distinction  between  the  roles  of  objects  with 
these  verbs:  O  suffix  ambitransitive  verbs  take  beneficiaiy/maleficiary  or  goal  objects 
(§4.2.4.1)  and  no-O-suffix  ambitransitive  verbs  take  patient  objects  (§4.2.4.2). 
4.2.4.1  O-suffix  ambitransitive  verbs,  beneficiary/maleficiary  and  goal  objects

4.2.5  Alternating  transitive  verbs 
Altemating  transitive  verbs  have  agentive  or  agent  and  goal  subjects  and  a  theme  object. 
They  can  function  as  either  transitive  or  ditransitive  verbs.  When  there  are  two  objects  an 
O suffix  indicates  an  added  recipient/goal  or  a  beneficiary,  depending  on  the  semantic 
nature  of  the  verb. 
4.2.5.1  Alternating  transitive  verbs  with  agentive  subjects  and  recipient/goal  objects

indicated  by  an  O  suffix  on the  verb.  Compare  the  following  examples  with  one  object  and 
with  two  objects.

usually  used  since  the  instrument  can  be  distinguished  by  an  instrumental  postposition  (§7.4.2.2).

4.2.6  Experiencer  object  verbs 
Experiencer  object  verbs  are  like  transitive  verbs  in  that  they  have  an  object  and  subject 
suffix  (see  §3.3.4.4).  However,  while  there  is  an object  NP  in  the  clause  there  is  no NP 
which  is  clearly  identifiable  as  the  subject  and  the  subject  suffix  can only  cross-reference  a 
third person  singular  referent  (cf  chapter  11).  An  example  is: 
(4.39)  (I)  mesiri  -se  -r  -a. 
Is perspire  -Ols  -PRES  -3s 
'I am  perspiring.' 
4.2.7  Copula  and  quasi-copula  verbs 
Copula  and  quasi-copula  verbs  have  a  subject  argument  and  a  complement.  The 
intransitive  verb  mene  'be,  stay,  exist'  can  function  as a copula  verb  (cf  §3.3.4.8.1).  The 
complement,  a  qualifier,  quantifier  or interrogative,  describes  the  state  of the  subject.  The 
quasi-copular  verb  horn  'become'  (cf  §3.3.4.8.2)  occurs  with  a  complement  such  as  a 
second  NP,  an  adjective  or a temporal.  The  complement  describes  the  resuh  of  the  process 
described  by  the  verb. 
(4.40)  Pensoro  hane  horn  -r  -a. 
pencil  short  become  -PRES  -3s 
'The  pencil  is  becoming  short.' 
4.2.8  The  negative  copula  verb  ia  'be  not' 
The  negative  copula  verb  ia  'be  not'  occurs  with  a  subject  argument  and  a  complement  (see 
§3.3.4.8.3  for  more  detail).  It  occurs  either  as  an independent  verb  clause  finally  or as a

4.2.10  Phasal  and  valency  changing  verbs 
There  are  two  phasal  verbs  which  express  aspectual,  valency  or  lexical  meaning  depending

and/or  valency  decrease  (§10.2.6).  The  following  examples  contrast  the  use  oiuri  'float'

Payne  (1997)  states  that  copula  verbs  tend  to  be  irregular  but  have  some  of  the  "moiphosyntactic  properties 
that  characterize  verbs  in  that  language"  (1997:115)  whereas  invariant  particles  are  not  marked  for 
"person/number/gender  of  the  subject,  or  the  tense/aspect  of  the  clause"  {1997:117).

4.2.11  Manner  verbs 
The manner  verb  name  'do  well,  be  careful'  can  carry  verbal  suffixes  but it  always  occurs 
in a  manner  serial  verb  construction  where  it  modifies  the  main  verb,  either  as  the  final 
verb,  or  as  a  penultimate  verb  before  a final  phasal  or  phasal  and  valency-changing  verb 
(cf. §  10.2.8.3.2).  The  intransitive  verbs  kiri 'be  ftill/tight'  and  horoko  'be  awkward,  noisy' 
also fianction  as  manner  verbs  in  manner  serial  verb  constructions. 
4.2.12  Quantifier  verbs 
The numeral  quantifiers  aterei 'one',  aere  'two'  and  ii  'three',  as  well  as  mipii 'many',

inflected  as  verbs,  in  the  following  context  at  least.  Like  manner  verbs,  they  can  modify  a 
main  verb  in  a  modified  serial  verb  construction  (see  §  10.2.8.3.3).

4.2.13  Prohibitive  verb 
The prohibitive  verb  is  the  verb  apaise 'leave'.  It  is used  in  prohibitive  constructions  (see 
§10.2.8.4.) 
4.2.14  Derived  verbs  and  Id eliding  verbs 
A small  number  of  verbs  occur  with  a  final derivational  suffix  -ne. The  verb  epone 'follow 
(someone)'  is  derived  fi-om the  basic  temporal  adverb  epono 'later'  (cf.  §4.7.2.2).  The 
source  of  other  examples,  such  as  kesane 'cut:scythe  (a  task  done  by  women)',  ketane 
'break,  snap  (something)',  ketine  'split,  chop  (something)  through  the  middle  lengthways)', 
and korone  'sweep,  broom  (something)'  is  unknown.

4.2.15  Borrowed  verbs

4.2.16  Generic  verbs 
Generic  verbs  have  different  semantic  overtones  in  different  environments.  They  are 
common  in  many  Papuan  languages  (see  Foley  1986,  Pawley  In  press,  Aikhenvald  2009). 
For example,  the  verb  u 'do'  is  often  used  with  borrowed  words  (see  §4.2.15)  or  in  the 
expression  u-pii-r-ia  [do-HAB-PRES-lp]  'we  do  it  like  that',  h  can  also  occur  with  a  finite 
complement  where  it  means  'say'  or  'quote'  (cf  §4.2.5.1,  §  12.3.2). The  verb  te  'get'  can 
also function  as a phasal  verb  (cf  §4.2.9  and  §10.2.4.5).  And  the  verb  oni  can  occur  in 
experiencer  object  constructions  meaning  'feel  like,  want  to'  or  'hunger/thirst  for'  (cf 
§ 11.3.3.3).  Oru  can  also  be  used  to  mean  'care  about,  give  hospitality'  (Priestley  2002b). 
Other  verbs  which  can  be  considered  here  are  the  ambitransitive  verbs  ue 'consume:eat.

4.3 Nouns 
4.3.1 Introduction 
Nouns  have  a  referential  function  and like  personal,  indefinite  specific  and demonstrative 
pronouns,  they  can  be  the  sole  constituent  of  an NP  and  can  function  as its head  (cf.  chapter 
5, particularly  §5.10).  They  are  distinguished  from  the closed  class  of  pronouns  (cf  §4.5) 
since  they  are  not  obligatorily  marked  for  person  and  number.  They  can  be  replaced  by 
meni 'whatyamacallit'^^  and  they  can  occur  in one  or  more  of  the  following  contexts. 
• with  'possessor/part  of  person-number  suffixes/enclitics 
• with  the  o 'genitive'  postposition 
• with  the  enclitics  =ama  'group'  and  =rare 'and/with' 
• with  =te  'prominent  subject' 
• in  expanded  NPs 
• as  objects  of animate,  inanimate,  or  inherently  locative  postpositions 
• in  vocative  constructions 
The distributional  criteria  listed  above  are  important  in  distinguishing  nouns  fi-om other 
word classes  and  in determining  noun  subclasses.  Two  of  these  criteria  are  exemplified 
below. 
(4.47) Mutu  =te  epon  pi  -a  =m.

'Mutu  stood  later.'T  1.9.13

4.3.2  Common  nouns 
Common  nouns  can  occur  in  fully  expanded  NPs  (§5.2).  They  are  described  below  in 
sections  on  inanimate  nouns,  inanimate  part  nouns,  verbal  nouns,  the  noun  rame  'one 
person',  animate  nouns  and  nature  nouns. 
Some  of  the  basic  differences  between  common  nouns  are  summarised  in  Table  4.1  above. 
Inanimate  and  verbal  nouns  have  an  optional  possessor  suffix  or enclitic  (see  chapter  6), 
inanimate  part  nouns  have  an  obligatory  possessor  suffix,  and  animate  and  nature  nouns  do 
not have  suffixes  or enclitics.  Animate  nouns  can  be  the  object  of  the  ahare 'animate' 
postposition  while  other  common  nouns  are  the  object  of  the  pa 'goal/locative'  or  pate 
'source/locative'  postpositions  (see  Table  4.1  above,  and  chapter  7). 
4.3.2.1  Inanimate  nouns 
Inanimate  nouns  denote  inanimate  things  and  can  be  the  object  o^pa  type  inanimate 
referent  'locative'  postpositions  or  the  instrumental  postposition  te.  They  select  the 
interrogatives  mana  'what?'  and  ani  'where?'  and  most  of  them  can  occur  with  a  possessor 
enclitic.  Table  4.2  lists  examples  ofinanimate  nouns.

4.3.2.2  Inanimate  part  nouns 
Inanimate  part  nouns  have  an  obligatory  -ne  'third  person  singular'  final  possessor  suffix 
and occur  in  possessive  nominal  constructions  with  dependent  NPs.  They  refer  to parts  of 
plants,  fires,  artefacts  and  abstract  things.  Examples  are  sere-ne 'its  seeds'  and  kini-ne  'its 
roots'  (see  §6.4). 
4.3.2.3  Verbal  nouns 
4.3.2.3.1  Introduction 
A number  of  words  can  be  used  as  common  nouns  or  as  verbs.  When  they  occur  as 
arguments  of  a verb  and  head  of  an  NP  they  are  referred  to  as  verbal  nouns.  These  nouns 
have  inanimate  referents.  As  nouns  they  can  occur  as  a  head  noun  in  a  possessive  nominal 
construction  with  possessor  enclitics  (for  examples  see  §6.5.3.1.3  and  §6.5.3.1.4)  and  as 
verbs  they  can  occur  with  verbal  inflections  (see  chapters  10  and  11).  There  is  no 
morphology  to  derive  verbs  fi-om  these  nouns  or  vice  versa.  For  morphosyntactic  and 
semantic  reasons  three  subtypes  are  proposed:  experiential,  descriptive,  and  expressive 
verbal  nouns.

4.3.2.4  The  noun  rame  'one/person' 
The  noun  rame  'one/person'  usually  has  a  human  referent.^^  It  functions  as  the  head  of  a 
rame NP  (see  §5.2.4)  and  can  be  modified  by  a  demonstrative,  pre-head  nominal  or 
indefinite  specific  article.  Unlike  common  nouns,  it  cannot  be  modified  by  adjectives  or 
quantifiers. 
4.3.2.5  Animate  nouns 
4.3.2.5.1  Introduction 
Animate  nouns  denote  people  or  animals.  They  fijnction  as  head  of  an  expandable  NP  and 
can be  dependent  nouns  marked  by  the  genitive  postposition  o  in  possessive  constnactions. 
There  are  several  postpositional  constituents  which  occur  with  nouns  that  have  animate 
referents  i.e.  the  ahare  'animate  locative'  postposition  (§7.3.4),  the  enclitic  =ama  'group' 
(§5.2.3.4.4  and  §5.12.3.2)  and  the  enclitic  =rare  'and/with'  (§5.12.3.1).  Animate  nouns 
can occur  with  the  enclitic  =te  'prominent  subject'  since  it  is  associated  with  semantic 
agency  (see  §4.12,  §5.11  and  §  13.5), and  they  select  the  inteirogative  me  'who'  (§4.14.2). 
Human  and  animal  nouns  are  subcategories  of  animate  noun  that  are  distinguished  for 
morphological  and  semantic  reasons. 
4.3.2.5.2  Human  nouns 
Human  nouns  are  nouns  other  than  proper  nouns  which  denote  people.  In  possessive 
constructions  they  can  occur  with  a  genitive  postposition  o  to  indicate  a  possessor  but  they 
do not  occur  as  head  nouns  with  a  possessor  person  and  number  enclitic.  Instead  kinship 
nouns  with  possessor  enclidcs  indicate  human  relationships  (cf  §4.3.3.2  and  §6.5.3.3). 
In one  rather  unclear  example  in  the  data  rame  appears  to  refer  to  an  inanimate  referent.

4.3.2.5.3  Animal  nouns 
Animal  nouns  are  used  to  denote  living  creatures  such  as  animals,  birds,  fish,  and  so  on. 
Therefore  they  can  have  the  semantic  role  of  agent  and  can  be  the  possessor  in  possessive 
constructions.  Alternatively  these  nouns  denote  close  associates,  natural  resources  or  food 
of humans  and  thus  they  can  be  the  possessee  with  possessor  person-number  enclitics  in 
possessive  constructions.  When  these  nouns  refer  to  animals  as  food  they  function  as 
inanimate  rather  than  animate  nouns.

4.3.2.6  Nature  nouns 
Nature  nouns  refer  to  things  in  the  natural  environment  which  can  sometimes  have  an  effect 
on people,  animals  or  things.  They  are  like  common  nouns  since  they  can  occur  with  pa 
the  'inanimate  referent'  type  locative  postpositions  (see  §7.3.2  for  details).  However,  they 
are also  like  animate  and  proper  nouns  since  they  can  function  as  effector  and  can  be 
" Appendix  4  has  many  other  examples  of  animal  nouns.

4.3.3  Proper  nouns 
4.3.3.1  Introduction 
Proper  nouns  refer  to specific  people,  animals  or  spirit  beings  and  function  as heads  ofNPs. 
These  kinship  nouns  and  personal  names  (cf.  §5.3  and  §5.4)  do not  occur  in  expanded  NPs 
with  demonstratives,  adjectives,  quantifiers,  or the  indefinite  specific  article.  Like  animate 
nouns  (§4.3.2.5)  they  can  occur  with  the  ahare 'animate  locative'  postposition^"  and  the 
enclitics  =ama 'group',  =rare  'and/with'  and  =te  'prominent  subject'.  They  select  the 
interrogative  me  'who'  and  can  function  as vocatives.  The  two  subclasses  are  bound 
kinship  nouns  and  personal  names. 
4.3.3.2  Kinship  nouns 
Kinship  nouns  based  on  birth,  marriage  and  initiation  relationships  are  used  to  refer  to or 
address  people.  They  are  bound  nouns  which  must  be  inflected  by  possessor  person-
number  (see  §6.5.3.3)  or  vocative  suffixes  (see  §4.3.3.4  below).  They  can  occur  with  a 
reflexive/emphatic  suffix  -moron 'self  (see  §5.3).

4.3.3.3  Personal  names 
Personal  names  are  used  for  people  and  for  animals  closely  associated  with  people.  They 
are not  marked  by  a  person-number  suffix  or  enclitic  apart  from  when  they  occur  with  the 
first  person  singular  possessor  suffix  and  the  affectionate  address  suffix,  as in  Arikao-mai-e 
[Arikao-Pls-AFF]  'my  dear  Arikao'  (see  §4.3.3.4  below  and  §6.5.3.2).  Specific  personal 
names  and  special  titles  can  be  distinguished  for  semantic  reasons. 
4.3.3.3.1  Specific  personal  names 
People  can  have  several  specific  personal  names.  Examples  of  male  names  are  Kunimi, 
Awai, and  Si  and  of  female  names  are  Kokit, Ahe  and  Youime.  Some  names  are  used  for 
both  males  and  females,  for  example,  Kerapesi.  Names  for  dogs  include  Sinti  and  Smoki. 

[PDF PAGE 164]
Word  Classes  135 
Names  can  be  given  soon  after  birth  or  later  on  in  life.  They  can  be  based  on  common 
nouns,  other  people's  names  or  the  names  of  spirits  of  ancestors  or  special  places.  The 
latter  are  often  said  to  be  revealed  in  dreams.  Names  can  also  be  based  on  personal 
characteristics  or  shared  experiences.  People  can  give  their  own  or  their  child's  name  to  a 
baby  and  establish  a  lasting  namii  'namesake'  relationship  with  that  child.^^  The  term 
iiamii 'namesake'  is  a  title  (see  §4.3.3.3.2  below)  rather  than  a  kinship  noun. 
Specific  personal  names  based  on  common  nouns  include  Airehetia^'^ 'kunai  grass  woman', 
Nahehena 'mami  (yam)  woman',  and  the  male  name  On  'Yam'.  An  example  of  a  personal 
name  based  on  a  personal  characteristic  is  Tamase,  from  tama 'mouth'  which  was  used 
because  the  baby's  lower  lip  protruded."^® The  name  Wapi-rane^^  which  incorporates  the 
noun  wapi  'arm,  hand'  was  given  to  a  woman  after  she  broke  her  arm  and  it  set  badly. 
Affinal  and  initiation  relationships  entail  some  degree  of  respect  and,  in  some  cases, 
avoidance  behaviour  so  instead  of  specific  personal  names  kinship  nouns  (see  §4.3.3.2), 
loanwords,  teknonyms  and  nicknames  are  used. 
When  a  name  is  based  on  a  common  noun  and  it  is  necessary  to  avoid  using  it,  both  the 
common  noun  and  the  name  can  be  replaced  by  borrowing  a  common  noun  from  another 
language.  For  example,  tepere  is  used  instead  of  nahe 'mami  (yam  type)'  andyanu  instead 
of 'yam'.  Possibly  some  words  come  into  the  language  in  this  way  (Sairam  Tomas 
2004:  Text  7.4). 
In 1976  Ahe  named  a  baby  after  her  daughter  Kitume  and  provided  extra  care  to  her  both  before  and  after 
her parents  died.  Since  Ahe died  her  daughter  has  cared  ftjr  her  namesake  and  namesake's  children  and  they 
help  her  in  return. 
In this  section  personal  names  are  written  in  italics. 
A grandson  was  later  given  this  name.  At  school  it  has  been  anglicised  to  Thomas. 
The  final  part  of  the  name  Wapi-rane  is  possibly  based  on  rame  'one/person'.

Teknonyms,''^  such  as  Enipa-ne  'Eni('s)  father',  refer  to a  person  by  referring  to  someone 
else,  usually  the  eldest  child  or  a  child  which  is  present  at  the  time  of  speaking.'*^  They 
consist  of  both  a  personal  name  and  a  kinship  noun  and  are  distinct  from  descriptive 
possessive  NPs  (cf  §6.5.3.2)  because  the  genitive  suffix  is omitted  from  the  initial  noun. 
Teknonyms  fianction  as  personal  names.  They  can  be  substituted  for  a name  that  is  'taboo' 
to a  speaker,  because  of  the  relationship  between  the  participants,  or  for  a kinship  noun  that 
is potentially  ambiguous  because  it  could  refer  to several  different  people.

late 1980s  many  people  have  adopted  English  names.  This  appears  to  be  a  result  of 
influence  by  settlers  from  the  Sepik  area. 
4.3.3.3.2  Special  titles 
Special  titles  are  used  to  refer  to people  in  relationships  that  are  not  based  on  kinship,  for 
example,  awe  'child',  herari  'initiation  leader,  initiate  of  older  generation',  taniaite  arene 
'big  man'  and  reciprocal  terms  such  as  natmi  'namesake'  (see  above)  and  namuka  'female 
agemate  (to  female  ego)'. 
The  term  teknonym  is  based  on  the  Greek  word  teknon  'child'  (Harold  Koch  pers.com.).  Teknonyms  are 
often  associated  with  Austronesian  languages  (e.g.  Geertz  and  Geertz  1975)  but  they  are  al.so  Found  in  a 
number  of  Papuan  languages,  e.g.  Anamuxra  (Ingram  2001:68)  and  Barupu  (Corris  2005:98). 
43 By extension  a  man  can  be  referred  to  as  his  dog's  father,  Sintipa-ncmu [Sinti  father-P3s]  'Sinti's  father'.

4.3.3.4  Proper  nouns  in  vocative  constructions 
Proper  nouns  can  occur  in vocative  constructions  used  to  address,  exhort  or  capture  the 
attention  of  another  person.'*'' These  constructions  can  occur  in  isolation,  for  example  when 
the speaker  is  calling  for  someone,  or  before  a clause.  Following  the  vocative  there  is  a 
pause  before  any  further  speech.  Human  nouns  (cf  §4.3.2.5.2)  are  also  sometimes  used  as 
vocatives. 
Vocatives  are  referential  but  they  are  not  argument  NPs  or  predicates  of  nonverbal  clauses. 
There  is  no  cross-referencing  on  the  verb  and  the  nouns  do  not  occur  with  qualifiers, 
postpositions,  no  'link'  or  =te  'prominent  subject'.  The  noun  awe  or  aiiya, 'my  child/little 
one (younger  person  in  ego's  care)'  appears  to  function  solely  in a vocative  construction. 
The noun  is  either  unmarked  or  followed  by  the  address  suffix  -ya ,  the affectionate  address 
suffix  -e, or  the  exclamatory  enclitic  =o.  Intonation  on  the  final  syllable  can  be  falling  or 
rising.  The  unmarked  specific  personal  name  in  the  example  below  has  rising  intonation  on 
the final  syllable. 
(4.71)  Seia,  were  arene  we  -r  -a  =mo. 
Seia,  sun  big  act  -PRES  -3s  =BM 
"Seia,  the  sun  is  very  hot."  T6.8.15 
The  address  suffix  -ya is  used  to  attract  attention  or  express  irritation  or  humour.  It  can 
follow  a kinship  noun  or  a person-number  suffix,  as in  moto-ya\ [brother-AD]  'brother!' 
and moto-ma-ya  [brother-PIs-AD]  'my  brother'  (female  speaker  to  older  male  sibling). 
The affectionate  address  suffix  -e can  be  affixed  to the  noun,  for  example,  in  moto-e 'dear 
brother'  or  it can  follow  the  first  person  singular  person-number  suffix  as in moto-mai-e! 
[brother-Pis  AFF]  'my  dear  brother'. 
The  exclamatory  enclitic  =o  is used  to  exclaim  at,  exhort,  or  to call  to  someone,  as  in the 
example  below  (cf  §3.2.1.6).  The  enclitic  in  this  example  has  rising  intonation. 
Animals  can  also  be  referred  to  with  personal  names  and  addressed  with  vocatives.

danger  and  in  the  unmarked  form  when  the  speaker  is  close  to  hand  and  has  been  the 
addressee  earlier  in  the  discourse.  In  the  recording  there  is  rising  intonation  on  the  final 
syllable  of  the  first  two  examples  while  in  the  final  example  the  intonation  simply  falls 
from  high  on  the  first  syllable  to  low  on  the  second.

4.3.4  Placenames 
Placenames  are  unique  names  of  settlements,  villages,  land,  gardens,  rivers  and  distant 
towns.  They  can  occur  as  required  arguments  of  motion  or  posture-taking  verbs  (cf  §3.5.2 
and §5.5).  There  are  three  types  of  placename:  local  placenames  which  occur  with  sa  type 
postpositions  (cf  §4.3.4.1),  river/distant  placenames  which  occur  with  pa  type 
postpositions  (or  no  postposition)  (§4.3.4.2,  and  placenames  with  an  incorporated  pa  ov  sa 
type  postposition  (cf  §4.3.4.3). 

[PDF PAGE 168]
Word  Classes  139 
4.3.4.1  Local  placenames  and  sa  type  postpositions 
Placenames  which  refer  to settlements  or  land  within  the  Koromu  or  nearby  language  areas 
can occur  as  object  of  the  postpositions  sa  'near:  goal/locative'  or  sate 'near: 
source/locative',  for  example,  Imari, Kesawai,  Korike,  Mauskare,  Sisari,  Sotoko  and 
Wetake, as  in  the  following  example. 
(4.76)  ...Sotoko  sa  erne  a  te  -pe  n-e-te,... 
Sotoko  G/L  land  come  get  -LTD:3p 
'...they  came  and  got  land  at  Sotoko...'  T5.23.4 
Sa 'near:goal/locative'  rarely  occurs  as  a  separate  postposition  with  river  names  but  it  can 
occur  in  the  expression  ya Kohu  sa  [river  Kohu  N:G/L]  'at  the  River  Kohu'  in  which  I 
propose  that  Ya  Kohu is  a  placename. 
4.3.4.2  River/distant  placenames  and  pa postpositions 
Placenames  of  local  rivers  and  distant  places  can  occur  with  the  inanimate  referent 
postpositions  pa 'goal/locative'  and  pate 'source/inessive'.  Enae,  the  local  name  for  the 
Ramu  River  and  Pakaia,  the  river  near  Kesawai 2,  are  examples  of  river  names  while 
Hemsisi, Kaiapit,  Mandan/Madan  (Madang),  Sosi/Saiisi,  Wataraisi,  Lae  and  Kainantu  are 
examples  of  distant  placenames. 
In the  first  clause  of  the  following  example  the  distant  placename  is  an  argument  of  a 
motion  verb.  In  the  second  clause  it  is the  object  of  the  postposition  pate 'source/inessive'. 
(4.77)  Sosi  yare  -pe  Sosipate  were  -i  =mo.  Warike  n  -a. 
Sosi  go  -SRSosiS/L  see  -Is  =BM  bad  STAY  -3s 
'I went  to  Sosi  and  in  Sosi  I  looked.  It  was  bad...'  T6.5.34 
The  following  example  shows  that  with  a  distant  placename  the  speaker  can  use  or  omit  the 
postposition/7a  'goal/locative'.

4.3.4.3  Placenames  with  incorporated  postpositions 
Some  placenames  of  rivers,  settlements  and  gardens  always  include  suffixed  pa 
'goal/locative'  or  sa 'near:goal/locative'.  Incorporated  sa  is  most  common  with  river 
names,  for  example,  Meansa,  Peretepesu  and  Sahosa  but  it  does  occur  in  the  names  of 
some  villages,  for  example  Weisa.  Many  placenames  incoiporatepa,  for  example  Eiorapa, 
Autopa, Karepupa,  Saspikipa,  Mantapa,  and  Otopa.  These  placenames  are  often  based  on 
common  nouns  which  indicate  a  feature  of  the  local  environment,  for  example  Waimeripa 
from  waimeri  grass  and  Kesaoyapa  from  kesao  'crayfish'  andj'a  'water'.  The  latter 
combines  a  pre-nominal  modifier  and  a  head  noun  with  the  postposition  pa (see  §5.2.2.2.2). 
Some  placenames  in  neighbouring  languages  also  include  pa, for  example  Saipa,  Keteiipa, 
Koropa. Placenames  with  incorporated  postpositions  never  occur  with  a  separate 
postposition.  For  example,  the  locative  goal  object  below.

example  shows  placenames  with  incorporated  sa  'near:goal/locative',  incoiporated  sate 
'near:source'  and  separate  postpositions. 
(4.80)  ...nene  no,  Peretepesa  mi  -pe

4.3.5  Temporal  nouns 
4.3.5.1  Introduction 
Temporal  nouns  are  a small  class  of  words  which  can  function  as  temporal  adverbs  (cf 
§4.7.2),  but  can  also  occur  as  objects  of  postpositions  (cf  §7.3.2.2)  and  complements  of 
quasi-copula  clauses  (cf  §3.3.4.8.2). 
4.3.5.2  General  temporal  nouns 
The  term  general  temporal  noun  (cf  §5.6)  is  used  to  refer  to nouns  such  as  sa 'time'  (cf 
§4.3.2.1),/)/  'time  (frequency)',  oto 'day',  asi  'month'  and  atotuhiinpa  'sometimes'. 
4.3.5.3  Part-of-day  nouns 
Part-of-day  nouns  refer  to specific  times  throughout  the  day.  These  times  are  based  on  the 
position  or  absence  of  the  sun. 
somoto 'morning,  from  sunrise  until  about  11  am  when  the  sun  is 
ascending' 
somont 'night,  the  time  when  the  sun  is  not  visible' 
wesekere 'middle  of  the  day,  from  about  11  am  until  2  pm  when  the  sun  is 
at its  greatest  height' 
arisapit 'afternoon,  from  about  2  pm  until  sunset  when  the  sun  is 
descending' 
Like  other  nouns  somoto 'morning',  somoni  'night'  and  wesekere  'midday'  can  be  the  O  of 
a postposition.  When  somoto  'morning'  occurs  with  pate 'source,  inessive'  an  early  time  is 
indicated. 

[PDF PAGE 171]
142 Chapter  4 
(4.81)  Somoto  pate  Kuaisa  top  -i. 
morningS/L  Kuaisa  climb  -Is 
'(Early)  in  the  moming  I  climbed  Kuaisa.'  T6.5.1 
A part-of-day  tenn  can  also  be  a  complement  in  a  quasi-copula  clause  (§3.3.4.8.2). 
(4.82)  ...arisapu  horn  -pit  -r  -a  no,... 
afternoon  become  -HAB  -PRES  -3s  GRD 
'...when  it  becomes  afternoon,...'  T  1.33.8 
4.4 Qualifiers 
Adjectives  (§4.4.1),  quantifiers  (§4.4.2)  and  the  indefinite  specific  article  (§4.4.3)  are  all 
qualifiers  which  occur  in  post-nominal  position  (see  also  §5.2.3).  Qualifiers  can  also  be  the 
sole  constituent  in  an  NP.  Adjectives  and  quantifiers  can  occur  in  headless  NPs  when  the 
referent  of  the  head  noun  is  recoverable  from  the  cultural,  real  world  or  discourse  context 
(cf  §5.2.5)  and  the  indefinite  specific  article  functions  as  the  indefinite  specific  pronoun  in 
some  contexts  (§4.4.3). 
4.4.1  Adjectives 
4.4.1.1  Introduction 
Simple  (non-derived)  and  derived  adjectives  function  as  post-nominal  modifiers  (§5.2.3) 
and can  also  be  the  sole  constituent  in  headless  NPs  (cf  §5.2.5).  They  can  also  function  as 
attributive  predicates  (§3.4.2.3)  or  as  complements  in  quasi-copular  clauses  (§3.3.4.8.2). 
An adjective  may  head  an  adjective  phrase  (§5.2.3.4)  which  consists  of  an  adjective  plus  an 
intensifier  (cf  §4.7.7).  These  possibilities  are  shown  below. 
(4.83)  Weti  arenepaya-r-u.  [house  big  G/L  go-PRES-3s]  'He  went  to  the  big  house.' 
Arene ku-r-a.  [big  come-PRES-3s]  'The  big  (one)  is  coming.' 
Muruni arene.  [lizard  (type.ol)  big]  '/V/a/7//7/are  big.' 
Arene hont-r-a.  [big  become-PRES-3s]  'It  is  becoming  big.' 

[PDF PAGE 172]
Word  Classes  143 
(4.84)  arene  herekani  [big  really]  'really  big'  (cf.  §5.2.3.2). 
Greater  scalar  proportion  can  also  be  indicated  by  lengthening  the  first  stressed  syllable  of 
dimension  adjectives. 
(4.85)  ....ya  ar^e/i^  w/-pe...[rain  big  move.down-SR]'...a  big  rain  fell...'  T5.24.14 
4.4.1.2  Simple  adjectives 
Simple  adjectives  describe  dimension,  age,  value,  visual  properties  (including  colour), 
physical  properties,  human  propensity,  position  and  similarity."^^ By  visual  properties  I 
mean  things  we  can  see  (cf  Wierzbicka  1996,  2004)  such  as  hue,  brightness,  saturation  , 
luster,  pronouncedness  and  other  characteristics  (cf  van  Brakel  1993:113  and  Beck  1972). 
Some  of  the  adjectives  in the  table  below,  for  example,  tesiini,  iimti  and  unman,  are 
glossed  with  English  colour  terms  for  convenience,  but  other  characteristics  which  are 
roughly  glossed  as  'dark',  are  an  important  part  of  their  meaning.  Furthermore,  in  response 
to translated  questions  about  'colour',  the  visual  propertyparere  'pattemed'  is  frequently 
emphasised  more  than  colour. 
Simple  adjectives  occur  immediately  following  a noun  (see  §5.2.3.1)  or  in  the  predicate  of 
an attributive  clause  (see  §3.4.2.3).  Compare  nokono  'good'  as  an  adjective  (below),  with 
riokono 'goodness'  the  noun  in  §4.3.2.1. 
(4.86)  ...wene  nokono  aire  -r  -a  =mo. 
food  good  come.up-PRES  -3s  =BM 
'...good  food  is  coming  up  (growing).'  T5.23 
Examples  of  simple  adjectives  are  given  in  Table  4.11.  Corresponding  nouns  with  the  same 
form  are  indicated  in  square  brackets. 
Dixon  proposes  four  core  semantic  types  of  adjectives:  dimension,  age,  value,  colour  (2004:4).  Some  of 
Dixon's  peripheral  types  are  also  adjectives  in  Koromu.

4.4.1.5  The  comparative  suffix  -ma

4.4.2  Quantifiers 
4.4.2.1  Introduction 
Quantifiers  indicate  the  number  of  referents  represented  by  an  NP.  Nouns  themselves  only 
express  general  number.  Therefore  when  they  are  not  modified  by  a  quantifier  they  may 

[PDF PAGE 178]
Word Classes  149 
refer  to one  or  more  items.^'  Quantifiers  follow  the  noun  or,  in  an  expanded  NP,  they 
follow  an  adjective.  There  are  three  types:  indeterminate  quantifiers,  numerals  and  the 
enclitic  ama  'group'. 
4.4.2.2  General  quantifiers 
General  quantifiers  describe  quantities  in  general  terms. 
asao/asa/atsao 'some  (some  others)'  [also  'part'] 
niipu 'many,  much,  all' 
pisi 'all  (used  to  refer  to women)' 
werai 'a  few,  a little'  [also  'a  short  time'] 
Werai 'a  little,  a  few'  can  be  reduced  to  rai to  indicate  'very  few'.  Niipii  'many'  can  be 
reduplicated  to  express  greater  quantity  or  the  first  (stressed)  syllable  can  be  lengthened  (cf 
§4.4.1.1  and  greater  scalar  proportion  is  expressed  by  lengthening  the  first  stressed  syllable 
in dimension  adjectives).  Also  wera  'child'  can  be  modified  by  kiri 'many'  or  kirikiri 
'many,  many'  and  the  suffix  -saine/seine 'many/all'  can  occur  with  nouns  such  as  hena 
'woman',  tamaite  'man',  na  'thing'  and  asi  'moon' 
(4.94)  Tamaite  nuupu  yar-e.  [man  many  many  go  STAY-3p]  'Many,  many  men  went.' 
A less  common  way  of  describing  greater  quantity  is  reduplication  of  nouns,  for  example 
asi asi  'many  months'  (T6.3.12). 
4.4.2.3  Numerals 
Numerals  express  exact  number.  Like  indeterminate  quantifiers  they  can  modify  nouns  but 
they  can  also  be  head  of  a numeral  phrase,  or  a modifier  in a temporal  (fi'equency)  NP (see 
§5.6).  Three  numerals  form  the  basic  counting  system. 
aterei 'one' 
acre 'two' 
Number  is  marked  by  subject  and  object  suffixes  on the  verb  which  cross-reference  nominal  arguments.

4.5 Pronouns 
4.5.1  Introduction 
Free  pronouns  and  genitive  pronouns  are  closed  word  classes  which  have  referential 
function  and  explicitly  specify  person  and  number.  Person  and  number  are  also  expressed 
by three  sets  of  bound  forms:  verbal  subject  suffixes,  verbal  object  suffixes  and  nominal 
person-number  suffixes/enclitics.  These  bound  forms  are  also  listed  here  for  comparision 
with the  fi-ee forms.  There  is  a  basic  distinction  between  singular  and  plural  in  all  these 
pronominal  forms.  Demonstratives  can  also  fijnction  as  pronouns  (see  §4.14.1). 
When  the  tables  in  the  following  sections  are  compared  it  is  evident  that  most  person-
number  forms  (except  some  first-person  singular  fornis)  have  similar  initial  consonants, 
while  verbal  subject  suffixes  (which  also  indicate  tense)  begin  with  a  vowel  or  with  /;. 
4.5.2  Personal  pronouns 
Personal  pronouns  can  occur  as  the  head  of  an  NP  (cf  §5.7).  They  function  as  core 
arguments  (and  can  occur  with  the  animate  referent  associative  enclitic  =rare  'and/with'  or 
=te 'prominent  subject').  They  can  occur  as  the  object  of  the  ahare 'animate  locative' 
postposition  and  they  select  the  interrogative  me  'who'.  Personal  pronouns  can  also  be 
qualified  by  quantifiers  (§4.4.2  and  §5.7)  and  can  occur  with  a  limiter  -nam  'alone'  or  the 
refiexive/emphatic  suffix  -moron '-self  (see  §5.7). 
The three  categories  ofperson:  first,  second  and  third,  and  two  categories  of  number: 
singular  and  plural  (non-singular),  are  outlined  in  the  table  below.

4.7 Adverbs 
4.7.1  Introduction 
Adverbs  are  modifiers  of  verbs,  clauses  or  adjectives.  They  generally  occur  before  verbs 
and clauses  and  after  adjectives.  The  number  of  adverbs  in  a  clause  is  kept  to  a  minimum 
but there  can  be  more  than  one  (cf  §3.5.3).  Some  of  them  can  modify  more  than  one  type 
of constituent.  A  number  of  semantic  subtypes  are  distinguished:  temporals,  locatives, 
manner  adverbs,  the  'only'  adverbs  {aisapii,  itini  and  miririi),  sentential  adverbs  and 
intensifiers. 

[PDF PAGE 187]
158 Chapter  4 
4.7.2  Temporals 
4.7.2.1  Introduction 
Temporals  describe  the  temporal  setting  of  an event.  They  function  as  clausal  adjuncts  and 
usually  occur  in  clause-initial  position  or  immediately  following  the  subject  NP.  Like 
nouns  they  can  also  be  marked  by  no  'ground'  as  a  'link'  or  'topic-like  element'  (see 
§14.3.2.4).  Based  on  differences  in distribution  there  are  two  subclasses:  basic  temporals 
(§4.7.2.2)  and  day  counters  (§4.7.2.3). 
Temporal  settings  are  also  expressed  by  nouns  such  as  sa 'time',  asi  'month'  and  somuni 
'night'  (§4.3.5),  noun  phrases  with  post-head  nominals  (cf  §5.2.3.3),  temporal 
postpositional  phrases  (§7.3.2.3),  temporal  link  expressions  (§  14.3.2.4),  and  the 
interrogative  enapii  'when?'(§4.14.2). 
4.7.2.2  Basic  temporals 
Basic  temporals  describe  time  in  general  terms. 
siinimapa/sumiirapa^^ 'before  now/long  ago' 
apii 'now' 
epoiio^^ 'later,  after' 
4.7.2.3  Day  counters 
Day counters  indicate  a  specific  day  on  which  an  event  occurred.  The  day  is  relative  to  the 
time  of  speaking.  Day  counters  can  occur  alone  or  as  the  first  constituent  in  a  temporal  NP, 
cf (§5.6). 
apii 'today'  (cf  use  as  general  use  as  'now')

arahii 'day  before  yesterday  and  days  before  that  up  to  a  week  or  two'

4.7.3  Locatives 
4.7.3.1  Introduction 
Locatives  describe  the  location  or  goal  of  an  action,  event  or  object.  In  verbal  clauses  they 
often  occur  as  oblique  arguments  before  the  verb.  They  can  also  display  nominal  behaviour 
as arguments  of  motion  and  posture  verbs.  In  nonverbal  clauses  locatives  can  be  the 
predicate  (§3.4.2.5)  or  they  can  be  optional  oblique  arguments,  clause  initially  (see  §3.5.3). 
Locatives  select  the  interrogatives  ani  'where',  anisa/ansa  'which  place/side'  and  anisate 
'fi-om  which  place/side'.  There  are  three  subtypes,  directional,  relational  and  general 
locatives  and  a  locative  complex  combines  directional  and  general  locatives. 
4.7.3.2  Directional  locatives 
Directional  locatives  indicate  directions  based  on  elevation  and  the  dominant  watercourses 
in the  environment  (see  chapter  8  for  more  detail).  Since  they  can  occur  as  the  object  of  a 
postposition  they  are  more  noun-like  than  other  locatives. 
aroho 'down  there/place  (down  river,  valley,  hill)' 
yoroho 'up  there/place  (up  river,  valley,  hill)' 
The  demonstratives  can  also  fianction  as  directional  locatives  and  while  mo  'this'  and  u 
'that'  cannot  occur  in  the  final  predicate  position  of  a  nonverbal  clause  eno  'over 
there/across  there  (across  a  river,  valley,  mountain,  road)'  can  (cf  §3.4.2.4). 
4.7.3.3  Relational  locatives 
Relational  locatives  describe  location  in  relation  to  something  else.  They  incoiporate  the 
postposition  sa  'neargoal/locative'  (cf  §4.8,  §7.3.3.2  and  §8.5.3).  Relational  locatives  can 
also  occur  in  complex  constructions  with  ahare  'animate  locative'  when  it  functions  as  a 
possessor  postposition  (see  §7.3.5).  There  are  three  subtypes  based  on  intrinsic,  directional 
and deictic  locations.

4.7.5  Aisapu,  itini  and  mirini,  the  'only'  adverbs 
The  adverbs  aisapu,  itini  and  mirini  have  similar  meanings  and  could  all  be  glossed  by

occur  before  the  verb  or  before  the  whole  clause. 
aisapu/aisoapu 'just,  merely,  simply,  only'  modifies  a  verb  or  a  clause 
tini/itini 'only,  truly'  modifies  a  verb  or  adjective

4.7.6  Sentential  adverbials 
Sentential  adverbs  usually  have  scope  over  the  whole  clause  which  follows  them.  Owing  to

si 'then,  so  then'  linking  adverbial 
nauto 'only  then'  linking  adverbial  (this  word  can  also  modify  an

pari 'again,  then,  eventually'  circumstandal  adverbial

4.8 Postpositions 
Postpositions  (cf.  chapter  7)  are subdivided  into  two  semantic  subclasses,  locative  and  non-
locative.  Nominals  and  demonstratives  and  locatives  which  are  nominal  in  character  can  be 
the object  of  these  postpositions.  In  addition,  the  postposition  sei  'orientation'  can  occur 
with  an  orientation  adverbial  clause  (see  §  12.6).

4.9 The  negative  particle  tai 
The  negative  particle  tai  'not'  precedes  and  negates  a  verb  (§3.3.5). 
4.10  Clause  final  modality  particles  and  enclitics 
The  epistemic  modality  particles  listed  below,  the  emphatic  particle  ne  (§3.2.2),  as  well  as 
the  =mo  'boundary  marking  enclitic'  (cf.  §3.2.1.2),  the  =e  question  enclitic  (Q)  (cf. 
§3.2.1.3)  and  the  =o  exclamatory  enclitic  (cf.  §3.2.1.6)  are  clausal  operators.  They  appear 
optionally  in  clause  final  position  where  they  have  scope  over  the  preceding  clause  and,  in 
some  contexts,  over  a  series  of  clauses,  (§9.4.2,  Priestley  2002:99-102).  The  three 
epistemic  modality  particles  are: 
puimo 'apprehensional'  (APP)  'might  (negative)' 
taiimo/taiio 'uncertainty'  (UNC)  'perhaps,  maybe' 

[PDF PAGE 200]
Word  Classes  171 
teimo/te 'possibility'  (POS)  'could' 
The  enclitic  =e  'question'  is  used  to  indicate  a  polar  interrogative,  while  the  final  boundary 
marking  enclitic  =mo  is  optional  in  declarative  and  exclamative  clauses  (see  §3.2.1.2). 
4.11 Conjunctions 
Conjunctions  which  conjoin  clauses  are  described  in  §  12.7 and  §  12.8. 
iimo 'but'  adversative  conjunction 
te/temo 'or'  disjunctive  conjunction,  follows  both  clauses  (cf.  modality 
particles) 
Listing  enclitics  can  follow  each  NP  in  a  list  of  items  (see  §5.12.3). 
=rare 'and/with'  conjoins  two  subject  NPs  with  animate  referents 
=ama 'group'  conjoins  two  or  more  proper  nouns  in  O  or  S  position 
4.12  The  'ground'  and  'prominent  subject'  particles/enclitics 
The  particle  uo  'ground'  and  the  enclitic  =te  'prominent  subject'  convey  information  about 
both  grammar  and  information  structure. 
The  particle  uo  'ground'  indicates  that  NPs,  temporals,  postpositional  phrases,  linking 
adverbials,  demonstratives,  and  clauses  are  background  material.  These  constituents 
combined  with  uo  'ground'  are  particularly  common  as  topic-like  elements  at  the  beginning 
of clauses  (see  §  14.2). Also  when  uo  'ground'  follows  a clause  it  indicates  that  the  clause 
is subordinate  to  a  main  clause,  for  example,  with  'when/given  that'  adverbial  clauses  and 
hypothetical  and  counterfactual  conditional  clauses  (§  14.3.3). 
The  enclitic  =te  'prominent  subject'  occurs  with  agentive  (or  effective)  subject  NPs  to 
disambiguate  A  and  O,  and  with  subject  NPs  and  some  predicate  NPs  (in  nonverbal 
clauses)  to  indicate  discourse  prominence  (see  §5.11  and  §  13.5). 

[PDF PAGE 201]
172 Chapter  4 
4.13  Interjections 
Interjections  express  emotions,  responses  and  greetings.  They  occur  in  a  distinct  intonation 
group  and  comprise  a  complete  utterance. 
Aiel 'Oh  no!' 
A/ef 'Poor  you!' 
Ese! 'That's  it,  that's  right!' 
la! 'No'  or  '(It)  is  not!'  (cf.  §3.3.4.8.3) 
Kiie! 'All  right!' 
O/Oo! 'Yes'  or  'Exclamation' 
Wao! 'Sorry!'  Said  when  someone  else  suffers  a sudden  misfortune.  The 
speaker  was  not  necessarily  the  cause  of  the  problem.  In  recent  years  wao 
has also  been  adopted  as  a  greeting  which  is  often  used  by  people  from 
neighbouring  language  groups  or  by  travelers  on  the  road. 
4.14 Semantically  defined  cross-cutting  classifications 
Demonstratives  and  interrogatives  are  semantically  defined  classes  of  words  which  occur  in 
a number  of  different  syntactic  classes.  They  are  discussed  in  the  sections  below. 
4.14.1  Demonstratives 
The  demonstratives  mo  'this/here',  u  'that/there'  and  eno  'that  over  there/over  there'  can 
function  as  demonstrative  pronouns  in  the  argument  positions  of  verbs  and  as  the  subject  of 
nonverbal  clauses  (cf  §5.8.1),  as  objects  of  postpositions  (see  §7.2),  as  pre-nominal 
modifiers  (cf  §5.2.2.1),  and  as  locative  adverbs  which  precede  and  modify  verbs  (cf 
§4.7.3.2).  Table  4.22  provides  examples  of  their  distribution.^''* 
Diessel  (1999:1)  proposed  four  syntactic  contexts  for  demonstratives:  pronouns  in  'the  argument  position  of 
verbs  and  adpositions',  determiners  'with  a  noun  in  a  noun  phrase',  adverbs  'as  verb  modifiers'  and  identifiers 
'in copuiar  and  nonverbal  clauses'.  In  Koromu  demonstratives  with  the  same  form  are  used  tor  each  of  these 
syntactic  contexts.

4.14.2  Interrogatives 
Interrogatives  are  a  small,  closed  class  of  words  which  are  used  to  ask  content  questions. 
Since  they  correspond  to  particular  word  classes  they  vary  as  to  whether  they  Rmction  as 
core  (cf  §3.3.2.1)  or  oblique  (cf  §3.5)  arguments.  Interrogatives  cannot  form  expanded 
NPs.

Chapter  5  Noun  Phrases 
5.1 Introduction 
This  chapter  examines  noun  phrases  (NPs).  The  following  sections  distinguish  common 
NPs  (§5.2),  kinship  NPs  (§5.3),  personal  name  NPs  (§5.4),  placename  NPs  (§5.5),  temporal 
NPs  (§5.6),  personal  pronoun  NPs  (§5.7),  pronominal  NPs  (§5.8)  and  nominalisation  NPs 
(§5.9).  Functions  of  NPs  (§5.10),  the  =te  'prominent  subject'  enclitic  (§5.11)  listed  NPs 
(§5.12)  and  appositive  NPs  (§5.13)  are  also  described. 
5.2 Common  noun  phrases 
5.2.1  Introduction 
This  section  examines  the  basic  type  of  common  NP  as  well  as  its  subtypes,  rame  NPs  and 
headless  NPs.  A  common  NP  has  a  common  noun  (cf.  §4.3.2)  as  the  head  noun  and 
optional  pre-head  and  post-head  modifying  constituents.  Pre-nominally,  demonstratives 
and possessors  are  optional  and  mutually  exclusive.  In  addition,  the  position  immediately 
prior  to  the  noun  can  be  filled  by  an  optional  pre-head  nominal.  The  position  immediately 
after  the  noun  can  be  filled  by  one  or  more  adjectives,  a post-head  nominal  or  an  adjective 
phrase.  A  subsequent  quantifier  or  indefinite  specific  article  is  also  optional.  The  basic 
structure  of  a common  NP  is  oudined  below. 
(Dem)  (Pre-head)  Head  N  (ADJ")  (Quantifier  ) 
(Possessor)  (Post-head)  (Indefinite  Specific  Article) 
(ADJ.P) 

[PDF PAGE 207]
178 Chapters 
Relative  clauses  can  occur  in  the  pre-head  slot.  Some  types  of  relative  clause  can  occur  in 
one of  the  adjective  positions  if  there  is  another  constituent  pre-nominally  (see  §  12.4 and 
§ 12.5 for  detailed  descriptions).  Demonstratives  can  occur  in  the  final  position  of  an NP 
following  post-nominal  relative  clauses  which  have  the  relative  pronoun  itne  (§  12.4.2.2). 
Some  possessors,  adjectives  or  quantifiers  can  occur  as  the  sole  constituent  in  a  headless 
NP (see  §5.2.5).  The  demonstratives  and  indefinite  specific  articles  can  also  function  as 
heads  ofpronominal  NPs  (see  §5.8).  Possessors  are  described  in  chapter  7. 
Common  NPs  are  headed  by  common  nouns.  The  examples  in  (5.1)  and  (5.2)  represent 
subject  and  object  arguments  respectively  and  occur  without  modifying  constituents.

5.2.2.2  Pre-head  nominals 
5.2.2.2.1  Introduction 
Common  nouns,  placenames,  NPs,  temporal  adjectives  and  nominalisations  with  the  suffix 
-apii can  occur  as  pre-head  nominals.  Both  the  pre-head  nominal  and  the  head  noun  have 
word  stress.  The  pre-head  nominal  specifies  a property  or  characteristic  of  the  referent  of 
the head  noun  (cf  Kratochvil  2007:149  on  Abui). 
5.2.2.2.2  Common  nouns  as  pre-head  nominals 
Common  nouns  (cf  §4.3.2)  which  occur  as  pre-head  nominals  act  to  restrict  the  category 
denoted  by  the  head  noun.  For  example,  they  can  indicate  the  substance  of  which  a  referent 
is made  or  the  flinction  it  perfonns. 
In the  examples  below  the  dominant  material  or  substance  of  the  entity  represented  by  the 
head  noun  on  the  right  is  indicated  by  the  common  noun  which  is  a pre-head  nominal.

5.2.3  Post-nominal  modifiers 
Qualifiers  (adjectives,  quantifiers,  the  indefinite  specific  article,  see  §4.4),  post-head 
nominals,  adjective  phrases  and  relative  clauses  can  function  as post-nominal  modifiers. 
5.2.3.1  Adjectives 
Adjectives  (cf  §4.4.1)  optionally  follow  and  modify  head  nouns  (5.39). 
(5.39)  Apati  putun  -au  =te  oro  ta  -e  =mo. 
weapon  explode-ADJ  =PS  shoot  END  -3p  =BM 
'They  shot  him  with  a  gun (lit.  an exploding  weapon).'  T5.23.52 
Adjectives  can  also  occur  as  predicates  in  nonverbal  clauses  (see  §3.4.3.2)  and  vowel 
lengthening  and/or  pailial  reduplication  is  used  to  indicate  greater  scalar  proportion  of 
simple  adjectives  which  describe  dimension  (see  §4.4.1). 
5.2.3.2  Adjective  phrases 
Adjective  phrases  follow  and  modify  head  nouns.  They  consist  of  an adjective  followed  by 
an intensifier,  such  as  herekaiii 'really',  sekau 'extremely',  itini  'really,  truly'  or  arenepate 
'extremely'.  For  example,orohoi  sekau  'extremely  long  neck'  (see  §4.7.6),  and  the 
example  in  squai'e  brackets  in  (5.40).
