5.2.3.3  Post-head  nominals 
A small  number  of  nouns  can  occupy  the  post-head  adjective  position,  where  they  restrict 
the category  of  the  first  nominal  by  indicating  the  kind  of  thing'  it  represents.  Some  of 
these  post-head  nominals,  for  example,  the  sound  made  by  yerie koe-koe  in  (5.46),  months 
or seasons  (5.48)  and  tomto  'meat'  can  stand  alone  as  nouns.^ 
(5.41)  ...na  tomto  hei  -apesi. 
thing  meat  search.for  -DES 
'...(we)  want  to  search  for  game'  (lit.  for  thing  meat)'  T1.33.16 
These  nominal  constructions  contrast  with  constructions  that  have  pre-head  nominals 
(§5.2.2.2).  As  Croft  (2001:241-280)  points  out  in  his  cross-linguistic  discussion  ofheads 
there  are  no  straightforward  tests  to  determine  the  head.  He  suggests  that  the  semantic  head 
"is the  primary  information-bearing  unit,  that  is,  the  most  contentful  item  that  most  closely 
profiles  the  same  kind  of  thing  that  the  whole  constituent  profiles"  or  the  one  which  has  the 
narrowest  extension  from  that  (2001:259). 
Many  snake  and  bird  species  (cf  Appendix  3)  are  identified  by  a  head  noun  and  a  post-
head nominal  in  a  semantically  generic-specific  construction  (as  in  Australian  languages). 
(5.42)  naire  amiimii  'python  (lit.  snake  python)' 
naire wamte  'death  adder  (lit.  snake  adder)' 
(5.43)  yene  aripuhe  'owl  (lit.  bird  owl)' 
yenepororo 'egret  (lit.  bird  egret)' 
' Further  research  is  needed  to  determine  the  source  of  all  the  post-head  nominals.

5.2.3.4  Quantifiers 
Quantity  can  be  expressed  by  general  quantifiers  (§5.2.3.4.1),  numerals  (§5.2.3.4.2), 
reduplication  or  reduction  (§5.2.3.4.3)  and  with  the  enclitic  =ama  'group'  (§5.2.3.4.4). 
Quantifiers  are  optional  since  quantity  is  also  expressed  by  singular  and  plural  subject  and 
object  verbal  suffixes.  The  latter  represent  all  persons  except  third  person  singular  object. 
Further  research  is  needed  with  people  on  the  south  side  of  the  valley  who  speak  less  Tok  Pisin. 
^°Mutu or  mittumi  can  be  used  as  either  a  verb  or  a  noun  meaning  'heap'.  It  can  refer  to  a  small  hillock. 
Yakere can  be  used  as  a  verb  or  noun  meaning  'split'  or  'laugh/smile'.

NPs  (see  §5.7). 
5.2.3.4.3  Reduplication  and  reduction 
Nupu 'many,  all'  can  be  reduplicated  to  indicate  greater  quantity,  while  werai  'a  few,  little' 
can be  reduced  to  its  final  syllable  to  express  lesser  quantity  (cf  §4.4.2.2). 
The  adjective  is  partially  reduplicated  to  indicate  greater  intensity  and  quality  (cf.  §4.7.7).

5.2.3.4.4  The  enclitic  =ama  'group' 
A noun  followed  by  the  enclitic  =ama  indicates  that  there  is  a  groupof  animate  referents 
together  with  the  referent  of  the  head  noun  (cf  §4.4.2.4).  The  enclitic  can  occur  in  some 
common  NPs  or  with  modifiers  in  headless  NPs  that  refer  to  human  referents.  It  can  also 
occur  in  proper,  kinship  and  numeral  NPs  but  it  does  not  occur  with  pronominal  and 
personal  pronoun  NPs.  The  following  example  occurs  in  a  common  NP. 
(5.55)  Wererip  o  arumu  -napa  =ama  mii  ka  -pe... 
Wererip  GEN  clan  -P3p  =group  sing  come  -SR 
' Wererip's  family  and  the  group  came  singing....'  T1.18.2 
An enclitic  of  the  same  form  is  used  to  indicate  items  in  a  list  (see  §5.12.3.2). 
5.2.3.5  Indefinite  specific  article 
The  indefinite  specific  article  ato  'a/one'  occurs  as  a  modifier  in  common  NPs  (cf  §4.4.3). 
It indicates  that  the  referent  is  a specific  objectively  referential  entity  which  is  indefinite 
and unidentifiable  for  the  hearer.'"'  Ato  'a/one'  follows  a  noun  in  a  subject  NP  in  (5.56),  an 
optional  adjective  in  an  object  NP  in  (5.57)  and  occurs  in  the  final  poshion  of  a  more  fully 
expanded  NP  in  (5.58). 
The  translation  for  =ama could  be  expressed  as  'mob',  as  in  Aboriginal  English. 
Du Bois  (1980:224)  states  that  "a  formally  indefinite  referential  mention  may  be  specific  or  non-specific. 
. ..although  the  hearer  is  not  able  to  identify  the  intended  referent,  the  speaker  at  least  has  a  specific  object  in 
mind."  An  entity  which  is  "objectively  referential"  is  an  "individuated  entity  in  the  message  world"  of  the 
speaker  (Payne  1997:263-264).

5.3 Kinship  NPs 
Kinship  NPs  consist  minimally  of  a bound  kinship  noun  (see  §4.3.3.2)  with  a  possessor 
suffix  (see  §6.5.3.3).  A  kinship  NP  can  function  as  a  core  argument  (5.71),  a  predicate  of  a 
nonverbal  clause  (cf  §3.4.2)  or,  like  other  NPs  with  human  referents,  as  an  object  of  the 
'animate  locative'  postposition  ahare  when  it  is  used  as  a  genitive  postposition  (cf  §7.3.5). 
(5.71)  ...ahi  -ma  =te  sasi  -s  -a.

'...my  mother  told  me.'  T5.3.5

5.7 Personal  Pronoun  NPs 
Personal  pronoun  NPs  have  a  personal  pronoun  (cf.  §4.5.2)  as  head,  as  in  (5.87)  below. 
They  are  distinct  from  pronominal  NPs  (cf.  §5.8)  because  the  personal  pronoun  indicates 
person  and  number.  Like  kinship  NPs,  personal  pronoun  NPs  can  include  the 
reflexive/emphatic  suffix  -moron 'self  and  like  common  NPs  they  can  include  quantifiers. 
The  limiter  suffix  -nam 'alone'  is  also  an  optional  constituent  of  personal  pronoun  NPs. 
A personal  pronoun  NP,  like  other  human  referent  NPs,  can  occur  as  a  core  argument 
(5.87),  a  predicate  of  a  nonverbal  clause  (cf  §3.4.2)  and  an  object  of  the  'animate  locative' 
postposition  ahare  when  it  is  used  as  a  genitive  postposition  (cf  §7.3.5).  However,  they 
cannot  occur  with  the  enclitic  =ama  'group'.

5.10 Functions  ofNPs 
The syntactic functions  that NPs can have  are: 
• subject  (5.91)  or object (5.96)  of a clause 
• predicate  of  a nonverbal  clause  (5.80) 
• complement  of  a negative  or quasi copula  clause  (5.82) 
• object  of  a postposition  (5.10) 
• a  locative argument  (5.79) 
• a  temporal  argument  (5.81) 
• a  pre-head nominal  (5.32) 
Table 5.1 indicates  the functions  of  common,  pronominal,  kinship,  personal  name, 
placename,  personal pronoun  and  nominalisations  NPs.  Other  nominals  and  headless  NPs 
vary as to how they function  syntactically  and are discussed in  the relevant sections  above.

An NP  has  a  syntactic  function  in  a  larger  construction.  This  mediates  semantic  and 
infonnation-sti-ucturing  flinctions.  Semantic  fianctions  specify  the  roles,  such  as  agent, 
patient,  and  benefactive  which  NP  referents  play  in  an  activity  or  state  of  affairs  (see  §3.3.3 
and chapter  10).  Infoirnation-stmcturing  functions  indicate  the  nature  of  the  information 
communicated.  They  take  into  account  the  participant's  worldview  and  current  knowledge, 
as well  as  spatial  and  temporal  perspectives  (see  chapters  13  and  14).  NPs,  like  temporals, 
locatives  and  clauses,  can  be  'ground'  (topic-like  or  tail  elements)  in  a  discourse  (see  (5.66) 
and chapter  13).

5.12  Listed  NPs 
Core  argument  NPs  can  be  grouped  together  in  a  list  and  cross-referenced  by  a  subject  or 
object  suffix  on the  verb.  An  intonation  juncture  follows  each  NP.  The  juxtaposition  of 
NPs  in  this  way  is  similar  to  asyndetic  coordination  (Haspelmath  2007:7).  Listed  NPs 
occur  in  a  simple  list,  in  a  list  with  a  final  consolidating  NP  ote/otepe  'all  (group)'  or  in  a 
list with  a  list  moipheme  following  each  item. 
5.12.1  Simple  listing 
NPs  which  have  either  inanimate  or  animate  referents  can  be  listed  as  follows. 
NP,NP,..." 
In the  example  below  a  list  of  NPs  with  inanimate  referents  are  cross-referenced  by  the 
object  suffix.^^ 
(5.106)  ...koia,  aiake,  ou  mo  pii  -pii  -r  -ia. 
sweet.potato  cassava  yam  here  plant  -HAB  -PRES  -Ip 
'...we  regularly  plant  sweet  potato,  cassava  and  yam  here.'  T  1.33.36 
Juxtaposed  NPs  with  human  referents  cross-reference  the  subject  suffix  in (5.107).  The 
enclitic  =te  'prominent  subject'  indicates  discourse  prominence  here  (see  §  13.5, 
particularly  §  13.5.3.3). 
The  pronunciation  oi=te  is  affected  by  vowel  harmony  in  this  example  (see  rule  2c,  §2.4.2.2,3). 
Tepere kie  means  'It  is  yam'  in  the  Sinsauru  (Kou)  language  and  Saipa  is  a place  in  that  area.

5.12.3  Listing  NPs  and  listing  morphemes 
Listing  NPs  can  have  an  identical  moipheme  following  each  item,^''  for  example,  the 
enclitic  =rare  'and/with'  and  the  enclitic  =ania  'group'  with  animate  referents,  and  the 
postposition  ore  'comitative  (with)'  with  inanimate  referents. 
5.12.3.1  Listing  animate  subject  NPs  with  =rare  'and/with' 
Two  animate  subject  NPs  can  be  listed  with  the  associative  enclitic  =rare  'and/with'

kinship  nouns)  or  animate  common  nouns.  One  of  the  NPs  and  hs  listing  morpheme  can  be 
omitted  if  the  referent  is  recoverable  from  the  verbal  suffix  or from  information  in  the 
discourse  or  real  world  context.^^  The  structure  is  therefore  as  follows. 
NP =rare. (NP =rare) 26

5.13  Appositive  NPs 
Appositive  NPs  describe  the  same  referent  in  different  terms  with  one  NP  standing  in 
apposition  to  another.  A  pause  can  occur  between  the  NPs.  The  initial  NP  can  be  a 
pronoun,  kinship  noun  or  common  noun,  as  in  the  examples  below,  while  the  final  NP  can 
be a  proper  noun,  common  noun,  nominal  compound  or  relative  clause.  An  example  of  the 
latter  is  given  in  example  (12.37)  in  §  12.4.2.3).

Chapter  6  Possessive  Nominal  Constructions 
6.1 Introduction 
This  chapter  examines  the  fonn  and  meaning  of  whole  part  and  possessive  nominal 
constructions.'  The  first  section  is  a  brief  discussion  of  terminology  associated  with 
possessives  (§6.2).  This  is  followed  by  a  section  on  the  basic  characteristics  of  possessive 
nominal  constructions  in  Koromu  (§6.3)  followed  by  more  detailed  sections  on  unmarked 
possessor  nouns  and  head  nouns  with  the  suffix  -ne 'P3s'  (§6.4)  and  possessive 
constructions  with  the  postpositions  o  'genitive  of  animate  referent  headed  NPs  (GEN)' 
(§6.5),  pao  'genitive  of  inanimate  referent  NPs  (IGEN)'  (§6.6),  sao 'genitive  of  animate 
referent  headless  phrases  (AGEN)'  (§6.7)  and  with  the  animate  locative  postposition  ahare 
(§6.8). 
6.2 Possession 
Structurally  possessive  constructions  are  two-member  syntagmatic  units  "with  the 
possessed  noun  as  head  and  the  possessor  as  its  modifier  or dependent"  (Nichols  1988:557). 
The  standard  linguistic  terminology  about  possession  is  potentially  misleading  semantically 
since  a  number  of  different  types  of  relationship  between  two  entities  can  be  indicated,  for 
example  ownership,  whole-part  relations  and  kinship  relations.  Lichtenberk  comments  that 
' Some  of  the  semantic  aspects  of  this  chapter  are  discussed  in  'The  semantics  of  inalienable  possession',  a 
chapter  in  Cross  Linguistic  Semantics,  edited  by  CliflFGoddard  (2008). 

[PDF PAGE 247]
218  Chapter  6 
...the  terms  'possessive  construction',  'possessor'  and  'possessed'  are  to  be 
understood  as  technical  terms.  A  possessive  construction  need  not  express  true 
possession,  i.e.  ownership,  as  in  my  house,  meaning  'the  house  I  own',  but  many 
other  types  of  relationship  between  two  enthies  (1983:148). 
The  teiTTis alienable  and  inalienable  possession  are  frequently  used  to  distinguish  types  of 
possession  in  Australian,  African,  American  and  Pacific  languages  (cf  Chappell  and 
McGregor  eds.  1996).  These  tenns  can  be  used  to  refer  to  structural  types.  The  tenn 
inalienable  is  used  to  label  nouns  which  occur  with  possessive  marking  while  alienable  is 
used  for  nouns  which  are  not  so  marked.  Semantically  inalienable  possession  indicates  "a 
permanent  and  inherent  association  between  the  possessor  and  the  possessed"  (Chappell 
and McGregor  1996:4).  It  often  refers  to 'parts'  of  a  whole. 
The  label  "possessive",  frequently  used  in  grammatical  descriptions,  has  no  constant 
semantic  content,  but  it  is  usually  used  with  respect  to  constmctions  whose  meaning 
involves  the  concept  of  PART. ^ For  example,  the  so-called  "inalienable  possession"  is 
usually  based  on  the  notion  of'a  part  of  a  person'  or  'a  part  of  a  person's  body' 
(often  extended  to  things  which  are  seen  as  'like  a  part  of  a  person')  Wierzbicka 
(1996:61). 
In contrast,  'alienable'  or  'separable'  possession  (Sapir  1917:86)  indicates  "a  variety  of 
rather  freely  made  associations  between  two  referents,  that  is,  relationships  of  a less 
permanent  and  inherent  type"  (Chappell  and  McGregor  1996:4)  or  as  Payne  puts  it  "the 
kind  of  possession  which  can  be  terminated"  (1997:105). 
6.3 Basic  characteristics  of  possessive  nominal  constructions 
Koromu  possessive  nominal  constmctions  are  distinguished  from  verbal  (§3.3.4.5)  and 
nonverbal  possessive  clauses  (§3.4.2.4).  There  are  several  different  types  of  possessive 
' The  semantic  prime  PART  has  a  narrower  range  of  use  than  English  part (Wierzbicka  1996:60). 

[PDF PAGE 248]
Possessive  Nominal  Constructions  219 
nominal  constnaction  which  overlap  in  some  characteristics.  Therefore  a few  basic  details 
are provided  in  this  section. 
First  of  all,  there  is  a basic  distinction  between  constructions  which  have  an  unmarked 
dependent  possessor  noun  and  a  head  noun  with  a  possessor  suffix,  and  constructions  in 
which  a  dependent  NP  has  a  genitive  case  postposition  and  is  followed  by  a  head  noun  with 
a possessor  suffix/enclitic  (cf  §  4.5.6). 
Possessor  N  Possessee  N  possessor  suffix  -ne 'P3s' 
Possessor  NP  o  Possessee  N  (possessor  -suffix/=enclitic) 
Constructions  with  an  unmarked  possessor  NP  and  a  head  noun  with  the  suffix  -ne 'third 
singular',  form  whole-part  constructions  in  which  the  possessor  is  not  referentially  distinct 
from  the  possessee,  for  example  tiri  kinin-ne  [tree  root-P3s]  'tree  root'.  In  contrast,  there 
are constructions  with  a  marked  possessor  NP  followed  by  a  head  noun  which  optionally 
occurs  with  a  person-number  suffix  or enclitic.  These  constructions  indicate  that  the 
possessor  is  referentially  distinct  from  the  possessee,  for  example  Winai  o  usii  [Winai  GEN 
pig]  'Winai's  pig'.^ 
Minimally,  a  possessor  NP  consists  of  a genitive  pronoun  or  a  head  noun  with  a  genitive 
postposition.  The  choice  of  genitive  postposition  depends  on  the  semantic  nature  of  the 
possessor.  O  occurs  with  animate  referent  NPs,pao  occurs  with  inanimate  referent  NPs 
and sao  follows  headless  NPs  or  animate  postpositional  phrases. 
Whole  part  constructions  with  the  possessor  suffix  -ne on  the  head  noun  and  possessive 
constmctions  with  genitive  postpositions  are  outlined  briefly  with  examples  in  Table  6.1. 
^ Nichols  (1988:563  ft)  discusses  various  patterns  of  possessive  marking  including  head-marked,  split-marking 
(head-  or  dependent  marked)  and  dependent-marked.  She  notes  that  in  some  Eurasian  languages  with  split-
marking  either  the  head  alone  is  marked  or  both  the  head  and  the  dependent  noun  are  marked  (for  example 
Tuva).  When  the  dependent  noun  is  marked  for  genitive  case  the  possessor  is  referential,  but  when  it  is 
unmarked  the  possessor  and  possessed  item  are  not  referentially  distinct  (Nichols  1988:566-567,  573). 
"Referentiality  or  definiteness  of  the  possessor  favors  dependent  marking  in  Ge'ez,  Tuva,  and  Turkish" 
(1988:581)  and  the  genitive  case  used  when  "the  possessor  is  referential"  in  Tuva,  a  Turkic  language  of 
Southern  Siberia,  "has  nothing  to  do  with  notions  such  as  'alienability'  and  ownership"  (1988:567).'

6.5 Possessive  constructions  with  a  possessor  NP  and  the  postposition  o 
6.5.1  Introduction 
Possessive  constnactions  with  an  animate  referent  possessor  NP  have  a  possessor  NP  which 
is a  genitive  pronoun  or  a  noun  followed  by  the  genitive  postposition  o.  The  possessor  NP 
refers  to  an  entity  which  is  referentially  distinct  from  the  referent  of  the  possessed  noun. 
The  possessor  NP  with  o  'genitive'  is  obligatory  with  an  unmarked  head  noun  (§6.5.2)  but 

[PDF PAGE 255]
226 Chapter  6 
it can  be  omitted  when  the  head  noun  has  a  possessor  suffix  or  enclitic  if  the  referent  is 
clear  from  the  context  (§6.5.3). 
6.5.2  Obligatory  possessor  NP  with  o  and  unmarked  head  noun  constructions 
Constructions  in  which  a  possessor  NP  has  a  genitive  pronoun  (see  Table  6.3)  or  genhive 
postposition  o  have  the  following  minimum  structure: 
Possessor  NP  o Possessee  N 
The possessor  NP  can  be  a  genitive  pronoun  with  incorporated  o  or  a  personal  name, 
kinship  noun  or  placename  followed  by  o 'genitive'  (see  Table  6.1).  This  NP  is  embedded 
in a  possessive  NP  with  an  unmarked  common  noun  as  head  noun.  The  possessor  and 
possessee  are  referentially  distinct  (cf.  Nichols  1988:567)  and  separable.  For  example,

'Winai's  pig  followed  me.'

6.5.3  Optional  possessor  NP  o  and  head  nouns  with  possessor  suffixes/enclitics 
6.5.3.1  Introduction 
Possessive  nominal  constmctions  which  have  a  possessor  suffix  or enclitic  on  the  head 
noun  indicate  a  close  or  inseparable  association  between  the  possessor  and  possessed  entity. 
The  possessor  NP  with  the  postposition  o  can  be  omitted  when  the  referent  is  recoverable 
from  the  context.  When  the  head  noun  is  a  common  noun  it  occurs  with  a  possessor 
enclitic  (§6.5.3.2)  and  when  it  is  a  kinship  noun  it  occurs  with  a  possessor  suffix  (§6.5.3.3). 
6.5.3.2  Optional  possessor  NP  o  and  common  nouns  with  possessor  enclitics 
6.5.3.2.1  Basic  characteristics 
A construction  which  has  a  possessor  NP  with  genitive  o  and  a  common  noun  with  a  person 
and number  possessor  enclitic  refers  to  things  that  are  closely  associated  with  a  person. 
Examples  of  these  things  are  body  parts,  personal  attributes  or  conditions  and  personal 
resources.  The  minimum  structure  of  these  constructions  is: 
(Possessor  NP  genitive  o/genitive  pronoun)  N  =possessor  enclitic 
With  common  nouns  possessor  person-number  is  expressed  by  an  enclitic  rather  than  a 
suffix.  Unlike  the  suffixes  which  attach  to  kinship  nouns  the  enclitic  attaches  to  the  right-
most  constituent  of  the  whole  NP  (or  to  locative  postpositions).  The  NP  examples  below 
show  the  enclitic  attaching  to  a  quantifier  in  (6.18)  and  an  adjective  in  (6.19).

• body  secretions,  products  and  conditions

6.5.3.2.2  Parts  of  the  body

mai-ked by  possessor  enclitics.  They  are  like  parts  of  things  or  parts  of  a whole'"'  in not 
being  owned  possessions.'^  Since  first  or  second  person  possessor  enclitics  indicate  a 
definite,  specific  referent  an  NP  with  a  genitive  postposition  o  can  be  omitted.

6.5.3.2.5  Personal  resources 
Personal  resources  are  things  people  do  many  things  with.  They  are  part  of  the  "personal 
domain  ...  associated  with  a  person  in  an  habitual,  intimate  or  organic  way"  (Bally  1996 
[ 1926]:33).^"  NPs  refeiring  to these  things  optionally  occur  with  a  possessor  enclitic  to 
indicate  a  person's  right  to  do  things  with  the  hem.  This  can  be  compared  with  a  person's 
exclusive  ability  to  do  things  with  parts  of  his/her  own  body. 
Personal  resources  include  manufactured  items,  natural  resources,  and  personal  places. 
NPs referring  to these  things  can  occur  with  a  possessor  enclitic.  Examples  are 
manufactured  artefacts  traditionally  made  from  local  products  by  the  person  who  uses  them 
such as  wesese 'trap',  /leri  'net  bag',  wesike  'purple  dye'  (6.45)  and  by  extension  mass-
produced  items.

6.5.3.3  Optional  possessor  NP  o  and  kinship  nouns  with  possessor  suffixes 
Constmctions  in  which  possessor  NPs  combine  with  kinship  nouns  that  have  a  possessor 
suffix  (see  Table  6.2  above)  refer  to  a  person  who  is  part  of  or  like  part  of  the  possessor's 
family.  The  possessor  NP  with  the  postposition  o  can  be  omitted  if  the  referent  is 
recoverable  from  the  discourse  or  real  world  context.  The  basic  structure  is: 
(Possessor  NP  <?/genitive  pronoun)  N^in  -possessor  suffix 
Kinship  nouns  refer  to people  who  are  related  by  birth,  marriage  or  initiation  (see  §4.3.3.2). 
These  bound  nouns  have  a  person  and  number  possessor  suffix  or a vocative  suffix  (cf. 
§4.3.3.4). 
A possessive  construction  refers  to two  distinct  referential  individuals  but  the  person 
indicated  by  the  kinship  noun  is  considered  to  be  like  a  part  of  the  same  thing,  a  family  or 
close-knit  group,  as  the  referent  of  the  possessor  NP.  For  example, 
(6.57)  fVeaii  =te,  Punti  o  pa  -ne, 
Weau  =PS  Punti  GEN  father  -P3s 
Weau =te  hoko  her  -a. 
Weau  =PS  make  PUT  -3s 
'Weau,  Punti's  father,  Weau,  made  it.'  T  1.17.2 
Cross-linguistically  kin  relationships  are  said  to  be  'inseparable'  on  the  basis  of  the 
unchangeable,  physical  link  between  mother  and  child:  "[they]  cannot  be  undone,  and  they 
cannot  be  established  in  any  other  way"  (Scheffler  1973:750).  The  people  involved  ai'e 
"necessarily  associated"  (Lyons  1968:301).  As  Sapir  (1917:88)  said  of  comparable 
constmctions  in  North  American  languages:  "MY  FATHER  is  not  one  who  is  owned  by 
me, but  rather  one  who  stands  to  me  in  a  certain  relation."  The  essential  semantic  content  is 
"pei-sonal  relation,  not  possession". 
Cultural  explanations  of  why  people  think  of  themselves  as  'parts  of  kinship  groups  are 
not pait  of  the  meaning  of  the  constmctions  as  such  since  the  choice  of  which  kin  terms  are 

[PDF PAGE 269]
240  Chapter  6 
marked  as  inseparable  varies  across  languages  and  can  be  quite  arbitrary  because  of 
diachronic  change.  However,  Koromu  kinship  nouns  refer  to  consanguineal,  affinal  and 
adopted  kin  as  well  as  male  agemates  who  experience  initiation  together.  Therefore  these 
kinship  nouns  generally  refer  to people  who  'live  in  the  same  place  for  a long  time'  and  'do 
many  things',  such  as  hunting  and  gardening  together,  as  if  they  were  all  'parts  of  one  thing 
(i.e.,  a  family)'  (cf  §4.3.3.2).^^  Marriage  and  initiation  ceremonies  establish  long-lasting 
relationships  such  as  this  and  are  described  in  the  same  type  of  linguistic  construction  as 
relationships  established  by  birth.

6.6 Possessive  constructions  with  a  possessor  NP  and  a  genitive  postposition  pao 
6.6.1  Introduction 
Possessive  constructions  with  possessor  NPs  that  refer  to an  inanimate  referent  consist  of  a 
possessor  NP  with  the  postposition  pao^^  'genitive  of  inanimate  referent  (IGEN)'  followed 
by a  head  noun.  The  head  noun  can  be  rame  'one'  (cf  §5.2.4)  or  a  common  noun  with  an 
optional  possessor  enclitic.  Many  of  the  examples  indicate  a  location  or  place  of  origin 
Personal  names  are  usually  unmarked  but  they  can  be  marked  by  the  first  singular  possessor  suffix  -mai and 
the affectionate  suffix  -e; for  example:  Arikao  mai-e  [Arikao  PI  s-AFF]  'my  dear  Arikao.'  to  indicate  a  close, 
affectionate  relationship:  'I  am  part  of  something;  this  person  is  part  of  the  same  thing'.  Similarly,  a 
teknonym  can  also  function  as  a head-marked  noun,  Makanipa-ne mai-e  [Makani  father-P3s  PI  s-AFF]  'my 
dear  Makani('s)  father'. 
^^ Pao appears  to  derive  from  the  goal/locative  postposition  pa combined  with  the  genitive  postposition  o.

Possessive  Nominal  Constructions  243 
associated  with  the  head  noun.^^ The  head  noun  can  be  omitted  when  it  is recoverable  from 
the discourse  or  real world  context.

Chapter  7  Postpositional  Phrases 
7.1 Introducrion 
This  chapter  describes  postpositional  phrases.'  §7.2  introduces  their  structure,  function  and 
distribution,  §7.3  presents  locative  postpositional  phrases,  §7.4  describes  non-locative 
postpositional  phrases,  §7.5  examines  postpositional  phrases  combined  and  §7.6  examines 
postpositional  phrases  and  anaphoric  reference. 
7.2 The  structure  and  function  of  postpositional  phrases 
Koromu  postpositional  phrases  function  as  clausal  adjuncts,  as  arguments  of  motion  and 
posture-taking  verbs  and  as  predicates  of  nonverbal  clauses.  A  simple  postpositional 
phrase  consists  of  a noun  phrase  or  a  directional  locative  followed  by  a  postposition.  All 
postpositions  can  govern  an  NP  but  only  pa forni  'locative'  postpositions  can  govern  a 
directional  locative  (adverbial). 
pp ^  |IVP  }  Postposition 
{DIRLOC  } 
' The  postpositions  o  'genitive',  pao  'inanimate  referent  genitive'  and  sao  'genitive  of  animate  referent 
headless  NPs'  are  described  in  chapter  6. 

[PDF PAGE 279]
250 Chapter  7 
Locative  and  non-locative  postpositional  phrases  are  further  subdivided  on  the  basis  of 
semantic  differences  between  postpositional  object  NPs  and/or  types  of  verb  with  which  the 
phrases  can  occur.^ 
7.3 Locative  postpositional  phrases 
7.3.1  Introduction 
Postpositions  which  can  function  as  locative  postpositions  are  pa 'goal/locative',  pt/^e 
'source/locative',  sa  'neangoal/locative',  sate  'near:source'^  and  ahare  'animate:locative'. 
The  semantics  of  the  object  of  the  postposition  affects  which  postposition  is  used  but  there 
is some  overlap  in  the  locative  functions  of pa and  sa  type  postpositions.  In  addition,  the 
pate and  sate  forms  can  be  used  to  express  manner  and  the  ahare postposition  has  some 
non-locative  functions.  Table  7.1  below  provides  an  overview  of  the  locative  fianctions  of 
these  postpositions,  the  overlap  between  them  and  the  semantics  of  their  objects. 
Table  7.1  Locative  postpositions:  their  functions  and  the  semantics  of  their  objects

The  postpositions  pa  and  sa  can  be  incorporated  into  placenames  (cf  §4.3.4),  sa and  sate 
can be  incorporated  into  relational  locatives  (§4.7.3.3)  and  pa can  be  incoiporated  into 
general  locatives  (§4.7.3.4).

genitive  postposition  (§7.3.5). 
7.3.2  Pa  form  postpositional  phrases 
7.3.2.1  Introduction 
Postpositional  phrases  with  the  postposition  pa ox  pate have  object  NPs  with  inanimate 
referents.  They  have  locative  meaning  and  in  the  case  of  pate  can  also  express  manner. 
Directional  locatives  can  be  objects  of  these  postpositions  and  location  in  time  is  expressed 
when  a  temporal  noun  is  the  object.  With  possessive  constructions  pa  becomes  an  enclitic 
(cf  example  (6.20)  in  §6.5.3.2.1). 
7.3.2.2  Constructions  with  pa 'goal/locative' 
Postpositional  phrases  headed  with  pa 'goal/locative'  (G/L)  llinction  as  arguments  of 
motion  and  posmre-taking  verbs,  as  locational  or  temporal  adjuncts,  and  as  nonverbal 
predicates.  The  constructions  in  which  these  phrases  occur  indicate  a  goal  or  location 
depending  on  the  semantic  nature  of  the  verb. 
The  following  constituents  can  occur  as  objects  of  the  postposition  pa 'goal/locative'. 
• an  NP  with  a  head  noun  or  noun  compound  that  is:

- a  placename  (cf  §4.3.4)  of  a  pailicular  large  river,  garden  or  distant  place  (7.2) 
• an  inteiTogative  (cf  §4.14.2)  ani  'where',  or  mamima  'what'  (7.3) 
• a  demonstrative  (cf  §4.14.1),  as  in  (7.4) 
• a  directional  locative  (cf  §4.7.3.2),  as  in  (7.5)

7.3.2.3  Constructions  with  pate 'source/locative'  or  'manner' 
Pate postpositional  phrases  function  as  clausal  adjuncts  which  either  have  a  locative  sense 
or they  express  the  'manner'  of  doing  something.  The  meaning  is  affected  by  the  semantic 
nature  of  the  verb  and/or  the  class  of  the  NP  which  is  object  of  the  postposition. 
7.3.2.3.1  Constructions  with  pate 'source/locative' 
Pate 'source/locative'  postpositional  phrases  express  either  the  'source'  from  which  a 
movement  begins  or  the  location  of  something  within  a  place.^  Common  nouns  describing 
location,  placenames  of  large  rivers,  gardens  or  distant  places,  interrogatives, 
demonstratives  and  directional  locatives  occur  with  pate 'source/locative'  as  they  do  with 
pa 'goal/locative'.

7.3.3.3  Constructions  with  sate  'near:source'  or  'manner' 
Sate postpositional  phrases  refer  to the  place  where  a  movement  began  or  the  manner  in 
which  an  action  is  performed.''  The  meaning  is  affected  by  the  head  noun  of  the  object  NP. 
7.3.3.3.1  Constructions  with  sate  'near:source' 
Postpositional  phrases  headed  by  the  postposhion  sate  'nearisource'"*  govern  inherently 
locative  NPs  such  as  local  placenames.  They  occur  in  constructions  with  motion  path  and 
transitive  motion  verbs  when  the  source  of  an  action  is  indicated. 
(7.43)  Korike  sate  ka  -pe  n-ia-te... 
Korike  N:S  come  -LTD:lp 
'We  came  from  Korike  and  ...'  T  1.13.2 
Locative  adverbials  which  incorporate  -sa  'near  side/place  and  the  interrogative  anisa  take 
the affix  '-re'  when  they  represent  the  source  or  starting  place  of  a movement,  as  in  anisate 
'from  which  side'  snAyorosate  'from  up  there'  (cf.  §4.7.3.3).  However,  with  placenames 
that  incoiporate  sa  other  constructions  are  used  for  example,  Meama  ya  pate  ka-r-a. 
[Meansa  river  S/L  come-PRES-3s]  'He  came  from  the  Meansa  river.' 
7.3.3.3.2  Constructions  with  sate  'near:manner' 
Constructions  in  which  the  sate postposition  occurs  with  an  NP  referring  to a  part  of  the 
body  indicate  a  means  of  transport  dependent  on  that  part.  For  example,  armete  'wallaby' 
use  their  two  back  legs  (one  side)  when  they  move  over  a  distance,  rather  than  the  fall  set 
of four  legs  used  when  grazing. 
(7.44)  Arusete  ehi  aterei  sate  tehei  -pit  -r  -e. 
wallaby  leg  one  N:MANN  walk  -HAB  -PRES  -3p 
'Wallabies  walk  on  one  leg.'"  (This  means  one  pair  of  legs,  the  back  legs.)  YTN2 
^ Sate may  be  derived  from  sa  and  one  of  the te forms.  When  sate  refers  to a location  -te  is  possibly  related  to

7.3.4  The  ahare  'animate  locative'  postpositional  phrase 
Ahare^^  'animate  locative  (ALOC)'  postpositional  phrases  have  an  animate  object.  They 
express  locative  (§7.3.4.1),  beneficiary/maleficiary  (§7.3.4.2)  or  referential  (§7.3.4.3) 
meaning  depending  on  the  semantic  nature  of  the  verb. 
7.3.4.1  Locative  constructions  with  the  ahare  postpositional  phrase

verbs.  This  reflects  the  inner  locative  or  participatory  meaning  expressed  with  the  pa and 
sa postpositions  and  described  in  the  sections  above. 
The  object  of  the  postposition  has  an  animate  referent  represented  by  a  personal  name 
(7.45),  a  kinship  noun  (7.46),  a  pronoun  (7.47)  or  a  human  (or  highly  animate)  common 
noun  (7.49)  in  the  examples  below.  The  first  two  examples  are  with  motion  path  verbs 
where  the  ahare postpositional  phrases  indicate  the  goal  of  motion  (as  in  English

7.4.1  Non-locative  postpositional  phrases  and  inanimate/animate  referent  NP  objects 
7.4.1.1  Introduction 
Non-locative  postpositional  phrases  with  inanimate  or  animate  referent  NP  objects  occur 
with  the  postpositions  ore  'comitative',  sei  'orientation',  seipa  'reason'  or  iiapii 'similitive'. 
These  postpositional  phrases  function  as  adjuncts  of  verbal  clauses.  With  the  exception  of 
seipa 'reason'  phrases,  they  also  function  as  predicates  of  nonverbal  clauses. 
7.4.1.2  Ore  'comitative'  postpositional  phrases 
Ore 'comitative'  postpositional  phrases  refer  to a  person  or  entity  that  accompanies,  or  is 
near  to  a  participant.  Although  ore  comitative  phrases  are  somewhat  similar  in  meaning  to 
listed  NPs  with  ore  'with'  (§5.12.3.3)  and  also  to  NPs  with  the  enclitics  =rare  'and/with' 
(cf  §5.12.3.1)  and  =ama  'group'  (cf  §5.2.3.4.4  and  §5.12.3.2)  they  are  not  identical 
semantically.  While  an  NP  with  ore  'comitative'  is  an  oblique  argument,  the  listed  NPs 
and NPs  with  =ama  'group'  flinction  as  core  arguments. 
The  head  of  the  object  NP  with  ore  'comitative'  can  be  a  common  noun  (7.67)  or  a 
demonstrative  (7.68). 
(7.67)  Esame  mipii  men  -e.  Esame  ore  ya  -r  -i. 
dog  many  be  -3p  dog  COM  go  -PRES  -Is 
'There  were  many  dogs.  1  went  with  the  dogs.'  T5.25.1 
(7.68)  Sowahe,  u  ore  horoni  -pii  -r  -e. 
ginger  that  COM  spit  -HAB  -PRES  -3p 
'Ginger,  they  habitually  spit  with  that.'  (..  .part  of  taro  planting  ritual)  D3.146.6 
The  head  can  also  be  a  pronoun  (7.69)  or  a  proper  noun  (7.70).  These  examples  also  show 
that locative  and  object  arguments  required  by  the  verb  occur  immediately  before  the  verb 
while  the  comitative  postpositional  phrase  comes  earlier  in  the  clause  following  the  subject.

7.4.1.3  Sei  'orientation'  postpositional  phrases 
Sei postpositional  phrases  indicate  the  pole  of  orientation  towards  which  the  predicate  is 
directed  (cf.  van  Hoecke  1996:18).  The  NP  with  sei  represents  the  puipose, 
cause/instigator,  intended/potential  object,  or  topic  of  the  action/state  which  is  oriented 
towards  it.  (It could  also  be  described  as  a  puiposive  dative.)  The  precise  meaning  of  the  sei 
postpositional  phrase  varies  to  some  extent,  depending  on  the  semantic  nature  of  the  verb  in 
the clause.  The  head  of  the  object  NP  with  sei  'orientation'  can  be  a  common  noun  (7.74), 
demonstrative  (7.76),  proper  noun  (7.77),  pronoun  (7.82),  a  nominalised  clause  with  pao 
(7.78)  (cf  §  12.5.3.4),  or  an  interrogative  such  as  me  'who'  (7.79). 
With many  dynamic  verbs  the  NP  with  sei  can  refer  to either  a  purpose,  "a  motivating  event 
which  must  be  unrealized  at  the  time  of  the  main  event",  or  a  reason  (cause  or  instigator), 
"a motivating  event  which  may  be  realized  at  the  time"  (Thompson,  Longacre  and  Hwang 
2007:250-251  [Thompson  and  Longacre  1985:185]).  With  the  motion  verb  in  the  first 
example  below,  the  sei postpositional  phrase  indicates  the  purpose  of  the  action.  In  the 
second  example  with  the  same  verb  a  reason  is  indicated.  In  both  cases  the  action  is 
'oriented'  towards  the  NPs  m  the  sei postpositional  phrases. 
(7.74)  Nene  no,  wau  sei  yar  -e  -te... 
3p GRD  banana  ORNT  go  -3p  -DR 
'They,  (they)  went  for  bananas...'  T1.15.72

pig fightNEC  get  PUT  -03  p -3  s

7.4.1.4  Seipa  'reason'  postpositional  phrases 
Seipa 'reason'  postpositional  phrases  refer  to the  reason  for  an  event  or  state.  The 
postposition  appears  to  be  a  combination  of  sei 'orientation'  and  pa 'goal/locative'.  The 
head of  the  object  NP  can  be  a  common  noun,  as  in  (7.88)  and  (7.89),  a  personal  name,  as 
in (7.90),  a  demonstrative,  as  in  (7.91),  or  the  interrogative  mana  'what',  as  in  (7.92).

7.4.1.5  Uapu  'similative'  postpositional  phrases 
Uapii 'similative'  postpositional  phrases  indicate  something  that  is  similar  to another  entity, 
time  or  action.  The  head  noun  of  the  object  NP  can  be  a pronoun  (7.93),  common  noun 
(7.94),  demonstrative  (7.95)  or  temporal  noun  (7.96).  In  nonverbal  clauses  the  object  of  the 
postpositional  phrase  in  the  predicate  is  described  as  similar  to a  person  or  thing  in  the 
subject  NP. 
(7.93)  Ne  i  uapu. 
2s Is  SIM 
'You  are  like  me.'  CS19.1 
(7.94)  Awai  o  toso  uapu. 
Awai GEN  torch  SIM 
'(It)  is  like  Awai's  torch.'DF 
In verbal  clauses  uapu postpositional  phrases  with  a  demonstrative  as  head  indicate  that  an 
action  in  the  real  world  or  discourse  context  is  similar  to the  action  described  by  the  verb. 
(7.95)  Ni  uo,  na  mo  uapu  ham  hore  -r  -a. 
3s GRD  thing  this  SIM  do  PUT  -PRES  -3s 
'He,  (he)  did the  thing  like  this.'  CS19.6 
When  a  temporal  noun  is  the  object  of the  postposition  uapu  'similative'  the  approximate 
time  or  duration  of  an event  is  indicated. 
(7.96)  Sonde  aterei  uapu  mene  -pe  a  mi  -e. 
Sunday  one  SIM  stay  -SR  come  move.down  -3p 
'They  stayed  about  one  week  (lit.  like  one  Sunday)  and  then  they  came  down.'

7.4.2  Non-locative  postpositional  phrases  and  inanimate  referent  NP  objects 
Non-locative  postpositional  phrases  with  aiau  'resemblative'  and  te  'instrumental'  can  only 
have  inanimate  referent  objects.  They  function  as  clausal  adjuncts. 
lA.l.X Aiau  'resemblative'  postpositional  phrases 
Aiau 'resemblative'  postpositional  phrases  like  iiupii postpositional  phrases  are  used  to  state 
that one  thing  resembles  another  thing.  However,  unlike  uapii  postpositional  phrases  they 
are not  used  to  describe  similarities  between  people  or  actions  or  to  describe  time.  The  NP 
object  of  the  postposition  can  only  be  a  common  noun. 
(7.97)  ...to  weti  aiau  uiri  -hera  =mo. 
GEN2p  house  RSM  become  -F3s  =BM 
'...he  will  become  like  your  house.'  Za8:9a  (Ps  91:9a) 
Aiau postpositional  phrases  commonly  occur  as  the  predicate  in  nonverbal  clauses.  The 
object  NP  of  aiau  'resemblative'  often  refers  to a  plant  or  part  of  a  plant. 
(7.98)  Mo  uo.  ware  aiau. 
this GRD  pumpkin  RSM 
'This,  (it  is)  Hke pumpkin.'  CS19.3 
A number  of  expressions  which  include  aiau 'resemblative'  describe  colour  (cf  §4.4.1.3.3). 
The  postposition  uapu  does  not  occur  in  this  context. 
(7.99)  Kururu  ami  -ne  aiau. 
butterfly  eye -P3s  RSM 
'(It  is)  like  the  eye  (yellow  spot  on  wing)  of  a  'kururu'  butterfly  (yellow).'

7.5 Postpositional  phrases  combined 
7.5.1  Introduction 
Postpostional  phrases  can  be  combined  in  juxtaposed  lists  and  in  apposition.  The  syntactic 
and semantic  relationships  involved  are  different  in each  case.  Postpositional  phrases 
which  occur  in  sequence  without  these  syntactic  and  semantic  links  are  discussed  in  §3.5. 
7.5.2  Juxtaposed  postpositional  phrases 
A series  of  postpositional  phrases  belonging  to  the  same  semantic  domain  can  be 
juxtaposed  in  a  list.  An  intonation  juncture  occurs  between  each  phrase.  The  examples 
below  include  te  'instrumental'  postpositional  phrases  (7.105),  ahare  'animate  locative' 
postpositional  phrases  (7.106),  and  ore  'comitative'  postpositional  phrases  (7.107).

(7.109)  the  initial  postpositional  phrase  is  more  specific  than  the  subsequent  phrase.

7.6 Postpositional  phrases  and  anaphoric  reference 
7.6.1  Introduction 
Postpositional  phrases  with  sei  'orientation',  seipa  'reason',  uapii  'similitive',  and  te 
'instrumental'  can  occur  with  the  demonstrative  u  'that'  when  it  makes  anaphoric  reference 
to a  participant  or  an  event.  References  to  participants  are  described  in  §7.4  and  in  §14.4.1. 
This  section  examines  anaphoric  reference  to  events  described  in  previous  clauses.

Chapter  8  Spatial  Reference 
8.1 Introduction 
This  chapter  examines  the  semantics  of  morpheme  categories  used  in  spatial  reference.' 
§8.2 is  an overview  of  the  theoretical  approach  to  spatial  reference  used  in  this  description. 
The subsequent  sections  describe  vertical  dimension  terms  (§8.3),  the  intrinsic  frame  of 
reference  indicated  by  relational  locatives  (§8.4)  and  the  absolute  frame  of  reference 
expressed  by  directional  locatives,  relational  locatives  and  motion  path  (directional)  verbs 
(§8.5).  Other  key  aspects  of  spatial  reference  such  as  lexical  items  (for  example,  sa 'place', 
ani 'where',  aiake  'far',  waimesa  'near'  and  placenames),  and  also  locative  and  complex 
locative  postpositional  phrases,  are  discussed  in  chapter  4 and  chapter  7  respectively. 
8.2 An  overview  of  systems  of  spatial  reference 
In a number  of  cross-linguistic  studies  Levinson  suggests  that  the  ways  in  which  languages 
refer  to the  location  of  objects  or  the  direction  of  movement  can  be  represented  by  frames 
of reference  (FoR)  which  label  "distinct  kinds  of  coordinate  systems"  in  the  horizontal 
dimension  (1996:1  10). 
Whereas  the  vertical  dimension  based  on  gravitation  with  all  its  effects  on our  balance 
and stance,  emerges  as  a universal  organizing  principle  for  spatial  conception,  the 
' Some  of  this  data  was  originally  presented  in  Priestley  2006. 

[PDF PAGE 317]
288 Chapter  8 
treatment  of  angles  on  the  horizontal  is  clearly  underdetennined  by  any  natural  force 
(Levinson  1998:13). 
Levinson  (1996:138-147,  2003:38-50)  proposes  three  frames  of  reference:  intrinsic,  relative 
and absolute  which  can  be  used  to  "identify  an  object  or  location  (the  referent  or  figure)  in 
relation  to  another  object  or  location  (the  relatum  or  ground)  by  projecting  off  the  relatum  a 
search  domain  in  which  the  referent  is  located"  (Palmer  2004:2). 
A language  can  have  more  than  one  frame  of  reference  (Levinson  2003:25,  Pederson  et  al 
1998:572).  Each  fi-ame  of reference  can  be  associated  with  distinct  linguistic  expressions, 
for example,  the  English  absolute  system  of  cardinal  directions  {north,  south,  east,  and 
west). Two  frames  of  reference  can  be  combined  (Levinson  2003:38)  or  individual  lexemes 
can be  used  in  two  different  fi-ames of  reference  (2003:38),  for  example  English  in  front of 
can occur  in  either  the  intrinsic  or  the  relative  frame  of  reference  (2003:41-46),  see  below. 
Intrinsic  reference  is  described  as  a binary  spatial  relation  since  it  involves  two  arguments, 
a figure/referent  and  a  ground/relatum  (2003:42).  The  figure  is  located  in  relation  to 
" 'inherent  features',  sidedness  or  facets  of  an object  used  as  the  ground"  (2003:41).  For 
example,  the  dog  is  at the  front of  the  truck  indicates  that  the  dog  is  in front  of  the  part  of  a 
truck  we  call  its  front,  the  part  that  lies  in  the  direction  of  motion. 
Relative  frame  of reference  is  described  as  temary  since  the  location  of  a  figure/referent  is 
expressed  in  terms  of  both  a  ground/relatum  and  the  viewpoint  of  a perceiver.  In  from 
Tom's viewpoint  the  dog  is  in  front of  a  tree  there  are  three  points  of  reference,  the  dog,  the 
tree  and  the  perceiver's  viewpoint.  For  English  speakers  the  tree  does  not  have  an  intrinsic 
front  but  the  front  is established  in  relation  to  the  viewpoint  of  the  perceiver  (2003:43-47). 
Levinson  (2003:47-50)  describes  absolute  frames  of  reference  as  binary  systems  which 
describe  a  figure  and  ground  in  relation  to  arbitrary  fixed  bearings  (see  also  1996:145),  for 
example,  the  dog  is  to  the  north  of  the  tree.  The  position  is  described  independently  of  the 
viewpoint  (relative  frame  of  reference)  or  of  inherent  features  of  the  ground/relatum 

[PDF PAGE 318]
Spatial  Reference  289 
(intrinsic  fi-ame  of  reference).  Absolute  systems  can  be  based  on  one  of  the  following  sets 
of "features  of  the  external  world"  (Palmer  2004:16). 
• North-South/East-West  (which  are  in  turn  based  on  observations  concerning  the  sun) 
• landward-seaward/parallel  to  the  coast 
• uphill-downhill  (fall  of  land)/across 
• upriver-downriver/away  from-towards  river 
• uphill-downhill  (elevational)/across  on  same  level  (Palmer  2004:3) 
All languages  have  a  deictic  system  of  spatial  reference,  in  which  location  and  direction  can 
be described  in  relation  to  the  context  created  by  the  speech  act  (Lyons  1977:637).  A 
deictic  component^  can  occur  in  each  of  the  frames  of  reference,  for  example,  the  dog  is  at 
my front  (intrinsic),  //'ow  my  viewpoint  the  dog  is  in  front of  the  tree  (relative)  and  the  dog 
is north  of  me  (absolute). 
As the  introduction  indicates  the  following  sections  examine  lexical  items  which  describe 
the vertical  dimension,  the  intrinsic  frame  of  reference  system  which  varies  in  relation  to 
the characteristics  of  specific  referents  and  the  absolute  reference  system  which  is  based  on 
dominant  features  of  the  landscape,  namely  elevation  and  watercourses  (see  Maps  1.1  and 
1.2).^ The  description  shows  that  the  absolute  reference  system  is  not  simply  a  binary 
system  based  on  arbitrary  fixed  bearings  (cf  Levinson  2003:47-50  above).  It  also  shows 
that  the  deictic  system  of  reference  is  sometimes  combined  with  the  intrinsic  or  absolute 
reference  systems. 
' Demonstratives  are  discussed  in  §4.14.1. 
' A  number  of  other  Papuan  languages  spoken  in  mountainous  country  use  an  elevation  based  absolute 
reference  system.  Examples  include  Nimboran  (Steinhauer  1997:269-280,  Voorhoeve  1997:281-285),  Yale 
(Heeschen  1997:180)  and  Yupno  (Wassmann  1997:143-174).

8.4 The  intrinsic  frame  of  reference

the sapiikotii  'path,  road'.  Entities  such  as  trees  do  not  have  fronts  and  backs  and  cannot  be 
refeiTed  to  by  the  relative  frame  of  reference  as  they  can  in  English  (cf.  §8.2).

8.5 The  absolute  frame  of  reference 
8.5.1  Introduction 
Levinson  states  that  languages  which  'make  extensive'  use  of  an  absolute  frame  of 
reference  "do  so  by  fixing  arbitrary  fixed  bearings  'cardinal  directions',  corresponding  one 
way or  another  to  directions  or  arcs  that  can  be  related  by  the  analyst  to  compass  bearings" 
(2003:48).  Terms  for  uphill, downhill  and  across  in  Tzeltal  are  used  in  a  "true  fixed-
bearing  system"  applied  to  objects  on  the  horizontal  and  on  slopes  and  to  objects  on  the 
same  compass  bearings  outside  Tzeltal  country  (1996:  111). 

[PDF PAGE 322]
Spatial  Reference  293 
However,  as  Palmer  (2004:6)  shows  in  languages  such  as  Manam,  landward  and  seaward 
absolute  reference  tenns  are  not  fixed  in  relation  to  compass  bearings  but  are  used  in  "an 
invariant  and  consistent  manner  in  any  location  on  the  island".  Also  terms  such  as  English 
downwind and  windward  are  detennined  by  wind  direction  at  the  time  they  are  used 
(2004:7)  and  "may  involve  directions  that  do  not  depend  on  a  predictable  conventionalized 
bearing"  (2004:6).  Therefore  Palmer  concludes: 
.. .absolute  FoR  requires  that  the  referent  be located  in  relation  to  the  relatum  on  the 
basis  of  a search  domain  projected  off  the relatum  in  a direction  based  on  an  object  or 
phenomenon  external  to  the  referent/relatum  dyad,  other  than  a  viewpoint.  This  does 
not logically  require  that  direction  to  be  fixed,  merely  identifiable  (2004:8). 
The connection  between  topography  and  linguistic  systems  of  absolute  spatial  reference 
discussed  by  Palmer  (2002:141-144,  2004:8-16)  is  summarised  below. 
• Within  a  language  or  group  of  related  languages  absolute  reference  systems  vary  in 
relation  to  topographical  differences.  For  example,  a  landward-seaward  axis 
interacts  with  an  east-west  axis  differently  on opposite  sides  of  an island. 
• There  are  differences  in the  absolute  reference  system  within  a  language  or  related 
group  of  languages  spoken  in  diverse  environments.  Asmat  speakers  (Papuan)  in 
"flat,  swampy"  river  country  use  a  "watercourse-based  system"  with  terms  for 
upriver  (against  the  current),  downriver  (with  the  current)  and  across  (away  from 
the bank).  On  the  coast  some  of  the  same  terms  are  used  for  northwest  (against  the 
coastal  current),  southeast  (with  the  coastal  current)  and  away  from  the  shore. 
• Similar  absolute  reference  systems  occur  in linguistically  and  areally  unrelated 
languages  in  topographically  similar  areas  such  as  Florutz  German  (Indo-European) 
and Samo  (Papuan)  which  both  have  elevational  and  watercourse  based  systems. 
The Koromu  absolute  frame  of reference  system  is  based  on  elevation  and  watercourses 
(see §  1.2 and  Maps  1  and 2)  and  therefore  can be  compared  to  Samo  and  Flomtz  German. 
Some  nouns  and  noun  phrases  refer  to these  topographical  features  (for  examples,  see 
§4.3.2.1  and  §5.2.2.2.2).  Many  locatives  and  motion  verbs  in  the  absolute  reference  system 
also reflect  the  importance  of  these  features  in people's  lives.  On  a  daily  basis,  people  walk 

[PDF PAGE 323]
294  Chapter  8 
many  miles  up  and  down  valleys  and  mountains,  and  along  and  across  rivers  to  get  water, 
crops,  firewood,  wild  game,  wild  edible  plants  and  building  materials,  as  well  as  to  interact 
with  other  people  (cf.  §8.2  and  §  1.5). Although  the>'a  'rivers'  can  hinder  movement  in  the 
wet season,  in  the  dry  season  the  river  beds  provide  good  walking  routes  through  the  keti 
'mountains',  tahene  'forests'  and  aire  'grasslands'. 
The  following  sections  examine  the  absolute  system  of  reference  expressed  by  directional 
locatives  (§8.5.2),  relational  locatives  (§8.5.3)  and  motion-path  verbs  (§8.5.4).  The 
interaction  of  these  constituents  with  adverbs  that  refer  to the  vertical  dimension  and/or 
intrinsic  and  deictic  systems  of  reference  is  also  discussed.  The  final  sections  compare  the 
use  of  directional  locatives  and  motion  path  verbs  (§8.5.5)  and  look  at  the  use  of  absolute 
reference  tenns  in  other  environmental  contexts  (§8.5.6).  Like  the  reference  system  of 
Manam,  the  Koromu  absolute  reference  system  is  shown  to  be  based  on  identitlable  rather 
than  arbitrary  bearings. 
8.5.2  Directional  locatives 
Directional  locatives  (see  §4.7.3.2)  which  specify  locations  or  directions  of  movement  are 
polysemous  since  they  can  be  used  to  refer  to location  or  direction  in  either  the  vertical  or 
the horizontal  domain.  The  locatives  listed  below  can  be  glossed  in  a  number  of  different 
ways  and  can  be  used  for  large  or  small  scale  reference.

8.5.3  Relational  locatives 
Relational  locatives  (see  §4.7.3.3)  describe  the  location  of  a  referent  in  relation  to 
something  else.  There  are  three  types:  intrinsic,  direction-based,  and  deictic. 
Intrinsic  relational  locatives  indicate  a  location  in  relation  to  inherent  features  or  sides  of 
something  else  (see  §8.4),  for  example,  eponsa  'behind'  below. 
(8.18)  Tamaite  aire  hare  eponsa  pe  n  -a. 
man  two  ALOC  behind  stand  STAY  -3  s 
'He  is  standing  behind  the  two  men.'  D3.112.17 
Direction-based  relational  locatives  are  linked  with  the  absolute  system  of  reference. 
Directional  locatives  in  reduced  fonn  can  incoiporate  the  postposition  sa}^ 
(8.19)  yorosa  'upper  side' 
aresa 'down/lower  side' 
Placenames  also  incorporate  (cf.  §4.3.4  and  §5.5)  and  it  is  possible  that  sa  is  derived  from  sa  'place'.

8.5.4  Motion-path  verbs 
While  motion-manner  verbs  indicate  the  manner  of  movement,  as  in  he  'move  quickly, 
walk  fast',  tehei 'move  at  a  steady  pace',  other  motion  verbs  indicate  the  path  of  movement 
(cf  §4.2.1.2).  These  motion-path  verbs  include  the  deictic  verbs  vwf'  'go'  and  ka  'come', 
the direction  verbs  mere  'move.up'  and  nii  'move.down'  and  a  number  of  transitive  motion 
verbs  with  locative  objects  such  aspo  'cross  (something)'  (see  §4.2.2.1  and  §4.2.2.2.3). 
The  deictic  verbs  can  occur  in  te  'get'-deictic  serial  verb  constnactions  (cf  §  10.2.9.1.2).  For 
example,  a  construction  with  te  ka [get  come]  'bring'  describes  someone  moving  an  entity 
toward  a  speaker  while  a  construction  with  te  yare [get  go]  'take',  describes  someone 
moving  an  entity  away  from  a  speaker. 
The  directional  verbs  mere  'move  up'  and  mi  'move  down'  (§4.2.1.2)  can  be  used  to  refer 
to the  vertical  dimension,  as  they  are  in  §8.3.  They  and  the  transitive  motion  verb  eue 
'move  across  (something)'  can  also  be  used  in  the  absolute  reference  system  to  refer  to 
movement  up,  down  or  across  the  Ramu  valley  or  river  and  to  movement  in  other  valleys 
and on  other  slopes.  These  verbs  are  common  in  serial  verb  constmctions  (see  §  10.2.8.2, 
§10.2.9.2.1,  and  §10.2.9.2.2).  In  the  example  below  reference  is  made  to  the  Ramu  Valley. 
(8.23)  ...eto  mani  =tapa  te  -pe  a  mere  -heru  =mo. 
tomorrow  money  =P2p  get  -SR  come  move.up-F3s  =BM 
'..  .tomorrow  he  will  get  your  money  and  come  up.'  T1.8.1  1 
The  suffix  for  1  s and  2s  has  the  same  form. 
The  terms  motion-manner  and  motion-path  verb  are  adapted  from  Tahny  (2007:71).  Motion  verbs  are 
common  in  Papuan  languages  (see  Nimboran,  Steinhauer  1997).  For  example,  in  Tauya,  there  are  at  least 
four  basic  motion  verbs  translated  as  'come,  go,  come  up'  and  'come  down'  (MacDonald  1990:186),

One naiTator  describes  a  joumey  by  truck  from  Kainantu  to  Goroka.  About  the  outward

Spatial  Reference  303 
there'.  When  describing  the  return  journey  he  uses  the  motion-path  verb  mere  'move  up' 
three  times,  as  in  heya mere-ia  [return  go  move.up-lp]  'we  returned  going  moving  up'.  It 
would  be  interesting  to  find  out  what  criteria  he  based  his  very  consistent  description  on

conventionalized  "worldwide  orientation"  (cf  Bowden  1997:  264-265)  with  j^oro/zo 'up 
there'  used  for  the  direction  to  the  east  where  the  sun  rises  and  aroho  'down'  used  for  the 
direction  to  the  west  where  the  sun  sets.  A  final  possibility  is  that  the  speaker  has  a  very 
acute  sense  of  elevation  since  Goroka  is  in fact  slightly  lower  than  Kainantu. 
About  50  kilometres  to  the  southeast  of  the  Koromu  area  the  Ramu  and  Markham  valleys 
merge.  Differences  in elevation  and  the  watershed  between  the  Ramu  and  Markham  rivers 
are scai'cely  discernible  and  while  the  direction  in  which  the  rivers  flow  indicates  which 
tenns  are  appropriate  the  deep  valley  and  high  mountains  are  so  dominant  it  is natural  to 
speak  of  one  valley.  Adzera  (Austronesian)  speakers,  who  migrated  in  recent  decades  from 
the Markham  to  the  Ramu  valley,  still  describe  directions  in  terms  of  their  Markham 
elevation  and  watercourse  based  absolute  reference  system  (pers.  com.  Arikao  Tomas).'"' 
Whether  Koromu  speakers  are  influenced  by  their  absolute  direction  system  when  in  the 
Mai-kham area  is  a subject  for  further  investigation. 
Further  discussion  witli  the  narrator  of  this  text  and  with  other  Koromu  speakers  is  needed  to  resolve 
questions  about  descriptions  of  locations  outside  the  Koromu  area.

Chapter  9 Verb  morphology 
9.1 Introduction 
This  chapter  provides  an  overview  of  verbal  morphology.  The  sections  below  describe  the 
basic  characteristics  of  independent  and  dependent  verbs  (§9.2),  the  morphology  of 
independent  verbs  (§9.3)  and  the  morphology  of  dependent  verbs  (§9.4). 
9.2 Basic  characteristics  of  independent  and  dependent  verbs 
Verbs  are  either  independent  or  dependent.  Independent  verbs  can  be  the  only  verb  in  an 
utterance,  the  final  verb  in  a  serial  verb  construction  or  the  final  verb  in  a  clause  chain.  A 
clause  chain  is  a  series  of  one  or  more  dependent  clauses  followed  by  a  final  independent 
clause.  The  head  of  each  dependent  clause  is  a dependent  verb  or  dependent  serial  verb 
constmction  with  its  own  core  and  peripheral  arguments.  These  dependent  verbs  are  only 
partially  inflected  for  tense-subject  and  aspect.  They  depend  on  the  closest  subsequent 
flilly  inflected  independent  verb  or  partially  inflected  dependent  verb  for  specification  of 
these  categories.  Independent  verbs,  other  than  ia  'be  not''  (cf  §4.2.8),  are  fiilly  inflected 
for tense-subject,  imperative  or  desiderative.  They  are  optionally  inflected  for  object  and, 
in non-fiature  tense,  for  habitual  aspect.  They  can  be  followed  by  a  boundary  marking 
enclitic,  a  question  enclitic  or  an  epistemic  modality  particle  (see  §3.2.1.6). 
' In  future  references  to  independent  verbs  and  their  inflections  the  qualification  concerning  ia  'be  not'  will 
not be  repeated  but  the  reader  needs  to  be  aware  of  it. 

[PDF PAGE 335]
306 Chapter  9

morphology  of  the  first  dependent  verb  indicates  that  the  next  verb  has  a  different  referent 
subject  (see  §9.4.3.4  below).  The  moiphology  of  the  second  dependent  verb  indicates  that 
the subsequent  verb  has  the  same  subject  (see  §9.4.2  below). 
(9.1)  C.  1 ...siti  poho  n  -ia  -te.

9.3 Independent  verb  morphology 
9.3.1  Introduction 
Independent  verbs  consist  minimally  of  a  verb  stem  with  inflections  that  indicate  the  tense-
subject  and  mood  of  the  verb.  The  term  'mood'  is  used  here  to  refer  to  a  "set  of  syntactic 
and semantic  contrasts  signaled  by  alternative  paradigms  of  the  verb"  (Crystal  1980:230). 
There  are  three  alternative  paradigms  for  Koromu  independent  verbs:  the  defauh 
portmanteau  tense-subject  indicative  suffixes,  the  second  person  singular  and  plural 
imperative  suffixes,  and  the  desiderative  suffix  -apesi  (cf  §3.2.1.1). 

[PDF PAGE 336]
Verb  Morphology  307 
9.3.2  Independent  verbs  with  tense-subject  suffixes 
9.3.2.1  Introduction:  niorphosyntactic  categories  and  properties 
Portmanteau  tense-subject  indicative  suffixes  occur  with  independent  verbs  in  declarative 
(cf §3.2.1.2),  interrogative  (§3.2.1.3)  or  exclamative  (cf  §3.2.1.6)  clauses,  which  express 
statements  (assertions),  questions  or  exclamations  respectively. 
A number  of  optional  suffixes  can  occur  with  a  verb  inflected  for  tense-subject.  The  verb 
stem  can  be  followed  by  an  object  (O)  or  reciprocal  (REC)  suffix,  and  then  by  habitual 
aspect  (HAB)  and/or  present  tense-aspect  (PRES).  In  addition,  a  verb  inflected  for  future 
tense  can  also  have  the  intentive  modality  suffix  (INT).  The  structure  of  fully  inflected 
independent  verbs  with  tense-subject  suffixes  is represented  schematically  below:^ 
Vstem  {(Object)  }(Habitual)  (PRES)  Tense-Subject  (Intentive) 
{(Reciprocal)  } 
The  following  sections  examine  the  morphosyntactic  categories  represented  on  these 
independent  verbs:  obligatory  portmanteau  tense-subject  suffixes,  the  optional  present 
tense-aspect  suffix,  optional  object  person  and  number  suffixes,  and  optional  reciprocal, 
habitual,  and  intentive  suffixes. 
9.3.2.2  Tense-subject  suffixes 
The  final  portmanteau  suffixes  of independent  verbs  express  person  and  number  of  the 
subject,  and  non-fiature  or  future  tense.  The  tense  locus  is  the  moment  of  speech;  the  future 
and non-future  time  distinguished  by  the  tense-subject  suffixes  reflects  "ascending  time" 
(Hewson  and  Bubenik  1997:4).  The  fiature  tense  has  seven  distinctions  in  person  and 
number  while  the  non-fiature  tense  has  four  distincdons  since  the  distinction  between  first 
and second  person  is  syncretised.  The  tense  and  subject  distinctions  are  outlined  in  Table 
9.1 below  and  explained  with  examples  in  the  following  paragraphs. 
^ Here  V  indicates  verb.  The  curly  brackets  {  J  indicate  that  one  of  the  items  within  the  brackets  can  occur. 
Within  curly  brackets  constituents  in  plain  brackets  are  optional.  If  there  are  no  plain  brackets  one  of  the 
constituents  must  occur  to  form  an  independent  verb.

9.3.2.3  The  present  tense  aspect  suffix  -r 
The  present  tense-aspect  suffix  -r  can  be  used  to  refer  to  the  moment  of  speaking  and  to 
periods  of  time  which  include  the  moment  of  speaking.  It  can  also  be  used  to  refer  to  time 
earlier  on  the  same  day  as  the  moment  of  speaking  (narrative  present)  and  to  extended 
ongoing  aspect.  Each  of  these  situations,  and  the  various  constmctions  that  the  suffix  can 
occur  in,  are  described  and  exemplified  below.  However,  the  fonn  of  the  suffix  and  the 
ablaut  rules  which  affect  the  preceding  verb  stem  are  described  first. 
The  underlying  form  of  -r  is  probably  -?-e  since  it  invariably  occurs  before  a  vowel  initial 
non-fiature  tense-subject  suffix  where  the  mid-vowel  /e/  is  affected  by  identical  vowel 
elision  (see  Rule  la,  §2.4.2.1)  or  pre-vocalic  /e/  elision  (Rule  3a  in  §2.4.3).  The  suffix  -r 
follows  the  verb  stem  and  an  optional  object  suffix. 
(9.7) O,  wera  ithitni  -se  -r  -a,"  ii  -a  -te... 
Oh child  be.heavy-Ols  -PRES  -3s  quote  -3s  -DR 
' "Oh,  the  child  is  heavy  forme,"  she  said'  T  1.15.74 
When  'present  tense-aspect'occurs,  a  preceding  verb  stem  with  a  final  high  vowel,  such 
as topi 'climb  up',  is  affected  by  ablaut  (see  Rules  5b  and  5c  in  §2.4.5.1).

constmctions  with  the  -r  suffix  are  more  restricted  than  the  rule  which  affects  phasal  and

verbs,  the  suffix  -r  originally  had  aspectual  meaning  alone. 
Cross-linguistically,  the  basic  meaning  of  present  tense  is  location  of  a situation  at  the 
moment  of  utterance.  Characteristically,  present  tense  is  used  to  refer  to situations  which

The  object:person  and  number  suffixes,  -se  'first  person  singular  object',  -seka  'first  person

9.3.2.6  The  habitual  aspect  suffix  -pu 
"Aspect  characterizes  the  relationship  of  a  predicate  to  the  time  interval  over  which  it 
occurs"  (Chung  and  Timberlake  1985:213).  Aspect  can  be  represented  in  Koromu  by  verb 
inflections  (cf  §9.3.2.3  and  §9.3.2.6),  by  phasal  verbs  in  serial  verb  constnactions  (cf 
§10.2.4,  §10.2.5,  §10.2.6)  or  by  aspectual  enclitics  in  serial  verb  constmctions  (cf  §10.2.7). 
The habitual  aspect  suffix  -pu  follows  the  verb  or  an  optional  object  suffix  and  indicates  a 
habitual  situation  or  event  with  verbs  inflected  for  non-tuture  tense.  It  does  not  occur  with 
the future  tense.  Instead,  other  means,  such  as  the  aspectual  enclitic  =apaie  'still, 
continuously'  (see  §10.2.7.2),  are  used  to  speak  of  activities  or  events  which  occur  on  a 
regular  basis  in  the  fiiture.  The  following  example  in  non-future  tense  is  inflected  for 
habitual  aspect. 
(9.22)  ...iisii  yo  -neka  -pu  -e. 
pig call  -03p  -HAB  -3p 
'...they  used  to  call  the  pigs.'  T1.25.6 
Habitual  and  present  tense-aspect  occur  together  to  represent  events  'occurring  regularly' 
over  the  event  frame.  The  event  frame  may  be  the  present  day  generally,  'sometimes', 
particular  times  and  seasons  or  universal  time.  Examples  can  be  glossed  by  the  English 
perfonnative  non-past  tense,  commonly  refen'ed  to  as  'simple  present'. 
' One  form  of  the  second  person  plural  is  -ie.  Here  the  final  /e/  of  this  suffix  has  been  elided  by  the  identical 
vowel  elision  rule  (rule  la  in  §2.4,2.1).

9.3.2.7  The  intentive  modality  suffix  -mpe 
Intentive  modality  is  expressed  by  a  suffix  -mpe 'intentive'  which  attaches  to  a  verb  marked 
for future  tense.  The  intentive  suffix  is a  root  modal  which  has  scope  over  the  core  level  of 
clause  structure  (see  Van  Valin  2005:9).  It  modifies  the  relation  between  a  core  argument, 
the  actor,  and  the  action.  In  contrast,  modality  particles  (see  §3.2.2)  modify  the  clause  as  a 
whole.  The  intentive  suffix  occurs  in  the  example  below:

Verbs  with  the  imperative  suffixes,  -ae 'IMP2s'  and  -ahe  'IMP2p',  distinguish  the  person

9.3.4  The  desiderative  suffix  -apesi 
Independent  verbs  with  the  suffix  -apesi 'desiderative'  occur  in  desiderative  clauses  and 
express  desires  and  wants  (cf  §3.2.1.5).  They  are  common  in  procedural  accounts  and 
comments  about  the  future.  When  verbs  are  inflected  by  -apesi the  subject  is  not  indicated 
and has  to be  determined  from  the  discourse  or  real  world  context.  The  verb  is  optionally 
inflected  by  the  object  or  reciprocal  suffix.  The  stixicture  is  as  follows:

{(Reciprocal)  }  {-Desiderative  suffix}

9.4 Dependent  verb  morphology 
9.4.1 Introduction 
Dependent  verb  morphology  indicates  whether  the  subsequent  verb  has  the  same  or  a 
different  subject,  the  same,  overlapping,  or  different  temporal  reference,  and  realis  or 
irrealis  status.  The  different  types  of  dependent  verb  moiphology  are  listed  below.  Notice 
that tense-subject  (T:S)  is  indicated  with  most  types  of  different  referent  suffix,  as well  as 
with the  loose  temporal  dependency  complex. 
Same  Referent,  Realis/Irrealis,  Close  Succession/Overlap  V  stem-pe^ 
Different  Referent,  Realis,  Temporal  Overlap  V  stem-?//e 
Different  Referent,  Realis,  Close  Dependency  V  stem-T:S-?e 
Different  Referent,  Irrealis,  Close  Succession/Dependency  V  stem-T:S-//e 
Different  Referent,  Irrealis,  Temporal  Overlap  V  stem-T:S-A;/e 
Same/Different  Referent,  Loose  Temporal  Dependency  V  stem-pe  n-T:S-te 
The different  types  of  dependency  constmctions  are  discussed  under  the  headings,  same-
referent  dependent  verb  morphology  (§9.4.2),  different-referent  dependent  verb 
morphology  (§9.4.3)  and  loose  temporal  dependency  (§9.4.4). 
^ The  Koromu  same  referent  dependency  form  -pe  and  different  referent  realis  fomi  -te  and  the  same  referent 
form-pa  and  different  referent  aorist  form-te  in  Tauya  (of  McDonald  1990:218  fO  are  very  similar.

independent  verb.

9.4.3  Different-referent  dependent  verb  morphology 
9.4.3.1  Introduction 
Dependent  verbs  with  one  of  the  three  different  referent  dependency  suffixes,  -te, -ne,  or 
-nte, indicate  that  the  subsequent  verb  has  a  different  subject  referent.  The  type  of  temporal 
relationship  between  the  dependent  and  the  final  independent  verb  and  the  realis  or  irrealis 
status  of  the  final  verb  is  indicated  by  whether  or  not  the  dependent  verb  is  inflected  for 
tense  and  subject,  and  by  the  choice  of  dependency  suffix.  The  following  structures  are 
possible: 
Verb  stem  +  Dependency  suffix  -nte 
Verb  stem  (Object)  (Aspect)  +  Tense-subject  + Dependency  suffix  -te/-ne/-nte 
The sections  below  introduce  the  realis-irrealis  distinction  in  dependent  verb  morphology 
(§9.4.3.2),  the  realis  different  referent  dependency  construction  which  does  not  have  tense-
subject  inflections  (§9.4.3.3)  and  the  realis  and  irrealis  different  referent  dependency 
constructions  which  do  have  tense-subject  inflections  (§9.4.3.4). 
9.4.3.2  The  realis-irrealis  distinction  and  dependent  verb  morphology 
Roberts  (1990,  1994  and  1997) presents  data  from  Papuan  languages  showing  a  binary 
distinction  between  realis  and  iiTcalis  status  in  the  morphology  of  dependent  switch 
reference  verbs.  He  states  that  "realis  relates  to events  that  the  speaker  believes  to  be 
actualized  or  realized"  while  "irrealis  relates  to  events  that  the  speaker  believes  have  not 
been actualized"  (Roberts  1994:50).  The  category  'irrealis'  in  these  constmctions  has  a  core 
semantic  meaning  of  "future-hypothetical"  but  the  range  of  categories  classified  as  irrealis 

[PDF PAGE 353]
324 Chapter  9 
varies  from  language  to  language  (1994:8),  from  ftiture  tense,  imperative  and  desiderative 
to counterfactual  and  past  habitual  (see  also  Roberts  1997:148-152). 
10 
To some  extent  the  realis-irrealis  distinction  in  Koromu  dependent  verb  morphology 
parallels  the  non-future  and  future  tense  distinction  (see  §9.3.2.2).  However,  the  dependent 
verb  suffixes  -ne 'different  referent  irrealis  close  succession  (DR:IR:CS)'  and 
-nte 'different  referent  irrealis  temporal  overlap  (DR:IR:TO)'  indicate  a  subsequent 
different  referent  verb  with  irrealis  status  where  the  latter  has  a  fiiture  tense,  imperative  or 
desiderative  suffix,  future  tense  and  intentive  -mpe,  or  habitual  aspect  with  present  tense-
aspect.  A  nonverbal  clause  can  also  have  irrealis  status."  Thus  in  Koromu,  realis  status  is 
used to  refer  to things  which  have  happened,  or  are  happening,  while  irrealis  status 
indicates  situations  which  cannot  be  described  as  either  true  or  false  in the  real  world. 
9.4.3.3  Different  referent  dependency  and  -nte:  realis  temporal  overlap 
A dependent  verb  with  the  suffix  -nte but  without  a  tense-subject  suffix  indicates  that  there 
is temporal  overlap  between  the  event  described  by  this  verb  and  the  next  verb.  Tense  is 
indicated  on  subsequent  independent  verbs,  different-referent  dependent  verbs  or  loose 
temporal  dependency  verbs  (cf  §9.4.4).  Aspect,  intentive,  imperative  or  desiderative 
suffixes  occur  on  subsequent  independent  verbs.  The  structure  of  the  dependent  verb  is: 
Verb  stem  Dependency  suffix  -nte 
Examples  of  this  type  occur  when  motion  or  posture  verbs  are  the  dependent  verbs.

tense,  imperative  mood,  or  desiderative  marking,  in  Erima  (1994:148,  151),  Gahuku  (1994:148-149,  151), 
Angaataha  (1994:149,  151)  and  Ambulas  (1994:149,  151);  irrealis  on  medial  verbs  when  the  tinal  verb  has

(1994:150,  151)  and  Wojokeso  (1994;I50,  151);  and  irrealis  on  medial  verbs  when  the  final  verb  is  future

A dependent  verb  with  a  tense-subject  suffix  and the  dependency  suffix  -ne indicates  that

tense-aspect  or  future  tense.  Present  tense-aspect  indicates  an  event  which  is  anterior  to  the 
event  with  irrealis  status  indicated  by  the  subsequent  verb.

different  referent  dependent  verb  is  inflected  for  present  tense-aspect  and  a  subsequent  verb 
has flie  future  tense  suffix.  The  dependent  verb  indicates  an  event  which  is  anterior  to the 
subsequent  fiature  event.

9.4.4  Loose  temporal  dependency  with  the  complex  -pe  n-T:S-te 
A dependent  verb  with  the  loose  temporal  dependency  complex'^  -pe  ii-T:S-te  indicates 
sequential  or  disjoint  temporal  reference.  Topical  reference  can  be  the  same,  referentially 
overlapping  or  different.  However,  in  the  majority  of  cases  it  remains  the  same.  The  verb 
is dependent  on  a  subsequent,  final  verb  for  the  expression  of  aspect,  present  tense-aspect 
and/or  desiderative  suffixes.  This  complex  moiphemic  sequence  is  given  one  gloss  which 
indicates  the  combined  core  meanings  of  loose  temporal  dependency  and  tense-subject  (cf 
variation  1  in §2.5.2). 
(9.54)  Taukate  pehe  re  -pe  n-e-te.  si  no,  men  -e. 
Taukate  hit  PUT  -LTD:3p  then  GRD  stay  -3p 
'They  hit  Taukate  and  then,  then,  they  stayed.'  T2.26.21 
The  complex  consists  of  the  suffix  -pe 'same  referent:close  succession'  (cf  §9.4.2),  the 
serial  verb  n-  'STAY'  (cf  §10.2.6),  a  future  or  non-fiature  tense-subject  (T:S)  suffix 
(§9.3.2.2)  and  the  dependency  suffix  -te which  occurs  in  constructions  which  represent 
'different  referent  realis:close  dependency'  (§9.4.3.4.2).'"^  The  complex  n-T:S-te,  forms  a 
separate  phonological  word  since  there  is  separate  word  stress  and  a  slight  pause  following 
-pe. The  pause  can  be  lengthened  when  a  speaker  hesitates  or  stops  to  think.  Example 
(9.55)  has  a  detailed  gloss  of  the  inflections  while  (9.56)  has  the  simplified  gloss  used 
throughout  the  remainder  of  the  thesis. 
(9.55)  ...hekeni  te  ka  re  -pe  n  -ia  -te, 
firewood  get  come  PUT  -SR  STAY  -Ip  -DR(?) 
" The  term  'loose  dependency'  was  originally  suggested  by  Ross's  (1994)  description  of  a  dependent  verb 
enclitic  in  Takia,  an  Austronesian  language  in  the  Madang  area  which  has  been  influenced  by  Papuan 
grammatical  structure. 
The  origin  of-te  is  difficult  to  determine.  As  indicated  it  occurs  in  two  different  dependency  constructions 
and  it  is  possibly  part  of  the  suffix  -nte  'different  referent:temporal  overlap'  (§9.4.3.44).  It  is  also  similar  in 
form  to  the  prominent  subject  enclitic  =te(§5.11,  §13.5)  and  the  instrumental  postposition  te  (§7.4.2.2).
