Chapter  10  Complex  Verbal  Predicates 
10.1 Introduction 
This  chapter  describes  complex  verbal  predicates.  The  two  basic  types  of  complex 
predicate  are  serial  verb  constructions  (§10.2)  and  adjunct-verb  constructions  (§10.3).  The 
final section  of  the  chapter  is  an  overview  of  verb  iteration  (§10.4). 
10.2 Serial  verb  constructions 
10.2.1  Introduction 
Serial  verb  constructions'  (SVCs)  form  complex  but  unified  predicates  which  combine  two 
or more  verbs.  In  the  following  sections  the  basic  characteristics  of  SVCs  are  described  in 
§10.2.2  and  the  classification  of  SVCs  in  §  10.2.3. These  introductory  sections  are  followed 
by a  description  of  phasal  SVCs  (which  specify  aspect)  in  §10.2.4,  phasal  and  valency 
changing  SVCs  with  here  PUT  in  §10.2.5,  phasal  and  valency  changing  SVCs  with  ne 
STAY  in  §10.2.6,  SVCs  with  aspectual  enchtics  in  §10.2.7,  coincident  SVCs  in  §10.2.8  and 
iconic  SVCs  in  §10.2.9. 
10.2.2  Characteristics  of  serial  verb  constructions 
Serial  verb  constructions  occur  in  Papuan,  Austronesian,  South-East  Asian,  East  Asian, 
West  African,  Australian,  Central  and  South  American  languages  and  in  some  pidgins  and 
Creoles.  Amongst  others  Durie  (1997:291),  Foley  and  Olson  (1985:18-32),  Crowley 
' An  earlier  description  of  serial  verb  constructions  is  given  in  chapter  four  of  my  MA  sub-thesis  (2002). 

[PDF PAGE 371]
342 Chapter  10 
(1987:38),  Givon  (1991:137-139)  and  Aikhenvald  (2006:1)  describe  some  cross-linguistic 
characteristics  of  serial  verb  constructions.  For  example,  Durie  states  "the  archetypal  serial 
verb  constmction  consists  of  a  sequence  of  two  or  more  verbs  which  in  various  (rather 
strong)  senses,  together  act  like  a  single  verb"  (1997:290).  The  constructions  have  the 
intonational  properties  of  a monoverbal  clause  but  there  is  no  morphology  indicating  clause 
boundaries  within  the  SVC.  The  component  verbs  share  tense,  aspect,  mood  and  polarity. 
They  can  share  core  and  other  arguments  and  each  verb  can  occur  as  an  individual  verb  in 
other  contexts.  In  addition: 
There  is  a  strong  diachronic  tendency  to  lexicalization  and  grammaticization  of  the 
meaning  of  serial  complexes:  this  can  involve  treating  the  whole  serial  complex  as  a 
single  lexical(ized)  item,  or  'demotion'  of  the  meaning  and  grammatical  status  of 
one  of  the  verbs  to  that  of  a modifier  or  case-marker  (Durie  1997:291). 
The  basic  criteria  which  identify  Koromu  serial  verb  constructions  are  outlined  below: 
(i) One  or  more  contiguous  verb  stems  terminate  in  a  verb  with  dependent  or 
independent  verbal  morphology.  Non-final  verb  stems  are  uninfleeted  apart  from 
optional  object  suffixes  and  optional  aspectual  enclitics. 
(ii) Tense,  subject,  aspect  and  mood  conveyed  by  final  inflections  are  applicable  to 
all the  verbs  in  the  construction. 
(iii) The  series  of  verbs  shares  a  single  subject  and  can  share  a  single  object. 
(iv) There  is  shared  polarity  since  the  negative  tai  precedes  and  has  scope  over  the 
whole  series  as  it  would  over  a  single  verb. 
(v) There  is  no  moiphology  indicating  clause  boundaries  or  syntactic  dependency. 
(vi) Each  verb  is  a  distinct  phonological  word  with  its  own  primaiy  stress  but  an 
SVC has  the  single  intonational  contour  of  a  mono-verbal  clause.  Pauses  associated 
with  clause  boundaries  do  not  occur. 
(vii)  Oblique  arguments  occur  before  the  construction,  not  within  it. 
(viii)  Each  verb  can  occur  as  a  simple  predicate  on  its  own. 

[PDF PAGE 372]
Complex  Verbal  Predicates  343 
(ix) A  phasal  or  phasal  and  valency  changing  verb  can  occur  in  an  SVC.  This  verb 
only  has  scope  over  the  verb  it  follows  (10.7).  The  resuhing  phasal  SVC  can  form 
pai1 of another  SVC  (see  §  10.2.9.2).^ 
Apart  from  infomiation  conveyed  by  phasal  verbs  (cf  (ii.)  above)  the  individual  verbal 
events  are  stripped  of  extra  infonnation  that  might  give  them  a  status  different  from  the 
next vei-b, for  example  a  different  subject.^

contiguous  verb  stems  ending  with  dependent  or  independent  verb  morphology  (criterion  i).

in each  constmction  (criterion  ii).  Each  series  of  verbs  shares  a  single  subject,  and  in  the

and vi).  Oblique  ai-guments  occur  before,  not  within,  serial  verb  constructions  (criterion 
vii).

10.2.3  Classification  of  serial  verb  constructions 
Classification  of  serial  verb  constructions  is  based  on  distinctions  in  composition  and 
meaning. 
PhasaP  serial  verb  constmctions  are  distinct  in  form  from  other  serial  verb  constructions 
since  the  main  verb  can  be  affected  by  ablaut  when  it  combines  with  a  phasal  verb 
expressing  aspect  or  aspect  and  valency  change.  Although  all  verbs  can  be  the  main  verb  in 
some  phasal  constmction  or  other  some  verbs  cannot  occur  with  certain  of  the  six  phasal 
verbs  because  the  verbs  are  semantically  incompatible.  Phasal  constructions  can  occur 
^ Capitals  indicate  a  phasal  verb.  I  use  this  device  to  indicate  that  the  verb  has  both  a  grammatical  function 
and  lexical  meaning.  In  some  examples  the  latter  remains  an  important  aspect  of  the  function  of  these  verbs. 
' The  term  phasal  (cf  Noonan  2007:118  [1985:107])  is  used  here  because  most  of  these  SVCs  are  used  to 
describe  beginning,  ending  or  continuing  something.

within  other  types  of  serial  verb  construction  so  they  are  described  first.  The  following 
sections  describe  phasal  serial  verb  constructions  (§  10.2.4),  phasal/valency  changing 
constructions  with  here  PUT  (§10.2.5)  and  phasal/valency  changing  constructions  with  ne 
STAY  (§10.2.6). 
Serial  verb  constructions  can  occur  with  aspectual  enclitics.  These  constructions  are 
described  in  §10.2.7. 
Coincident  serial  verb  constructions  (§10.2.8)  have  one  verb,  from  an  open  or  a  restricted 
class,  that  represents  a  main  event  and  one  verb  from  a restricted  class  that  modifies  it  in g 
some  way.  Motion  verbs  are  common  in  these  constructions  but  they  can  also  occur  in 
phasal  or  iconic  constructions. 
Iconic  serial  verb  constructions  (§10.2.9)  have  at  least  two  verbs,  either  a  phasal  SVC  and  a 
verb  or  two  phasal  SVCs.  Each  verb  or  phasal  SVC  represents  a  component  in  an  event

10.2.4  Phasal  serial  verb  constructions 
10.2.4.1  Introduction 
Phasal  serial  verb  constructions  consist  of  a main  verb,  in  which  the  final  vowel  can  be 
affected  by  ablaut,  and  a  phasal  verb  which  expresses  aspect.  The  stmcture  of  these 
constmctions  is: 
V affected-by  -ablaut[K/iiR V  phasal 
Phasal  verbs  are  verbs  which  have  lexical  meaning  and  grammatical  function.  They  can 
have  a  grammatical  function  as  the  final  verb  in  a  complex  predicate  (see  §  10.2.4,  10.2.5 
Foley  and  Olson  comment  that  cross-linguistically  ^'intransitive  verbs,  particularly  active  intransitive  verbs 
of motion,  location,  or  posture,  are  favoured  in  a  restricted  slot  to  fonn  nuclear  junctures  with  another  verb  in 
an open  slot"  (1985:41). 
' Koromu  appears  to  be  similar  to  Alamblak  where  Bruce  states  that  "only  commonly  associated  notions 
(states,  events,  participants,  ideas  etc)  can  be  encoded"  in  serial  verb  constructions  (1984:152),

and §  10.2.6).  Verbs  with  the  same  form  can  be  the  sole  verb  in  a  simple  predicate  (see 
§10.2.4.5.1)  or  the  main  lexical  content  verb  in  a  complex  predicate  (see  §10.2.5.2.  When 
these  verbs  occur  as  final  phasal  verbs  they  are  glossed  with  the  basic  lexical  meaning  but 
they  are  written  in  capitals  to  indicate  their  grammatical  function.  The  main  verb  and  the

10.2.5.4  Here  PUT  constructions  and  valency-increase 
10.2.5.4.1  Introduction 
Here PUT  constructions  can  also  indicate  valency-increase.  There  are  several  types  of 
valency  increase  depending  on  the  semantic  nature  of  the  main  verb  and  the  semantic  roles 
of the  core  arguments  (cf  §3.3.4  and  §4.2).  An  agentive  subject  can  be  added  to  stative-
like verbs  (§10.2.5.4.2),  the  subject  of  verbs  with  agent  and  theme  subjects  can  become 
solely  agentive  (§Error!  Reference  source  not  found.)  and  some  verbs  have  an  added 
locative  goal  object  (§  10.2.5.4.4),  beneficiary  object  (§10.2.5.4.5)  or  patient  object 
(§10.2.5.4.6). 
10.2.5.4.2  Adding  agentive  subjects  to  stative-like  verbs 
Stative-like  verbs  include  stative  and  stative-inchoative  verbs  with  theme  subjects  (cf 
§4.2.1.3  and  §4.2.1.4),  experiencer  subject  verbs  (§4.2.2.2.4)  and  experiencer  object  verbs 
(cf  §4.2.6).  When  these  verbs  combine  with  here  PUT  an  agentive  subject  is  added. 
In the  formula  below  the  subject  of  an intransitive  verb  is  represented  on  the  left  of the 
arrow  and  the  arguments  of  the  transitive  here  PUT  construction  with  that  verb  are 
represented  on  the  right.  The  theme  or  experiencer  role  of  the  subject  which  occurs  with 
the intransitive  verb  becomes  the  role  of  the  object  in  the  resulting  classic  causative 
construction.  A  subscript  x  indicates  that  the  subject  (S)  of  the  intransitive  verb  and  the 
object  (O)  of  the  transitive  constnjction  have  the  same  or  a  similar  semantic  role.  In  these 
formulas  1  retain  the  notation  S  for  the  subject  of  transitive  constructions. 
Sx = Theme  or  Experiencer  S  = Agent,  Ox = Theme  or  Experiencer

in context  i.e.  'I  knew  him  up  to  a  point'  and  otherwise  is  lexicalised  as  'met  (him/her)'.

10.2.5.4.7  Adding  a  more  completely  affected  object  patient 
Prototypical  transitive  verbs  have  a  subject  with  the  single  semantic  role  of  agent,  and  an 
object-patient.  The  object  has  something  happen  to  it  that  clearly  affects  it  (Andrews 
1985:68).  With  some  of  these  verbs,  there  is  not  the  same  need  to  increase  valency  or 
adjust  the  semantic  roles  in  a  here  PUT  construction.  With  these  verbs,  for  example  sopo 
'strike,  kill'  orpihi  'touch,  hit'  (cf.  §4.2.2.2.1),  it  appears  that  the  object  is  more  completely 
affected  and  the  subject  acts  with  greater  intensity  when  the  verb  occurs  with  here  PUT. 
The  prototypically  transitive  verb  sopo  'strike/kill'  refers  to  striking  or  clubbing  an  animate 
being.  The  referent  of  the  object  NP  is  clearly  affected  by  the  action.  It  is  stunned  by  the 
blow  and  may  bleed  and  suffer  broken  bones.  Although  the  subject  acts  with  intention,  the 
creature  does  not  necessarily  die  immediately,  for  it  is  common  practice  to  stun  an  animal 
or bird  and  carry  it  away  from  the  hunting  ground  still  alive.  The  following  example  also 
shows  that  the  verb  sopo  'strike/kill'  is  inherently  telic.  In  serializaton  with  the  inherently 
telic  grammaticized  verb  here  PUT,  telicity  is  reaffinned. 
(10.97)  ...iisii  airi  -pii  -e  -te  itsii  oro  -pe

yeue sopo  -neka  -pe  ii  -pii  -r  -ia. 
bird strike/kill-03p  -SS  quote  -HAB  -PRES  -Ip 
'...a  pig  arrives,  we  shoot  it  and  we  club  the  birds.  That's  what  we  do.' 
When  sopo  'strike/kill'  occurs  with  here  PUT  the  referent  of  the  object  NP  actually  dies. 
The  object-patient  is  more  thoroughly  affected.  The  action  is  taken  through  to  its  ultimate, 
irreversible  conclusion.  (It  may  be  that  the  subject  acted  with  greater  intensity  or 
intention.)  The  semantic  roles  of  subject  and  object  remain  the  same.

10.2.6  Phasal/valency  constructions  with  ne  STAY 
This  section  examines  the  use  of  constaictions  with  ne  STAY  under  the  headings  of  stative 
aspect  (§10.2.6.1),  stative  aspect  and  valency  reduction  (§10.2.6.2)  and  verbs  that  do  not 
occur  in  ne STAY  constructions  (§10.2.6.3). 
10.2.6.1  Stative  aspect 
Stative  durative  aspect  is  expressed  by  ne STAY  constructions  with  verbs  which  have  non-
agentive  subjects  (stative-like  verbs),  verbs  which  have  subjects  with  the  dual  semantic 
roles  of  agent  and  goal  (body  placement  verbs)  and  verbs  with  agent  and  theme  subjects 
(intradirective  verbs).  When  verbs  combine  with  ne  STAY,  the  reduced  fonn  of  niene 'be, 
stay,  exist',the  semantic  role  of  the  subject  becomes  closer  to  the  theme  role  and  Hirther 
from  the  agentive/effector  role.  Stative-like  verbs  retain  non-agentive  subjects 
(§ 10.2.6.1.1),  body  placement  verbs  have  subjects  with  reduced  agency  (§  10.2.6.1.2)  and 
intradirective  verbs  lose  the  agentive  role  of  the  subject  (§10.2.6.1.3). 
10.2.6.1.1  Retaining  the  non-agentive  subject  role  of  stative-like  verbs 
Stative-like  verbs  retain  non-agentive  subject  semantic  roles  in  ne  STAY  constructions.  It 
appears  that  a  much  more  permanent  state  of  affairs  can be  indicated  when  ne  STAY  occurs 
with these  stative-inchoative,  experiencer  object  and  some  experiencer  subject  verbs. 
Compare  the  stative-inchoative  verb  (with  a  theme  subject)  in  the  simple  predicate  and  the 
complex  predicate  with  ne  STAY  below.  The  latter  indicates  a  state  of  affairs  which 
remains  for  a long  time. 
" In  Tauya  there  is  an  existential  verb  and  stative  auxiliary  mene-  (MacDonald  1990:192)  and  Siroi  has  the 
auxiliary  WW-  'be'  (Wells  1979:58).

10.2.8  Coincident  serial  verb  constructions 
10.2.8.1  Introduction 
Coincident  serial  verb  constructions  consist  of  two  verbs  (which  are  not  phasal  or  phasal 
and valency-changing  verbs)  that  each  encode  components  of  one  event.  In  some  cases  the 
second  verb  modifies  the  first.  In  all subtypes  one  or  both  verbs  are  from  a restricted  class. 
There  are  four  subtypes:  coincident  motion  (§10.2.8.2),  modifying  (§10.2.8.3),  prohibitive 
(§10.2.8.4)  and  descriptive  (§10.2.8.5). 
10.2.8.2  Coincident  motion  constructions 
10.2.8.2.1  Introduction 
Coincident  motion''^  serial  verb  constiuctions  consist  of  two  intransitive  motion  verbs 
which  refer  to facets  or  aspects  of  one  monophasal  event.  There  are  two  types:  deictic-
movement  and  manner-direction  of  movement  constmctions. 
The  teiTTi coincident  motion  is  adopted  from  Durie  (1997:336). 

[PDF PAGE 413]
384 Chapter  10 
10.2.8.2.2  Deictic-movement  serial  verb  constructions 
Deictic  movement  serial  verb  constructions  consist  of  an  initial  deictic  verb  and  a 
subsequent  direction  or  motion-manner  verb.  The  deictic  verbs  jare  'go'  and  ka  'come' 
describe  direction  in  relation  to  the  speaker.  They  appear  in  the  reduced  forms  jw 'go'  and 
a 'come'  in  the  initial  slots  of  serial  verb  constructions.  The  direction  verbs  mere  'move 
up'  and  mi  'move  down'  describe  absolute  direction  while  motion-manner  verbs  describe 
manner  of  movement,  for  example  alio  'crawl',  aiiri  'swim',  he  'move  fast',  here 'fly', 
heteri 'run',  kekere  'jog,  dance',  koru  'move  up  and  down,  ripple,  bubble'  kiione  'shake 
head (side  to  side),  soroiie 'jump',  tehei  'walk'.  The  construction  is: 
Vdeictic  Vdirection/motion-manner

10.2.9.1.2  Te  'get'-deictic  constructions 
Te 'get'-deictic  constructions  combine  te  'get'  and  a  deictic  verb  to  describe  the  transfer  of 
an object  in  a  deictic  direction.  These  constmctions  te  ka  [get  come]  'bring'  or  te  yure [get

come]  'bring')  or  away  {te  yare [get  go]  'take')  away  from  the  speaker  (cf  §8.5.4).

10.2.9.2  Sequential  serial  verb  constructions 
Sequential  serial  verb  constructions  describe  a  sequence  of  events.  The  three  main  types, 
are initial  motion,  final  motion  and  two-main-verb  sequential  constructions. 
10.2.9.2.1  Initial  motion  sequential  constructions 
Initial motion  sequential  constructions  consist  of  a directional  verb  expressing  deictic  or 
elevational  movement  followed  by  a verb  which  expresses  the  main  event.  The  main  verb 
determines  the  transitivity  of  the  construction  as  it does  in phasal  SVCs  (cf.  § 10.2.4 to 
§10.2.6).  The  verbs  express  a  sequence  of  events  (10.161)  ahhough  in  some  cases  there  is 
possibly  a  purposive  relationship  (10.162).  The  constructions  can  occur  within  phasal 
SVCs.  The  structure  is: 
Vdirection  VITR/IR 
In initial  position  the  deictic  verbs,  ka 'come'  andyare  'go'  appear  in the  reduced  forms  a 
'come'  and  ya 'go'.  In  the  following  examples  these  verbs  occur  in sequence  with  stative 
mene 'be,  stay'  and  a  posture-taking  verb  respectively.

10.3 Adjunct-verb  constructions 
Adjunct-verb  constructions  consist  of  a  lexical  element  or  adjunct  followed  by  a  verb. 
These  constituents  ftjnction  together  as  a  complex  verbal  predicate.  The  adjunct  is  closely 
bound  to  the  verb  but  it  is  not  an  argument  and  it  is  not  cross-referenced  on  the  verb. 
Verbal  morphology  controlling  the  number  of  arguments  occurs  on  the  verb. 
A number  of  the  experiencer  object  constructions  discussed  in  chapter  11  consist  of  an 
adjunct  and  a  verb.  This  section  examines  adjunct-verb  constructions  in  which  a  lexical 
element  expresses  the  meaning  of  the  construction  and  is  followed  by  a  generic  verb  such 
as II  'do'  and  te  'get'  (cf  §4.2.16  and  §4.2.5.1).^ 
Most  borrowed  verbs  (cf  §  4.2.15)  from  Tok  Pisin^^  occur  with  the  generic  verb  ii  'do'  (cf 
§4.2.16).  The  constructions  indicate  that  an  agent  perfonns  an  activity  indicated  by  the 
borrowed  word.  The  structure  is 
Vborrowed  verb  V  u  'do' 
Some  borrowings  from  Tok  Pisin  are  haim  'h\xy\pasim  'stop',  ruitim  'write',  salim  'sell', 
skulim 'teach',  daunim  'swallow'.  One  of  these  occurs  in  the  following  example. 
Adjunct-verb  constructions  (verbal  adjunct  constructions)  are  common  in  highlands  TNG  languages  (Foley 
1986:119).  For  extensive  examples,  see  Kalam  (Pawley  et  al  2000,  Pawley  1993  and  Pawley  In  press).

10.4 Verb  iteration 
Iteration  of  verbs  in  serial  verb  constructions  is  one  aspect  of  complex  verbal  predicate 
formation.  Fully  inflected  verbs  can  also  be  repeated  to  express  prolonged,  continued  or 
repeated  actions,  so  both  serial  verbs  and  Rjlly  inllected  dependent  and  independent  verbs 
are included  in  the  examples  below  (cf  chapter 
Repetition  of  constituents  occurs  in  other  word  classes.  For  example,  expressing  intensity 
with  adverbs  (in  §4.7.4)  or  increased  quantity  or  quality  with  quantifiers  (in  §4.4.2.2).  With 
verbs  iteration  indicates  repeated/prolonged  actions  perfonned  or  experienced  by 
participants.  This  is  indicated,  to  some  extent,  in  partial  reduplication  in  the  fonnation  of 
some  human  nouns  from  verbs  (see  §4.3.2.5.2),  and  in  some  experiencer  object 
constructions  (see  §  11.3.3.2). 
Repeated  serial  verb  constructions  express  prolonged  action  in  the  example  below. 
Some  of  the  data  given  here  is  repeated  from  the  Appendix  on  iteration  in  my  MA  (Priestley  2002). 

[PDF PAGE 430]
Complex  Verbal  Predicates  401

'The  dogs  poured  and  poured  towards  me  (they  kept  coming  and  coming).' 
T2.32.21 
A same  referent  dependent  verb  can  also  be  repeated  to  express  extended,  continued  action. 
It is  common  for  motion  verbs  such  as  deictic  direction  verbs  to  be  repeated  in  this  way. 
They  are  not  repeated  as  uninflected  verb  stems.

'I ran  and  came  and  came  and  came  and  came  and,  came  and  stayed...'  T2.14.6 
Final independent  verbs  can  be  repeated  to  express  a  repetitive  action.

In the  first  line  of  the  following  example  a  fully  inflected  serial  verb  construction  is 
repeated.  The  repetition  indicates  prolonged  action  and  it  also  provides  a  location  for 
further  information  to  be  added.  In  the  next  two  lines  a  whole  clause  is  repeated.  Both  the 
partially  repeated  clause  and  the  fully  repeated  clause  are  a  means  of  expressing  tail-head 
linkage  (cf  §14.4.3)  and  the  repetition  can  serve  as  a  hesitation  device  or  gap  filler  which 
provides  the  speaker  time  to  think  before  making  the  next  point.

Chapter  11  Impersonal  experiencer  object  constructions 
11.1 Introduction 
This  chapter  describes  impersonal  experiencer  object  constructions.'  These  constructions 
refer  to  involuntaiy  physical  and  psychological  conditions  or  sensations  and  form  the  basis 
of the  impersonal  experiential  clauses  described  in  §3.3.4.4.  Following  a  brief  introduction 
to impersonal  experiencer  object  constructions  in  Papuan  languages  (§  11.2), Koromu 
experiencer  object  constmctions  are  discussed  under  the  following  headings:  basic 
characteristics  of  experiencer  object  constructions  (§  11.3),  basic  condition  verb  experiencer 
object  constructions  (§  11.4),  experiencer  object  constructions  with  adjunct  nouns  (§  11.5), 
experiencer  object  constmctions  with  a  stimulus  noun  as  subject  and  a  body  part  noun  as 
adjunct  (§  11.6),  reasons  why  adjunct  nouns  are  not  analysed  as  subjects  (§  11.7) and 
experiencer  object  constmctions  and  the  switch  reference  system  (§  11.8). 
11.2 Impersonal  experiencer  object  constructions  in  Papuan  languages 
Experiencer  object  constmctions  are  impersonal  constmctions  which  describe  an 
uncontrolled  state  or  event.  Impersonal  constructions  are  common  in  Papuan  languages  as 
a means  of  describing  bodily  and  mental  processes  which  are  not  initiated  or  controlled  by 
the experiencer  (Foley  1986:121-124,  Pawley  et  al  2000:154).  The  temiinology  used  to 
describe  these  constmctions,  their  fonn  and  the  way  they  work  varies  from  language  to 
language.  However,  they  generally  have  a  third  person  singular  subject  suffix  on the  verb 
for which  the  referent  is  not  easily  identified  and  an  object  NP,  or  object  suffix,  which  has 
In the  remainder  of  the  chapter  these  constructions  are  referred  to  as  experiencer  object  constructions. 

[PDF PAGE 433]
404 Chapter  11 
the semantic  role  of  experiencer.  In  many  cases  there  is  at least  one  nominal  participant  for 
which  it  is  difficuh  to identify  the  grammatical  role.  Robert's  (2001)  detailed  description 
of lexical  impersonal  constructions  in  the  Madang  language  of  Amele,  shows  that  both  the 
experiencer  NP  and  a  second  NP  in  these  constructions  exhibit  some  properties  of  subjects. 
The  experiencer  NP  refers  to the  pragmatic  topic  while  the  other  NP  refers  to  the  semantic 
agent  which  is  cross-referenced  as  subject  on  the  verb.  Pawley  et  al  (2000)  and  Pawley 
(2007)  discuss  experiencer  object  (involuntary  experience)  constructions  in  the  Madang 
language  of  Kalam.  Pawley  (2007)  states  that  this  type  of  verbal  construction  is  the  most 
difficult  to analyze  and  suggests  that  while  some  condition  nominals  can  be  analysed  as 
subjects,  some  are  adjuncts  and  some  function  as  both  subject  and  adjunct.  Anamuxra 
(Ingram  2001:319-321),  Erima  (Colbum  1979),  Hua  (Haiman  1980:357-360),  Siroi 
(1979:64-65),  Tauya  (MacDonald  1990:  187-191)  and  Usan  (1987:139-140,203-204)  are 
amongst  many  other  languages  which  have  impersonal  constructions.

(11.3)  Ea  i  perani^  -s  -a.

1: 'Yesterday  I  was  hungry.'

Like  Koromu  the  English  translation  in  (1)  has  one  core  NP  argument.  Although  the 
translation  does  not  reflect  the  fact  that  in  Koromu  there  are  two  core  argument  suffixes  and 
that the  experiencer  is  an  object  rather  than  the  subject,  the  English  subject  does  lack 
control  over  the  state  just  as  the  object  experiencer  does  in  Koromu. 
Translation  (2)  has  two  core  arguments  so  although  it  reflects  the  structure  of  the  verb  it 
does  not  reflect  the  structure  of  the  whole  construction.  It  is misleading  conceptually 
because  it  suggests  a  third  person  stimulus  which  does  not  occur.  If  this  type  of  translation 
is used  the  third  person  singular  subject  suffix  is best  understood  as  a  dummy  subject  as  in 
'it is  raining'.^ 
Translation  (3)  has  two  core  arguments  and  the  added  verb  'affect'  because  the  condition 
expressed  by  the  Koromu  verb  is  expressed  in  English  by  the  NP  subject.  The  English 
noun  reflects  the  nominal  character  of  experiencer  object  constructions,  insofar  as  the 
Koromu  verb  roots  also  function  as  nouns. 
The  importance  ofthe  experiencer  object  is  confirmed  by  the  fact  that  the  reflexive,  which 
normally  only  occurs  with  subject  NPs,  can  occur  with  the  object  NP  (cf  §3.3.2.6).  in

which appears  to derive  from  pera 'taro'  and  orii  'insides.' 
' An  impersonal  or  dummy  subject  'it'  is  not  used  in  this  context  in  English.

11.5 Experiencer  object  constructions  with  adjunct  nouns 
11.5.1 Introduction 
Some  experiencer  object  constructions  have  an  adjunct  noun  immediately  before  the  verb. 
They  are  described  here  as  condition  verb  experiencer  object  constructions  with  stimulus 
nouns  (§  11.5.2),  condition  verb  experiencer  object  constructions  with  body  part  nouns 
(§ 11.5.3),  and  si  'give'  experiencer  object  constructions  with  condition  nouns  (§  11.5.4). 
^ The  animate  -  inanimate  distinction  has  proved  to  be  significant  in  other  areas  of  the  grammar.  For  example 
O suffixes  refer  to  animate  referents  (cf  §4.2.2.1  .and  §4.2.4,1)  and  there  are  different  locative  postpositions 
for  animate  and  inanimate  referents  (cf  §7.3).

11.5.2  Condition  verb  experiencer  object  constructions  with  stimulus  nouns 
11.5.2.1  Basic  characteristics  of  experiencer  object  constructions  with  stimulus  nouns 
In condition  verb  experiencer  object  constructions  with  stimulus  nouns  a  non-referential 
noun  which  is  'adjunct'  to  the  verb  expresses  the  stimulus  for  the  condition/sensation 
expressed  by  the  verb.  An  optional  experiencer  object  NP  can  occur.  The  structure  is: 
(NPOexperiencer)  Ntheme:stimulus  Vcondition-Osx-3s.sx 
This  group  of  experiencer  object  constructions  can  be  subdivided  into  three  groups,  set 
adjunct-verb  constructions  (§  11.5.2.2),  free  adjunct-verb  constructions  (§  11.5.2.3)  and  non-
finite complement  clause  adjunct  constructions  (§  11.5.2.4). 
11.5.2.2  Set  adjunct-verb  constructions 
Set adjunct-verb  constructions  are  set  expressions  in  which  a  specific  adjunct  noun 
combines  with  a  specific  verb.  The  constmctions  refer  to  physical  or  psychological 
conditions  or  sensations.''  Of  these  examples  there  is  no  evidence  that  the  adjunct  teri 
'cold'  can  be  possessed,  quantified  or  questioned.  However,  eri  'fear'  and  oni  'insides 
(body  part)'  can  both  occur  as  referential  nouns  in  other  grammatical  contexts. 
' The  expressions  teri  mete  'cold  body',  eri  mete  'fear  body'  and  oru  mere  'insides  move  up'  can  all  function 
as NPs  and  the  latter  can  also  fijnction  as  a dynamic  verb.  Apart  from  non-isolable  teri  'cold'  the  constituents 
within  the  compounds  are  derived  from  other  word  classes.  Eri  'fear'  and  oni  'insides/feel'  can  occur 
elsewhere  as  nouns  or  verbs,  mere  'move  up'  is  a  verb  and  mete  functions  as  the  noun  'body'  or  as  the 
reduplicated  verb  form  metemete 'sense'.  Nokonoh)  is  derived  from  the  adjective  nokono 'good'.

11.7 Reasons  why  adjunct  nouns  are  not  analysed  as  subjects 
In experiencer  object  constructions  it  is  initially  a  little  difficult  to detennine  whether  the 
third  singular  subject  suffix  cross-references  an  impersonal  referent,  or  the  adjunct  noun. 
Many  of  the  tests  for  identifying  subjects  are  indetenninate  in  this  context.  For  example, 
the pronominal  test  does  not  apply  since  stimulus  nouns  cannot  be  represented  by 
pronouns.  In  addition,  subject  agreement  cannot  apply  because  (a)  bodily  function  nouns 
are uncountable  and  (b)  the  third  singular  subject  suffix  can  be  used  for  inanimate  subject 
nouns,  such  as  plants  and  crops,  even  when  they  are  plural  (cf  (3.24)  in  §3.3.2.2.1  and 
(9.18)  in  §9.3.2.3). 

[PDF PAGE 446]
Impersonal  experiencer  object  constmctions  417 
However,  there  is  evidence  from  grammar  and  information  structure,  in  both  natural 
recorded  text  and  elicited  data,  that  in  most  experiencer  object  constructions  stimulus,  body 
pai1 and  condition  nouns  are  adjunct  nouns  (cf.  §  11.5, and  for  an exception,  see  §  11.6). To 
begin  with,  the  nouns  cannot  be  expanded  into  full  NPs  like  subject  NPs.  Furthermore,  the 
order  of  core  arguments  and  the  position  of  the  negative  particle  tai  before  the  adjunct 
suggest  that  these  nouns  are  adjuncts. 
The  default  word  order  in  the  basic  clause  structure  of  transitive  verbal  clauses  is  AOV  (see 
§3.3.4.2  and  §  13.3). OAV  word  order  only  occurs  when  the  O  is  a  link  (with  or  without  uo-
marking).  There  are  no  O  links  with  no-marking  (see  §  14.3.2.2),  that  represent  stimuli, 
body  parts  or  conditions,  in  either  natural  or  elicited  experiencer  object  constructions.  The 
evidence  below  indicates  that  O  links  without  ;/o-marking  (see  §  14.4.2)  do  not  occur  either. 
In other  verbal  constructions,  when  O  is  an  unmarked  link,  either  =te  'prominent  subject' 
follows  A to  disambiguate  it  from  initial  O  (see  §  13.5.4),  or  it  is  clear  from  the  discourse 
context  that  the  initial  noun  is  an  O  link  (see  §14.4.2).'^  However,  in  experiencer  object 
constructions  the  animate  experiencer  object  NP  always  occurs  before  the  stimulus,  body 
part  or  condition  noun  (11.8).  If  one  of  the  latter  were  the  subject  it  could  be  expected  to 
occur  in  initial  position,  or  with  the  =te  'prominent  subject'  enclitic,  at  least  some  of  the 
time,  but  this  does  not  happen.  Thus  the  following  sentence  is  only  acceptable  without  the 
=te 'prominent  subject'  enclitic.

Chapter  12  Basic  Clause  Combining 
12.1 Introduction 
This  chapter  introduces  some  of  the  basic  structures  which  combine  two  or  more  clauses.  It 
begins  with  a  brief  overview  of  clause  chains  (§12.2)  (cf  §9.4).  Further  sections  describe 
complement  clauses  (§12.3),  relative  clauses  (§12.4),  non-specific-subject  nominalised 
clauses  withpao  as  NPs  (§12.5),  adverbial  sei  'orientation'  clauses  (§  12.6), clauses 
combined  with  iimo  'adversative'  (§12.7)  disjunctive  clauses  combined  with  temolte 
'possibility'  (§12.8)  and  the  pre-quote  structure  with  the  basic  quotation  structure  (§12.9). 
Compared  to  Indo-European  languages  there  are  few  adverbial  and  complement  clause 
types.  However,  some  adverbial  clauses  and  the  conditional  clauses  are  expressed  in  link 
constructions  with  (;o-marking  (see  §14.3.3).  In  addition,  orientation,  reason,  similitive  and 
instrumental  concepts  can  be  expressed  by  postpositional  phrases  in  which  u  'that'  is  the 
object  of  the  postposition  and  makes  anaphoric  reference  to earlier  information  (see  §7.6). 
12.2 Clause  chains 
Clause  chains  consist  of  one  or  more  dependent  clauses  followed  by  an  independent  clause 
(cf  §9.4).  The  dependent  clauses  are  not  subordinate  to  the  final  independent  clause. 

[PDF PAGE 455]
426  Chapter  12 
Instead  each  clause  has  its  own  set  of  core  and  peripheral  arguments  and  forms  part  of  a 
chain  of  clauses.' 
Each  dependent  clause  has  a  dependent  verb  or  a  serial  verb  construction  with  a  final 
dependent  verb.  Dependent  verbs  have  a  dependency  suffix  and  may  be  partially  inflected 
for tense,  subject  and  indicative  mood  (cf  §9.4).  They  are  dependent  for  llill  specification 
of tense,  subject,  aspect  and  mood  on  the  nearest  subsequent  verb  which  is  fiilly  inflected. 
Independent  clauses  are  headed  by  independent  verbs  or  by  serial  verb  constructions  with  a 
final independent  verb.  These  clauses  can  be  the  only  clause  in  an  utterance  or  the  final 
clause  in  a  clause  chain.  Independent  verbs,  apart  from  ia  'be  not'  have  tense-subject 
indicative  suffixes,  imperative  or  desiderative  suffixes  (cf  §9.3).  Aspect  suffixes  are 
opfional  and  they  can  be  followed  by  modality  enclitics  or  particles  (cf  §3.2.2.2). 
In the  clause  chain  below  four  dependent  verbs  are  followed  by  a  final  clause  in  which  a

When  describing  clause  chains  in  Papuan  languages  Foley  (1986:177)  states  "They  do  not  function  as 
arguments  of  some  main  clause.  They  do  not  function  as  embedded  parts  within  a  whole,  but  are  linked  to  a 
fully  inflected  verb  in  a linear  string,  much  like  beads  on  a  necklace." 
Temporal  succession  and  temporal  overlap  are  common  characteristics  of  clause  chaining  in  Papuan 
languages  (Roberts  1997:139-142).

12.3 Complement  clauses 
12.3.1  Introduction 
A complement  clause  flmctions  as  an  argument  of  a  complement-taking  predicate  (CTP) 
(Noonan  2007:53  [1985:43]).  Complement  clauses  are  described  in  the  following  sections 
on finite  complement  clauses  (§  12.3.2),  non-finite  complement  clauses  with  -upu  (§  12.3.3) 
and non-finite  complement  clauses  with  -apesi  (§12.3.4). 
12.3.2  Finite  complement  clauses 
A finite  complement  clause  occurs  in  a  basic  quotation  structure  which  describes  the 
transfer  of  info  iTnation by  an  agentive  subject.  The  quoted  speech  (a  word,  discourse, 
thought  or  sound)  is  the  complement  which  contains  the  transferred  information  (Noonan 
2007:121  [1985:110]).  The  complement-taking  predicate  is  the  altemating  transitive  verb  it 
'quote'  (see  §4.2.6)  on  which  tlie  addressee  is  optionally  cross-referenced  as  the 
recipient/goal  by  an  O  suffix  (cf  §3.3.3).  The  agentive  subject  is  optionally  represented  by 
an NP.  The  order  of  the  main  constituents  is  fixed,  as  indicated  in  the  structure  below. 
(NPS)  COMP=  direct  speech/intention  V  =  u  'quote'  (with  optional  O  suffix) 
A sentential  adverb  (cf.  §4.7.6)  or  an  adverb,  such  as  aisapu 'just'  (cf  §4.7.5),  can  occur 
before  the  quoted  speech.

thematic  argument  structure  Sx=  Agent,  Oiy=  Goal,  02=  (quote)  Theme.

12.3.3  Non-finite  complement  clauses  with  -apu 
Non-finite  complement  clauses  with  -apu  'nominalisation'  are  described  in  sections  on 
their  basic  characteristics  (§12.3.3.1),  the  experiencer  S  immediate  perception  predicate  ese 
'hear'  (§12.3.3.2),  the  experiencer  S  knowledge  predicated/para/  'know'  (§12.3.3.3),  the 
experiencer  O  desiderative/non-desiderative  predicates  o/7/  'feel  like/want'  and  maikohii 
'do  not  feel  like,  do  not  want  to'  (§12.3.3.4),  the  experiencer  O  mental  predicates  iiriiriiu 
'think  about/consider'  and  iipu  iimnm  'sense'  (§12.3.3.5)  and  the  serial  verb  construction 
warike here  'cause  harm'  (§12.3.3.6). 
12.3.3.1  Non-finite  complement  clauses  with  -apu:  basic  characteristics 
A non-finite  complement  clause  with  -apu  'nominalisation'  forms  a  nominalised  predicate. 
This  can  be  an  argument  of  a complement-taking  predicate.  The  clause  has  a  verb  stem  (or 
final verb  in  a  serial  verb  construction)  that  has  no  tense-subject,  object,  aspect  or  mood 
inflections.  The  verb  stem  is  followed  by  the  suffix  -apu. Nominalised  verbs  with  -apu 
also  function  as  pre-nominal  modifiers  (cf  §5.2.2.2.6)  and  heads  of  NPs  (§5.9). 
The  time  reference  of  non-finite  complement  clauses  with  -apu  is  dependent  on  the  time 
reference  of  the  complement-taking  predicate.  Non-finite  complement  clauses  are  objects 
of complement-taking  experiencer  subject  predicates  (§4.2.2.2.4)  and  adjuncts  of 
complement-taking  experiencer  object  predicates  (cf  §4.2.6  and  §  11.5.2.4).  The 
nominalised  predicate  in  a  non-finite  complement  can  have  a  notional  subject  argument  in 
an associafive,  possessive  relationship  with  the  predicate  (see  §  12.3.3.2). 
The  examples  below  show  that  object  NPs  and  oblique  arguments,  like  postpositional 
phrases,  can  occur  in  non-finite  complement  clauses.  The  notional  object  of  the 
nominalised  predicate  retains  the  form  it  has  in  basic  clause  structure.  The  second  example 
also  shows  an  adjunct-verb  construction  (see  §  10.3) within  a  non-finite  complement.

12.4 Relative  clauses 
12.4.1  Introduction 
Relative  clauses  modify  the  head  noun  of  an  NP.  Within  them  the  NPrd,  or  relativized  noun 
phrase  (Payne  1997:325),  is  coreferential  with  the  head  noun  of  the  matrix  clause  (Andrews 
2007:206).  The  restrictive  type  of  relative  clause  restricts  the  set  of  potential  referents  of 
the head  noun  "by  giving  a  proposition  that  must  be  tme  of  the  actual  referents  of  the 
overall  construction"  (Comrie  1989:143)  while  non-restrictive  relative  clauses  provide 

[PDF PAGE 466]
Basic Clause  Combining  437 
extra infoimation  about  a  referent  that  is  already  flilly  identifiable.  The  sections  below 
describe  Koromu  postnominal  relative  clauses  (§12.4.2),  internally  headed  relative  clauses 
(§ 12.4.3),  prenominal  locative  relative  clauses  with  the  postposition  o  (§12.4.4)  and  relative 
clauses  with  the  postposition/^ao  (§12.4.5).  These  are  all restrictive  relative  clauses. 
12.4.2  Postnominal  relative  clauses 
12.4.2.1  Introduction 
Postnominal  relative  clauses  have  a  finite  verb  and  describe  specific  incidents  connected 
with the  referent  of  the  head  noun.  There  are  two  types:  posmominal  relative  clauses  with 
the relative  pronoun  une  and  postnominal  relative  clauses  with  a  gap for  NPrei-
12.4.2.2  Postnominal  relative  clauses  and  the  relative  pronoun  une 
Posmominal  relative  clauses  can  have  a  relative  pronoun  une  representing  the  argument 
which  is  coreferential  with  the  head  noun  of  the  main  clause.  Une  can  refer  to a  subject, 
direct  object,  indirect  object,  oblique  or  object  of  a postposition  and it  retains  the  position 
required  of  the  ai'gument  to  which  it  refers.  In  the  example  below  une indicates  the  subject

12.4.5  Nominalised  clauses  with  the  postposition  pao as  relative  clauses 
12.4.5.1  Introduction 
Nominalised  clauses  followed  by  the  postposition  pao 'inanimate  referent  genitive" 
(IGEN)'  (cf  §6.6)  consist  minimally  of  a verb  marked  for  tense  and  subject  person-number. 
Aspectual  suffixes  and  object  and  oblique  arguments  occur  with  these  clauses  in  some 
contexts.'^  These  chai-acteristics  are  similar  to  those  in  clausal  nominalisations  described 
by Comrie  and  Thompson  (2007:376  [1985:392]): 
The  characteristic  feature  of this  type  of  nominalization  is  that  there  is  no  evidence 
in favor  of  viewing  its  head  as  a  lexical  noun.  That  is,  the  verb  in  such  a  clause 
typically  has  no  nominal  characteristics  and  often  has  such  verbal  characteristics  as 
person  and  number,  though  it  may  be  lacking  in  tense-aspect  marking.'^ 
Nominalised  clauses  with  the  postposition  pao 'inanimate  genitive',  commonly  fianction  as 
relative  clauses  in  the  pre-nominal  or  postnominal  modifier  positions  (§5.2.1).  In  example 
(12.43)  the  nominalised  clause  occurs  prenominally  like  prenominal  locative  relative 
clauses  with  the  postposition  o  'genitive'  (§12.4.4).''^ 
" Inanimate  referent  genitives  are  referred  to  as  inanimate  genitives  after  this  point. 
Tauya  has  geioindive  nominahsations  which  fijnction  as  pre-nominal  quahfiers  or  as  nouns.  Marked  by  the 
suflTix -mo they  are  "invariably  inflected  with  the  l/2sg.  aorist  desinence  /e/"  (McDonald  1990:110). 
For example,  Lakhota  has  clausal  nominalisations  in  which  the  article  is  suffixed  to  a  sentence  which  has 
"no  change  whatsoever  from  its  fomi  in  a finite  sentence"  (Comrie  and  Thomson  2007:377  [1985:392-393]). 
Comrie  and  Thomson  (2007:379  [1985:394-395])  discuss  examples  of  nominalisations  which  function  as 
relative  clauses  in  Luisefio,  a  Uto-Aztecan  language,  in  Dieguefio,  a  Yuman  language,  in  Quechua  and  in  a 
number  of  languages  of  the  American  west  and  southwest.

" "Reduced  clauses  have  a  restricted  range  of  tense-aspect-mood  marking...  and  may  furthermore  have  some

12.6 Sei  'orientation'  adverbial  clause 
A sei 'orientation'  adverbial  clause  indicates  the  reason  or  purpose  for  the event  expressed 
in a subsequent  main  clause  (cf.  §7.4.1.2).  For  morphophonological  reasons  these 
adverbial  clauses  have  first  or  second  person  singular  subjects. 
When  sei  'orientation'  is  expressed  following  a clause  with  a  first or  second  person  plural, 
third person  singular  or  third  person  plural  subject,  an anaphoric  demonstrative  pronoun  ii 
'that'  is  object  of  the postposidon  sei  'orientation'.  This  pronoun  refers  back  to 
'orientation'  information  in  the  preceding  clause  (cf  §7.6.2).  These  subject  suffixes  all end 
with mid  or  low  vowels  (cf  §9.3.2.2).  The  high  back  vowel  of  u 'that'  is  not affected  by 
the presence  of  these  vowels  as  it is by the  final  high  front  vowel  /i/  in the  first  and  second 
person  singular  subject  suffixes.  Following  the  high  fi-ont vowel,  the  subsequent  anaphoric 
pronoun  ii  'that'  is  elided  and  thus  sei follows  immediately  after  the finite  clause  to  form  a 
'reason/purpose'  adverbial  clause.  For  examples  see  (12.65)  and  (12.66)  below.^' 
When  the  main  clause  has  a  different  subject  the  sei 'orientation'  clause  expresses  a  reason 
tor the  main  event. 
(12.65)  /  ka  -r  -i  sei  eri  -r  -a. 
Is come  -PRES  -Is  ORNT  fear  -PRES  -3s 
'Because  I  am coming  he  is afraid.'  D3.129.1b 
When  the  main  clause  has  the  same  subject  as  the  sei 'orientaiton'  clause  it  appears  that 
either  a reason  or  a puipose  can  be  expressed. 
These  clauses  are  further  examples  of  subordinate  clauses  in  the  same  environment  as  nouns  (cf.  §12.4.4)

12.9 The  pre-quote  strategy  and  the  basic  quotation  structure 
The pre-quote  strategy  consists  of  an utterance  verb  which  gives  details  on the  nature  of  a 
speech  act.  This  is  the  minimal  constituent  in  a pre-quote  formula  which  occurs  as  a 
separate  clause  juxtaposed  in  front  of  a basic  quotation  structure  (see  §  12.3.2).^^ 
(Pre-quote)  Complement  clause  u-  'quote' 
The pre-quote  formula  consists  of  an optional  subject  NP,  an  optional  recipient  object  NP 
and an  utterance  predicate.  It  does  not  include  quoted  speech.  The  pre-quote  structure  is: 
(NPS)  (NPO)  Vutterance 
Utterance  verbs  that  can  occur  in  the  pre-quote  are: 
sasi 'tell  non-third  singular  referent' 
sau 'tell  third  singular  referent' 
to/tohoi 'ask' 
yo 'call' 
The speech  verb  in  the  pre-quote  fonnula  and  the  utterance  predicate  ii 'quote'  can  both 
have  an  object  suffix  which  refers  to the  recipient.

Chapter  13  NP Realisation,  Omission  and  Prominence 
13.1 Introduction 
This  chapter  is  concerned  with  aspects  of  grammar  and  information  structure  described  in 
sections  on  principles  of  information  structure  (§13.2),  NP  realisation  (§13.3),  NP  omission 
(§13.4),  and  subject  NPs  with  the  =te  'prominent  subject'  enclitic  (§13.5). 
13.2  Principles  of  information  structure 
13.2.1  Introduction 
This  section  provides  a  background  to  understanding  Koromu  grammar  and  information 
structure  with  a  brief  introduction  to  information  packaging  (§13.2.2),  information-status 
(§ 13.2.3)  and  topic  continuity  (§13.2.4). 
13.2.2  Information  packaging 
Two  important  elements  of  information  packaging  in  the  sentence,  recognised  by  many 
different  approaches,  are  the  focus-background  distinction  and  optional  sentence-initial 
topic-like  expressions.  Thus  Vallduvi  (1992:46)  proposes  that  information  packaging  in 
the  sentence  consists  of  the  FOCUS  and  the  GROUND  and  that  the  latter  can  be  subdivided 
into  the  LINK  and  the  TAIL: 
S=  {FOCUS,  GROUND} 
GROUND  =  [LINK,  TAIL]. 

[PDF PAGE 487]
458  Chapter  13 
In this  approach  the  focus  is  the  "informative",  "nonelidable  part  of  the  sentence,  since  it  is 
the only  contribution  to  the  hearer's  knowledge  store  at  the  time  of  utterance  (or  so  the 
speaker  assumes)"  (1992:46).  The  focal,  informative  part  of  the  sentence,  in  Koromu,  is 
described  in  this  chapter. 
In some  contexts  the  whole  clause  is  new,  informative,  focus  infoirnation.  Examples  of 
these  "all-focus  structures"  (cf  §  13.3) are  in  general  descriptions,  "[pThe  BOSS  called]",  in 
pure  existential  sentences:  "Waiter!  [pThere's  a  fly  in  my  cream  of  broccoli  soup]!",  and  in 
sentence  fragments:  "What  doesn't  the  boss  like?"  "BROCCOLI."  (1992:51).  Answers  to 
the question  "What's  happened?"  are  also  all-focus  structures,  for  example,  in  the  response 
"John  found  a  sheep  in  the  house." 
In the  response  below,  "a  sheep"  is  the  only  contribution  to  the  hearer's  knowledge-store. 
The  remainder  of  the  sentence  is  the  ground  (see  chapter  14),  which  includes  the  link  and 
the tail  (in  English  part  of  the  tail  can  occur  before  the  focus). 
(13.1)  A.  "What  did  John  find  in  the  house?" 
B. "John  found  a  sheep  in  the  house." 
LINK  TAILl  FOCUS  TAIL2 
13.2.3  Information-status 
Some  key  aspects  of  infonnation-status  which  are  relevant  to  a  discussion  of  infonnation 
structure  are  the  concepts  of  hearer-old  and  hearer-new  infonnation,  discourse-old  and 
discourse-new  infonnation  and  inferrable  infonnation  (Prince  1992:300-3  10). 
Hearer-old  infonnation  is  infonnation  which  the  speaker  assumes  that  the  hearer  knows. 
For example,  someone  who  says  "I'm  waiting  for  it to  be  noon  so  I  can call  Sandy 
Thompson" assumes  that  the  hearer  knows  of  an  entity  with  the  proper  name  Sandy 
Thompson. In  contrast,  hearer-new  information  is  expressed  when  the  speaker  assumes  that 
the entity  is  not  known  to  the  hearer  as  in  "I'm  waiting  for  it to  be  noon  so  I  can cafl 
someone". Discourse-old  infonnation  is  infonnation  which  has  already  been  mentioned 

[PDF PAGE 488]
NP Realisation,  Omission  and  Prominence  459 
earlier  m  a  discourse.  Discourse-new  information  has  not  been  mentioned  earlier  in  the 
discourse.  When  infonnation  is  hearer-new  it  is also  discourse-new  (1992:303-304). 
InfeiTable  infonnation  or  entities  are  technically  hearer-new  and  discourse-new.  However, 
the speaker  may  assume  that  the  hearer  is  able  to  infer  the  existence  of  an entity  since  there 
is a trigger  entity  in  the  discourse  (discourse-old)  with  which  the  inferrable  entity  is 
associated.  For  example,  in  "He  passed  by  the  Bastille  and  the  door  was  painted  purple" 
the door  is  discourse  -new but  it  is  treated  as  though  it  is known  to  the  hearer  because  the 
speaker  assumes  that  the  hearer  knows  that  a  building  like  the  Bastille  will  have  a  door 
associated  with  it  (1992:304-305). 
13.2.4  Topic  continuity 
In this  description  the  terni  "topic"  is  used  to  refer  to the  "topic  continuity"  of  participants 
or entities  in  a  discourse  (Givon  1983).  U  is "most  common  for  one  topic  to  be  the 
continuity  marker",  representing  "the  participant  most  cnicially  involved  in  the  action 
sequence",  "most  closely  associated  with  the  higher-level  theme  of  the  paragraph"  and 
"most  likely  to  be  coded  as  the  primaiy topic  -  or grammatical subject  -  of the  vast  majority 
of sequentially  ordered  clauses/sentences"  (Givon  1983:8). 
13.3 NP  realisation 
Clauses  in  which  core  argument  NPs  ai'e  expressed  in  fiill  occur  at  points  in  a  discourse 
where  participants  are  introduced  or  reintroduced  as  part  of  the  informative,  non-elidable 
focus  (Vallduvi  1992:46).  In  constructions  of  this  type  the  whole  clause  is  in focus.' 
All-focus  clauses  can  occur  in  thetic,  presentational  contexts  (Vallduvi  1993:11),  such  as 
responses  to  questions,  where  the  questions  provide  no  infonnation  about  the  core 
argument(s).  In  such  responses  the  core  argument  NPs  are  new  and  informative,  and  if  the 
clause  is  transitive  the  default  word  order  is  AOV  (cf  §3.3.2.3  and  §3.3.4.2). 
' Constructions  in  which  all  the  constituents  are  in  focus  are  described  as  all-focus  sentences  in  Vallduvi 
(1992:51-52)  and  as  event-reporting  sentences  and  sentence-focus  structures  in  Lambrecht  (1987:366  and 
1994:222-223,233-235).

13.4 NP  omission 
13.4.1  Subject  NP  omission 
Subject  NPs  are  omitted  when  there  is  'topic  continuity'  in  a  discourse  because  'what  is 
continuing  is  more  predictable'  and  'what  is  more  predictable  is  easier  to  process'  (Givon 
1983:12).  The  most  continuous/accessible  topics  can  be  coded  by  zero  anaphora  or  by 
"unstressed/bound  pronouns  or  grammatical  agreement"  (1983:17).  Koromu  continuous/ 
accessible  topics  are  minimally  marked  by  grammatical  agreement  for  the  subject  on  both 
independent  and  dependent  verbs.^ 
Table  13.1  gives  information  about  transitive  clauses  from  recordings  of  approximately 
four  hours  of  text.  Itshows  that  while  there  are  68  examples  of  overt  subject  NPs  in  AOV 
order  transitive  clauses  (cf  §  13.3) there  are  at  least  270  clauses  which  have  subject  marking 
on the  verb  but  no  subject  NPs  and  64  examples  of  AV  clauses  in  which  O  is  omitted 
^ Complete  zero  anaphora  only  occurs  when  a  verb  occurs  with  the  desiderative  suffix  -apesi  since  this  suffix 
is mutually  exclusive  with  tense-subject:person-number  suffixes  (see  §9.3.4).

13.5 Prominent  NPs  and  the  =te  'prominent  subject'  enclitic 
13.5.1  Introduction 
The  enclitic  =te  'prominent  subject'  (cf  §3.3.2.4  and  §5.11)  is  optional  with  subject  NPs. 
It has  the  same  form  as,  and  probably  derives  from,  the  instrumental  postposition  te.  which 
suggests  that  it  may  have  indicated  ergative  case  in  the  past.  Synchronically,  =te 
'prominent  subject'  provides  syntactic  and  discourse  infomiation.  It  occurs  with  inanimate 
referent  subject  NPs  which  are  effectors  (§13.5.2)  and  with  the  animate  referent 
interrogative  word  me  'who'  in  all  clause  types  (§13.5.3).  h  distinguishes  the  subject  NP  in 
transitive  clauses  in  contexts  where  there  would  otherwise  be  ambiguity  between  the 
subject  and  object  NP  (§13.5.4).  h  is  also  widely  used  in  transitive,  intransitive  and 
nonverbal  clauses  to  indicate  that  an  NP  is  the  most  salient,  prominent  referent  at  a 
particular  point  in  a  discourse  (§13.5.5).  For  example,  in  a  narrative  about  an  accident 
which  happened  when  several  men  were  hunting  pig,  the  enclitic  =te  'prominent  subject' 
attaches  to  the  NP  which  refers  to  the  man  who  actually  shot  the  pig. 
(13.19)  ...Maks=te  it  pate  oro  ho  -r  -a. 
Max =PS  there  S/L  shoot  PUT  -PRES  -3s 
'...Max  shot  h  (a  pig)  there.'  T6.5.21 
Prominence  with  subject  NPs  is  similar  to  the  concept  of  prominence  discussed  by  Choi 
"the  salient  or  prominent  part  which  is  the  center  of  interest  in  the  cuirent  discourse" 
(1999:77)  and  the  "standing-out  property"  which,  like  contrastive  focus,  selects  a  value 
from  a  set  of  alternatives  (1999:88).  However,  in  Choi's  discussion  prominence  only  occurs 
either  in  the  focus  part  of  the  clause,  or  in  the  link  (the  topic-like  element  in  the  ground) 

[PDF PAGE 496]
NP Realisation,  Omission  and  Prominence  467 
(1999:92).  In  Koromu  a  prominent  subject  NP  can  occur  in the  focus  (as in the  example 
above),  the  link,  as  in (13.50)  in  §  13.5.5.2.1,  or  the  tail,  as in (13.51)  in §  13.5.5.2.1. 
The use  of  =te  'prominent  subject'  is  also  affected  by  semantic  factors  (cf  the  animacy 
hierarchy  in  Silverstein  1976).  With  an  inanimate  referent  NP  in  a  transitive  clause  =te  can 
indicate  that  the  NP  is  an  effector  rather  than  a  non-agentive  subject  (§13.5.2);  it  is 
obligatory  with  the  animate  inten'ogative  word  me  'who'  (§13.5.3);  and  when  NPs  have  the 
same  relative  animacy  as  each  other  =te  disambiguates  the  subject  from  the  object  if  the 
meaning  of  the  verb,  word  order  or  verbal  suffixation  does  not  do  so  (§ 13.5.4). 
Table  13.2  below  was  originally  compiled  to  provide  an  overview  of  the  use  of  =te 
'prominent  subject'  in  transitive  clauses  widi  overt  subject  and  object  NPS.^  It  shows  that 
=te occurs  with  the  subject  NP  in  42 of  the  68  AOV  clauses.  The  transitive  or  intransitive 
clauses  section  gives  data  on  clauses  with  one  core  argument  NP.  These  examples  are  either 
intransitive  clauses  or  transitive  clauses  in  which  only  one  core  argument  NP  is  realised. 
Most of  the  data  in  the  sample  is  from  narrative  but  examples  of  in  nonverbal  clauses 
are more  common  in  conversation.  Most  of  the  nonverbal  clauses  in  this  data  occur  in  direct 
speech  or  in  descriptive  texts  about  language  borrowing  and  land  ownership.  The  number 
of clauses  which  have  no  overt  NPs  is  very  high  and  has  not  yet  been  counted.

In descriptions  of  many  of  these  languages  the  terms  'ergative'  and  'nominative'  are  used

languages  such  as  Turkish,  Hindi  and  Spanish,  even  though  accusative  marking  only  occurs 
when  the  object  is  definite  in  Turkish,  or  specific  and  animate  in  Hindi  and  Spanish  (Blake 
1994:120-121).  In  describing  Koromu  the  term  'prominent  subject'  is  used,  instead  of  a 
case  marking  terni.  This  is  because  =te  is  used  extensively  to  indicate  discourse 
prominence  of  subject  NPs  in  transifive,  intransitive  and  nonverbal  clauses,  as  well  as  to 
distinguish  subject  from  object  NPs  in  transitive  clauses.  There  is  a  close  link  logically 
between  the  syntactic  and  discourse  functions  ofsince  in  each  case  a  member  of  a set  is 
highlighted  to  distinguish  it  from  the  remainder  of  the  set  of  potential  referents.  Since  the 
enclitic  commonly  indicates  discourse  prominence  of  intransitive  subjects  where  clearly  it 
cannot  have  the  syntactic  lunction  of  disambiguating  between  subject  and  object,  I  see  no 
need  to  use  a  syntactic  term  for  something  that  has  this  equally  important  discourse 
fiinction. 
The  fianctions  of  =te  'prominent  subject  are  outlined  in  the  following  sections.  In  some 
contexts  the  enclitic  has  more  than  one  of  these  fiinctions. 
13.5.2  Inanimate  referent  NPs  as  effector  subjects 
Inanimate  referent  NPs  commonly  occur  as  object  NPs  with  the  semantic  roles  of  theme  or 
patient.  However,  when  they  are  effector  subject  NPs  with  dynamic  transitive  verbs  they 
can be  followed  by  the  enclitic  =te  'prominent  subject'.  In  the  first  example  below  an 
inanimate  referent  NP  is  the  object  in  an  instmmental  postpositional  phrase  while  in  the 
second  example  the  subject  NP  with  =te  'prominent  subject'  has  an  inanimate  referent. 
The  prominent  subject  is  cross-referenced  by  a  subject  suffix  on  the  verb  and  an  object 
suffix  indicates  an  animate  patient.  There  is  also  implied  discourse  prominence  since  tau 
'axe'  is  one  member  of  a set  of  instruments  which  could  have  caused  the  injury.

Similarly,  Scott  (1996:167)  suggests  that  in  Fore  optional  ergative  mari<ers  "raise  noun  phrases  to  the  top  of

Donohue  and  Donohue  (1997:90)  argue  that  the  Fore  ergative  marker  is  nominative.

13.5.4.2  Disambiguating  inanimate  and  animate  referent  NPs  as  A  and  O 
The  inanimate  referent  noun  hekerii  'fire'  is  like  human  referent  nouns  in  that  it  is

13.5.4.3  Disambiguating  animate  referent  A and  O 
In a transitive  clause  with  two  animate  referent  NPs  the  A  can  be  followed  by  =te  if  there  is 
a need  to  disambiguate  between  A  and  O.  This  is  not  always  necessary  because  A  can  be 
distinguished  fi-om  O  by  object  and  subject  suffixes,  by basic  AOV  word  order  (cf  §  13.3) 
and/or  because  with  some  verbs  the  relative  animacy  of  the  NPs  is  sufficient  to distinguish 
the subject.  So  for  example,  with  te  'get',  in  the  first  clause  below,  the  relative  animacy  of 
the NPs  and  the  AOV  word  order  disambiguate  the  subject  from  the  object.

confii-ms  that  the  object  NP  is  fi-onted  as  a  link  (cf  §  14.4.2).

13.5.5.1  Inanimate  referents  and  prominence 
Inanimate  referent  subject  NPs  which  are  not  effectors  can  occur  with  =te  'prominent 
subject'  when  the  NP  has  discourse  prominence.  In  the  example  below  two  parallel 
statements'^  compare  two  inanimate  members  of  a  set.  The  enclitic  =te  indicates  the 
discourse  prominence  of  the  subject  NP  in  the  first  statement. 
(13.34)  lo  weti  =te  arene  men  -a.  No  weti  werane. 
GEN  Is  house  =PS  big  be  -3s  GEN2s  house  small 
'My  house  is  big  (bigger).  Your  house  is  small.'  (My  house  is  bigger  than  yours.) 
D4.149.1 
In the  following  dialogue  the  predicate  NPs'^  in  both  the  question  and  the  response  have  the 
prominent  subject  enclitic  =te.  The  speakers  are  discussing  small  pieces  of  ash  floating  in 
the  air.  Both  the  interrogative  word  and  the  NP  in  the  response  refer  to one  of  a  set  of 
potential  referents,  things  that  commonly  fall  from  above,  such  as  rain,  leaves  and  ash.''* 
Clearly,  =te  does  not  have  an  instrumental  use  in  these  nonverbal  clauses  as  neither  of  the 
speakers  wanted  to  use  hekeniposoro  'ash  pieces'  to  do  something.  Note  that  the  predicate 
in these  contexts  is  more  directly  referential  and  subject-like  than  the  anaphoric 
demonstrative  which  can  either  occur  in  the  left-most  position  of  the  clause  or  be  omitted. 
Further  discourse  context  is  not  available  for  this  example  but  I  think  it  was  a  response  to  a  question  about 
the comparative  size  of  two  houses,  in  which  case  this  is  an  instance  of  contrastive  topic,  and  in  Dik's  terms 
there  is  parallel  focus  (1989:394-395). 
In Dik's  framework  this  type  of  example  could  perhaps  be  considered  as  having  completive  focus  on 
information  presented  to  fill  an  information  gap  (1989:282,  285).  However,  Dik  states  that  there  is  no 
contrast  involved  with  information  in  completive  focus  and  I  suggest  that  in  Koromu  when  te  occurs  there  is 
an implied  contrast  or  prominence. 
In the  early  to  mid  dry  season  tracts  of  grass  land  are  burnt  off  for  hunting  puiposes  and  to  form  fire  breaks. 
When  this  happens  there  is  usually  a  lot  of  ash  in  the  air.

The  discourse  prominence  of  one  animate  referent  NP  can  be  marked  in  transitive, 
intransitive  or  nonverbal  clauses.  For  example,  in  the  dialogue  below  the  first  speaker  hears 
Mam 'what'  can  refer  to  events  and  entities  so  unlike  me  'who'  it  does  not  have  to  occur  with  te

Chapter  14  Ground  - links  and  tails 
14.1 Introduction 
This  chapter  describes  the  ground  (cf.  § 13.2.2)  and  its  role  in  grammar  and  information 
packaging.  The  ground  can  be  either  a  link  (topic-like  element)  or  a  tail.  The  sections 
below  describe  basic  characteristics  of  the  ground  (§14.2)  links  with  /<o-marking  (§14.3), 
links  without  no-marking  (§14.4)  and  tails  (§14.5). 
14.2 Basic  characteristics  of  the  ground 
The  ground  corresponds  to  the  background  (Chafe  1976),  the  presupposition,  the  topic,  or 
the open-proposition.  In  terms  ofVallduvi's  approach  (1992:46-47)  the  ground  is: 
"..  .a vehicular  frame  for  the  informative  focus,  i.e.  it guarantees  an  appropriate 
entry  of  information  into  the  hearer's  knowledge  store,  indicating  to  the  hearer 
where  and  how  the  information  must  be  entered.  Since  the  focus  is  the  information 
in the  sentence,  it  follows  that  the  ground  does  not  make  any  contribution  to  the 
hearer's  knowledge-store.  The  knowledge  encoded  in  the  ground  portion  of  a 
communicated  proposition  is  knowledge  the  speaker  assumes  that  the  hearer 
already  possesses". 
The  ground  "exists  only  if  necessary  to  guarantee  a  successftjl  retrieval  of  the  information 
encoded  in  the  sentence"  (1992:48).  For  example,  in  "The  boss  CALLED",  "the  boss"  is 

[PDF PAGE 515]
486  Chapter  14 
the ground  (specifically  the  link,  see  below)  and  "CALLED"  is  the  informative  focus 
(1992:50). 
As has  been  noted  in  §13.2.2  the  ground  can  be  sub  divided  into  the  link  and  the  tail 
(Vallduvi  1992:46).  Links  function  as  topic-like  elements  which  refer  to  identifiable 
information  in  the  preceding  discourse  or  the  real  world  context.  Lambrecht  (1994:77-78) 
describes  an  identifiable  referent  as: 
...one  for  which  a  shared  representation  already  exists  in  the  speaker's  and  the 
hearer's  mind  at  the  time  of  the  utterance,  while  an  unidentifiable  referent  is  one  for 
which  a  representation  exists  only  in  the  speaker's  mind 
Links  point  to  (or  link  the  hearer  to)  the  place,  or  address,  where  subsequent  'focus' 
informafion  can  be  entered  into  the  hearer's  knowledge  store.  In  the  example  "The  boss  [F 
visited  a  broccoli  plantation  in  COLUMBIA]"  the  link  (also  the  subject)  is  "the  boss"  and 
the focus  is  the  information  in  brackets  entered  under  the  address  or  link  (Vallduvi 
1992:50).  A  link  can  be  a  preposed  complement  as  in:  "The  bossi  [F  I  wouldn't  BOTHER 
ti]",  and  there  can  be  mukiple  links  as  in:  "Broccolii  the  boss  [F  doesn't  EAT  t|]" 
(1992:50). 
Links  in  Koromu  are  more  common  than  tails.  They  occur  before  other  clause  constituents, 
at the  beginning  of  a  sentence  or  following  a  dependent  verb.  There  are  two  different  types 
of links,  those  with  the  particle  no  'ground'  and  those  without  it. 
The  tail  is  "an  element  that  acts  as  a  signaling  fiag  to  indicate  exactly  how  the  information 
carried  by  the  sentence  must  be  entered  under  a  given  address"..  .it is  "the  nonfocal, 
nonlink  part  of  the  sentence"  (1992:49).  Tails  in  Koromu  are  usually  right  detached  but 
they  can  occur  within  the  clause.  They  occur  with  or  without,  the  particle  uo  'ground'  (see 
§14.5).  The  first  tail  in  the  example  below  refers  back  to  infonnation  in  an  earlier  clause. 

[PDF PAGE 516]
The  Ground  487

14.3 Links  with  uo-marking 
14.3.1  Basic  characteristics  of  links  with  u<7-marking 
Link  constituents  marked  by  uo  'ground'  occur  in  the  left-most  position  of  a  clause.  They 
form  a  distinct  intonation  group  with  falling  intonation,  that  ends  with  the  final  particle  uo 
'ground'  and  is  followed  by  a  pause  before  the  main  body  of  the  clause.  There  is  no 
anaphoric  pronoun  in  the  subsequent  focal  part  of  the  clause,  but  coreferential  subject  and 
object  arguments  can  be  represented  by  verbal  suffixes. 
The  following  constituents  can  occur  as  links  with  uo  'ground':  noun  phrases,  temporals, 
locatives,  postpositional  phrases,  the  linking  adverbial  si  'then,  so  then',  and  clauses  in 
realis  or  iirealis  mode  which  fonn  adverbial  and  conditional  clauses  respectively. 
The  ;/o-marked'  constituents  have  a  number  of  semantic  and  informational  characteristics. 
J7o-marked  noun  phrases^  are  often,  although  not  necessarily,  coreferential  with  the  subject 
' The  fomi  uo  may  derive  from  it  'that',  the  demonstrative  which  is  widely  used  for  anaphoric  reference,  and 
the enclitic  =o  'exclamation'  or  the  postposition  o  'genitive'.  A  number  of  Papuan  languages,  for  example 
Usan  and  Korafe,  also  have  forms  that  combine  a  determiner/deictic  with  a  further  constituent  or  other  forms 
which  function  in  similar  ways  in  "domain-creating  constructions"  (Reesink  1994). 

[PDF PAGE 517]
488 Chapter  14 
and object  arguments  of  the  verb  which  follows.  f7t>-marked  temporals,  locatives, 
postpositional  phrases,  linking  adverbials  and  clauses  refer  to temporal,  spatial,  or  other 
background  information  for  the  clause  and  therefore  compare  with  Chafe's  "topic" 
(1976:50)  which  sets  "a  spatial,  temporal,  or  individual  framework  within  which  the  main 
predication  holds". 
t/o-marked  links  are  common  at  the  beginning  of  a discourse  where  they  refer  to the 
narrator,  other  people/entities  present  in  the  real  world  context,  or  real  world  conditions 
such as  time,  location  or  events.  They  are  also  common  within  a  discourse  when  they  refer 
to a  topic  which  has  been  mentioned  earlier.  With  NP  links,  particularly,  this  occurs  at 
points  where  there  is  a  shift  in topic.  Temporal  or  locative  /(^-marked  links  can  occur  when 
there  is  a shift  in time  or  location. 
Interrogative  words  which  naturally  bear  pragmatic  focus,  and  constituents  which  cannot 
stand  alone,  such  as  postpositions,  particles,  clitics,  conjunctions,  subordinators  and  some 
modifiers,  cannot  occur  as  the  ground  and  therefore  they  cannot  occur  as  links.

background  information  is  retrieved  when  there  is  a switch  in  topic,  fi-om heuahina 'old 
woman'  back  to  ahi-ma  [mother-Pis]  'my  mother'.

14.3.2.1.3  Uo-marked  subject  NP  links  in  contrast  to  subject  NPs  and  suffixes 
The  subject  of  a  clause  can  be  indicated  by  a  subject  NP,  verbal  suffixes  or a subject 
coreferential  NP  link.  The  subject  coreferential  links  exemplified  above  contrast  with 
subject  NPs  which  occur  in  presentational  contexts  when  a  new  or  unpredictable  participant 
is introduced  (cf  §  13.3, as  in  (14.13)).

When  there  is  "topic  continuity"  from  preceding  clauses  this  can  be  indicated  by  dependent 
verbs  marked  for  saine  or  different  subject  following  (see  §9.4).  Subject  NPs  are  often 
omitted  from  the  focus  and  the  ground  following  same-referent  dependency  suffixes  since 
in that  context  topic  continuity  is  maintained  and  there  is  no  need  to  indicate  a  focal 
referent  or  a  link  to  one  in  the  knowledge-store. 
14.3.2.1.4  f/o-marl^ed  subject  NP  links,  identifiable  referents  and  topic  change 
Subject  coreferential  NP  links  indicate  a  referent  which  is  identifiable  at  points  in  a 
discourse  where  there  is  some  discontinuity  in  the  topic.  Thus  they  can  occur  at  the 
beginning  of  a  discourse  when  reference  is  made  to  the  narrator  or  other  real  world 
participants,  who  are  present  at  the  time  or  who  have  been  mentioned  in  earlier  discussion. 
They  can  also  occur  within  a  discourse,  following  final  verbs  or  verbs  with  different 
referent  marking,  if  there  is  a  shift  back  to  a  topic  mentioned  earlier. 
First  person  pronoun  links  can  occur  at  the  beginning  of  personal  histories  and  procedural 
accounts  which  involve  the  speaker  when  the  narrator  and  the  addressee  have  discussed  the 
topic  earlier.  Thus  the  first  person  referents  are  identifiable  from  the  real  world  and  the 
information  about  the  first  person  referent(s)  provides  a  link  for  subsequent  infomiation.

14.3.2.2  Object  coreferential  NP  links  with  uo-marking 
14.3.2.2.1  Introduction 
Object  NP  links  with  ((o-marking  are  described  in  the  following  sections  on  /(o-marked 
object  links  in  contrast  to  object  NPs  and  suffixes  (§14.3.2.2.2)  and  object  links  and 
identifiable  referents  (§  14.3.2.2.3). 
14.3.2.2.2  f/o-marked  object  NP  links  in  contrast  to  object  NPs  and  suffixes 
The  object  of  a clause  can  be  indicated  by  an  object  NP  within  the  clause,  verbal  suffix 
marking  or  an  object  coreferential  link.  Overt  reference  to  the  object  can  be  omitted  when 
it is  clear  there  is  "topic  continuity"  from  a  preceding  clause. 
An object  NP  is  part  of  the  new  focus  information  when  it  occurs  before  the  verb  in  a 
clause  with  AOV  word  order  (14.27). 
(14.27)  ...serie  ya  nn  -pii  -r  -ia. 
2p water  drink  -HAB  -PRES  -Ip 
'...we  drink  the  water.'  T5.20.43 
Object  NP  links  are  fronted  to  initial  position  before  a  subject  NP  but  if  the  subject  NP  is 
marked  by  =te 'prominent  subject'  this  is  sufficient  to indicate  that  the  object  NP  is  a  link 
(see §  14.4.2 below).  However,  the  link  is  f/o-marked  if  there  is  a possibility  that  the  object 
NP might  not  be  recognised  as  link  infonnation  or  if  it is  also  a  general  or  major  topic  in 
the discourse. 
When  a  subject  NP  is  omitted  from  a  clause  (because  oftopic  continuity  of  the  subject 
referent)  it is  not  possible  to  tell  whether  O  is  fronted  as  a  link  unless  it  is  marked  by  no.

14.3.3  Clauses  as  initial  links 
14.3.3.1  Introduction 
Clauses  can  occur  in the  same  environment  as  a noun  (cf.  § 12.4.4 and  §  12.4.5) and be 
followed  by  no 'ground'.  They  function  as links  to subsequent  information  in  the  main 
clause.  Some  of  these  topic-like  elements  in  sentence-initial  position  correspond  with 
Haiman's  findings  (1978)  that  "conditional  clauses  and  topics  are  marked  identically  in  a 
number  of  unrelated  languages"  (1978:564).'^ 
The precise  nature  of  clause  links  varies  depending  on  whether  the  //o-marked  clause  is  in 
realis  or  irrealis  mode,  and  on  the  semantic  nature  of  the main  clause.  The  following 
sections  describe: 
• realis  /<o-marked  clause  links  -  'when/where/given  that  (about)'  subordinate  clauses 
• irrealis  /^o-marked  clause  links  -  hypothetical  and  counterfactual  conditionals'^ 
Similar  constructions  occur  in  otiier  Papuan  languages  such  as  Usan,  Korafe,  Folopa,  Enga  and  Dani 
(Reesink  1994:98).  In  Usan  the  "domain-creating"  e«g-construction  is  used  with  given  noun  phrases,  relative 
clauses,  conditionals,  "when"  clauses,  antitheticals,  "peak"  information  and  independent  sentences. 
" In  Hua  (Haiman  1978:581)  hypothetical  and  "when/given  that"  clauses  have  identical  morphology.  In 
English  hypothetical  and  counterfactual  conditional  clauses  have  similar  morphology  in  "If...(then)..." 
sentences. 

[PDF PAGE 541]

14.3.3.2  Realis  M^>-marked clause  links 
Realis  no-marked  clause  links  form  subordinate  clauses  which  indicate  the  temporal  setting 
(§ 14.3.3.2.1),  the  locative  setting  (§14.3.3.2.2)  or  the  topic  (§14.3.3.2.3)  of  a main  clause. 
As subordinate  clauses  they  lack  modality  marking  but  are  otherwise  like  main  clauses. 
14.3.3.2.1  Temporal  clause  links 
The  realis  i/o-marked  clause  provides  a  link,  in  the  fonn  of  a  subordinate  clause,  which 
expresses  the  temporal  background  of  a  main  clause  when  both  the  link  and  the  main  clause 
are verbal  clauses  in  realis  mode.'''  In  the  majority  of  examples  the  temporal  link  has  a 
final verb.  Temporal  clause  links  indicate  temporal  background  based  on  infonnation 
earlier  in  the  discourse,  in  the  real  world  or  in  the  overall  topic  of  the  discourse.

refers  to shared  knowledge  from  the  real  world  context.

14.3.3.3  Irrealis  wo-marked  clause  links:  conditionals 
Irrealis  z(o-marked  clause  links  express  conditions  for  irrealis  main  clauses.  Following  a 
brief  introduction  (§14.3.3.3.1)  two  types  ofiirealis  //o-marked  conditional  clauses  are 
described:  hypothetical  conditionals  (§14.3.3.3.2)  and  counterfactual  conditionals 
(§14.3.3.3.3). 
14.3.3.3.1  Introduction 
Irrealis  no-marked  clause  links  are  part  of  the  ground  that  acts  as  a  'frame  for  the 
informative  focus'  (Vallduvi  1992:46).  They  can  be  compared  with  conditionals. 
' The  shortened  form  of  the  boundary  marking  enclitic  =mo  is  common  in  rapid  speech. 

[PDF PAGE 544]
The  Ground  515 
.. .conditionals,  like  topics,  are  givens  which  constitute  the  frame  of  reference  with 
respect  to  which  the  main  clause  is  either  true  (if  a proposition)  or  felicitous  (if  not). 
(Haiman  1978:564) 
A conditional  clause  is  (perhaps  only  hypothetically)  a  part  of  the  knowledge  shared 
by the  speaker  and  his  listener.  As  such,  it  constitutes  the  framework  which  has 
been  selected  for  the  following  discourse.  (Haiman  1978:583) 
14.3.3.3.2  Irrealis  uo-marked  clauses:  hypothetical  conditionals 
An irrealis  ;;o-marked  clause  marked  for  future  tense,  imperative  mood  or  desiderative 
mood  provides  a  hypothetical  conditional  link  to  a  subsequent  irrealis  main  clause  in  future 
tense.  Some  of  the  information  in  the  conditional  link  may  be  part  of  the  knowledge  store 
shared  by  the  speaker  and  hearer  (cf  Haiman's  comment  given  above). 
In many  examples  the  irrealis  »o-marked  clause,  or  protasis,  is  in  the  fliture  tense.  The 
main  clause  can  also  be  in  the  future  tense,  as  in  (14.58),  where  the  future  tense  link  refers 
to ya kohomi  'deep  water'  which  has  been  described  in  previous  clauses.

14.3.5  i/o-marked  link  strings 
A sentence  can  have  multiple  links  in  a  link  string.  Each  no-marked  constituent  can  be  a

The  hearers  are  instructed  to  go  to  these  multiple  addresses  to  enter  the  information  given 
(Vallduvi  1992:48).  Alternatively,  a  second  link  provides  further  information  on  an  earlier 
hnk.

discussion  of  what  and  when  the  text  is  to be  about.  The  order  in  which  the  links  occurs 
reflects,  to some  extent,  the  order  in  which  constituents  occur  in  basic  clause  structure  (see 
§3.3.4.3  and  §3.3.4.3.5).  For  example,  the  linking  adverbial  si and  temporals  occur  before 
other  links,  such  as  subject  coreferential  NP  links.  However,  a  loosely  connected  NP  link 
(cf  §14.3.2.3),  can  precede  a  temporal  link.  Clause  links  follow  other  types  of  links.  A 
temporal  link  occurs  before  a  subject  NP  coreferential  link  in  the  following  example.

14.4.3  Clauses  without  wo-marking:  tail-head  linkage 
Clauses  without  i/o-marking  are  the  "head"  in  "tail-head  linkage".  Tail-head  linkage  is  a 
repetitive  device  whereby  some  of  the  information  in  the  final  clause  of  a sentence  is 
repeated  at  the  beginning  of  the  following  sentence.  This  device,  described  as  the  "life 
blood  of  narrative  discourse  in  most  Papua  New  Guinea  languages"  (Johnston  1976:66),  is 
a means  of  maintaining  discourse  cohesion  in  oral  narrative.^'  Koromu  tail-head  linkage 
can  be  expressed  by  lexical  repetition  (§14.4.3.1)  or  pro-verb  substitution  (§14.4.3.2).  The 
repeated  information  is  the  link,  or  background  information,  for  the  new  information  in  the 
subsequent  clause. 
14.4,3.1  Lexical  repetition 
A link  in  tail-head  linkage  by  lexical  repetition  involves  partial  or  fiall repetition  of  the  final 
clause  of  a  sentence  at  the  beginning  of  the  next  sentence.  Partial  repetition  occurs  more 
frequently  than  flill  repetition.  This  strategy  enables  a  speaker  to  end  a  sentence  and  link  it 
to the  following  sentence  by  repeating  the  final  verb  along  with  information  in  inflections 
about  tense  and  subject.  Examples  occur  in  narratives  and  procedural  accounts.^^ 
Johnston  (1976:66)  points  out  that  vernacular  speakers  want  to  cut  this  type  of  Hnk  out  of  written  versions 
of the  same  narratives. 
^^ The  repeated  information  is  highlighted  in  bold  print.
