14.5 Tails 
14.5.1  Introduction 
Tails  are  non-initial  constituents  which  are  part  of  the  ground  (cf.  § 14.2). They  can  occur 
within  a  clause  but  they  are  most  commonly  found  at  the  end.  Vallduvi  argues  that,  like 
links,  they  guarantee  "an  appropriate  entiy  of  information  into  the  hearer's  knowledge 
store"  (1992:46)  and  they  also  perform  "a  more  specific  task  regarding  the  exact  way  in 
which  information  is  retrieved  and  entered  under  a  given  address"  (1992:49).  Thus  tails 
consolidate  or  expand  information  already  given.  There  are  two  different  types  of  tails  in 
Koromu:  those  with  no  'ground'  and  those  without  no  'ground'. 
14.5.2  Tails  with  Mo-marking 
Non-initial  position  ;(o-marked  noun  phrases  and  clauses  are  like  link  expansions  in  link 
strings  in  that  they  provide  a  repetition,  expansion  or  consolidation  of  known  information 
and indicate  that  'I  (or  you)  said  something  about  something  before  and  1  want  to  say 
something  more  about  this'.  In  the  example  below,  the  initial  //o-marked  subject  NP  is  a 
link and  the  final  ((o-marked  NP  is  a  tail  that  provides  more  detail  about  its  antecedent  /(re-
marked  NP. 
(14.90)  Si,  u  tamaite  uo,  upit  mo  men  -a,  Hoiha  uo. 
then  that  man  GRD  now  here  be  -3s  Hoiha  GRD 
'Then,  as  for  that  man,  now  he  is  here,  Hoiha  that  is.'  T1.14.21 
Like  links,  non-initial  »f;-marked  constituents  repeat  known  information  from  the  previous 
discourse  or  the  real  world  context.  In  the  example  below  a  non-initial  no-marked  clause 
reiterates  the  temporal  setting  discussed  before  the  recording  was  made.

14.5.3  Tails  without  H^>-marking 
Tails  without  ;?o-marking  provide  specific  background  information.  They  clarify  details 
which  may  not  have  been  specified  in  the  discourse  but  which  are  closely  connected  to 
information  already  given.  Thus  they  perform  "a  more  specific  task  regarding  the  exact  way 
in which  information  is  retrieved  and  entered"  into  the  knowledge  store  (1992:49). 
In example  (14.99)  the  infomiation  in  the  no-marked  tails  is  recoverable  from  the  preceding 
conversation  and  the  discourse.  The  infonnation  in  the  unmarked  tails  (underlined)  was 
also recoverable  fi-om the  hearer's  knowledge-store.  However,  within  the  discourse  context 
karepate 'with/by  car'  in  Line  5  points  the  hearer  back  to  the  car  mentioned  in  Line  3  and 
Line  8  provides  foil  details  of  the  referents  indicated  on  the  verb  in  Line  7.  For  the  speaker

Appendices 
Appendix  1:  List  of  texts 
The  texts  below  are  the  main  database  used  in  this  study.  The  texts  are  personal  stories  and 
histories,  procedural  accounts,  traditional  stories  or  legends,  exhortations,  descriptions  of 
families  and  land,  stories  passed  down  from  parents,  and  a  small  amount  of  elicited  data. 
The  texts  in  bold  italic  in  the  lists  below  are  transcribed  in  Appendix  2.  The  texts  and  the 
examples  in  the  thesis  are  referred  to  by  the  identifying  number  on  the  cassette  tape  (with  T 
for Tape  file).  The  tape  number,  speaker's  name  and  short  titles  (mostly  in  Koromu)  are 
used to  identify  the  texts  in  the  original  handwritten  files  and  the  shoebox  file.  Texts  with 
the same  title  can  be  distinguished  by  the  other  information.  Many  of  the  2004  recordings 
were  also  recorded  in  audio-visual  format  but  T.K.v.2  is  only  in  audio-visual  format.

We dig  a  hole  and  we  put  compost  down  and,  we  put  yams  above  it  and  we  cover 
them  with  soil  and,  yams  and  mami,  the  two  of  them  lie  there,  we  bury  them.  We 
dig a  hole  and  bury  them.  So  then  some  food  things,  sweet  potato,  cassava,  taro, 
we don't  do  like  that.  We  don't  dig  a  hole  and,  we  don't  bury  them.  No.  We 
plant  them.  That  is  all,  the  talk  about  planting  yam  and  mami.' 
Text  2  Keti 'Following  a  mountain  pig  hunt'  Sarip  Kesapun  (T6.8)^ 
This  story  was  recorded  at  Otopa,  Kesawai  1  in October  2004  with  Sarip  who  was  about  55 
at that  time.  Sarip  grew  up  at  Kesawai  1.  She  married  Yot  and  lived  at  Waimeripa  and 
Autopa  until  they  moved  to  Kesawai  1  when his  health  was  poor.  She  and  her  children 
remained  at  Kesawai  1  after  Yot  died.  Her  story  is  about  a  hunting  expedition. 
Men often  hunt  on  their  own  using  various  techniques  (T1.26)  but  in  the  windy,  dry  months 
of August  and  September  people  of  all ages  enjoy  hunting  together  in  the  wide  open  spaces. 
Large  areas  of  kunai  grassland  are  set  alight,  usually  by  men  and  boys  who  chase  the  wild 
pigs,  bandicoots  and  birds  that  flee  the  flames.  Women  and  children  watch  from  high 
vantage  points  and  if  they  are  not  caring  for  small  children  they  run  to  help  cut  up  the  meat 
and load  it  into  netbags  for  transport.

Text  3  Koromu sakine  kinine  'Roots  of  the  Koromu  language'  -  Menato  Epati  (T2.33) 
This  text  was  recorded  at  Otopa,  Kesawai  1  in August  2000.  At  that  time  Menato  was 
about  60.  He  was  the  eldest  living  member  of  the  patrilineage  which  owns  the  Sotoko  land. 
Before  his  death  in  2006  he  lived  at  a  small  settlement  near  the  Monpea  River  between 
Kesawai  1  and Kesawai  2.  Highly  regarded  for  his  oratory  Menato  captivated  people  with 
his fluency  and  his  humourous  stories  caused  laughter  years  after  they  were  recorded. 
Code-switching  with  Tok  Pisin  may  result  from  the  years  he  spent  on  plantations  as  a 
young  man.  Tok  Pisin  words  and  phrases  from  the  original  are  retained  in  the  transcription, 
but a  Koromu  translation  is  given  in  the  footnotes.  Lines  (45)  and  (46)  are  based  on 
Menato's  account  when  we  did  the  transcription  since  his  speech  was  too  rapid  to  hear.'^

Appendix  3:  Koromu  to  English  wordlist  and  English  to  Koromu  finderlist 
The lists  below  are  based  on  the  wordlists  at  the  back  of  a small  book  called  Yene,  tomto.  mire 
'Birds  wild  animals  and  snakes'  (Tomas,  Mutu,  Priestley.  In  press.).  The  book  is  based  on  scripts 
based  on  pictures  and  translations  written  by  Sairam  and  Winis  some  years  ago.  We  checked  these 
in 2004  and  the  booklet  is  now  being  prepared  for  printing.
